### 3.2 CSI Denoising Preprocessing

As demonstrated in the previous section, the gesture can be portrayed by the change of phase-shift in CSI. Unfortunately, for commodity WiFi devices, as the transmitter and receiver are not synchronized, there exists a time-varying random phase offset e−j​θoffsete^{-j\theta\_{\text{offset}}}:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | H⁡(f,t)=e−j​θoffset​(Hs​(f,t)+Hd​(f,t))=e−j​θoffset​(Hs​(f,t)+A⁡(f,t)​e−j​2​π​d⁡(t)λ),H(f,t)=e^{-j\theta\_{\text{offset}}}(H\_{s}(f,t)+H\_{d}(f,t))=e^{-j\theta\_{\text{offset}}}\left(H\_{s}(f,t)+A(f,t)e^{-j2\pi\frac{d(t)}{\lambda}}\right), |  | (4) |

where A⁡(f,t)A(f,t), e−j​2​π​d⁡(t)λe^{-j2\pi\frac{d(t)}{\lambda}}, and d⁡(t)d(t) denote the complex attenuation, phase-shift, and path length of dynamic components, respectively. This random offset thus prevents us from directly using the CSI phase information.

Therefore, we need to eliminate e−j​θoffsete^{-j\theta\_{\text{offset}}}. Fortunately, for commodity WiFi cards, this random offset remains the same across different antennas on the same WiFi network interface card (NIC) as they share the same RF oscillator. Thus, it can be eliminated by the CSI-ratio model [16, 25]:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Hr​(f,t)=H1​(f,t)H2​(f,t)=e−j​θoffset​(Hs,1+Hd,1)e−j​θoffset​(Hs,2+Hd,2)=A1​e−j​2​π​d1​(t)λ+Hs,1A2​e−j​2​π​d1​(t)+Δ​dλ+Hs,2,H\_{r}(f,t)=\frac{H\_{1}(f,t)}{H\_{2}(f,t)}=\frac{e^{-j\theta\_{\text{offset}}}(H\_{s,1}+H\_{d,1})}{e^{-j\theta\_{\text{offset}}}(H\_{s,2}+H\_{d,2})}=\frac{A\_{1}e^{-j2\pi\frac{d\_{1}(t)}{\lambda}}+H\_{s,1}}{A\_{2}e^{-j2\pi\frac{d\_{1}(t)+\Delta d}{\lambda}}+H\_{s,2}}, |  | (5) |

where H1​(f,t)H\_{1}(f,t) and H2​(f,t)H\_{2}(f,t) are the CSI of two receiving antennas. When two antennas are close to each other, Δ​d\Delta d can be regarded as a constant. According to Mobius transformation  [[39](#bib.bib39)], (5) represents transformations such as scaling and rotation of the phase-shift e−j​2​π​d1​(t)λe^{-j2\pi\frac{d\_{1}(t)}{\lambda}} of antenna 1 in the complex plane, and these transformations will not affect the changing trend of the phase-shift[[40](#bib.bib40), [41](#bib.bib41), [42](#bib.bib42)].

CSI to Phase.
Phase PP extracted from HrH\_{r} can be used to describe gestures:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | P​h​a​s​e=a​n​g​l​e​(Hr),Phase=angle(H\_{r}), |  | (6) |

where a​n​g​l​e​(⋅)angle(\cdot) denotes the phase extraction function. For a complex z=abs​(z)⋅ej​θz=\text{abs}(z)\cdot e^{j\theta}, we can use a​n​g​l​e​(⋅)angle(\cdot) to obtain the phase of zz, θ=a​n​g​l​e​(z)\theta=angle(z).The visualized Phase image is shown in Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Method ‣ Wi-CBR: WiFi-based Cross-domain Behavior Recognition via Multimodal Collaborative Awareness")(a).

CSI to DFS.
The DFS captures frequency changes due to gesture motion, such as hand speed. To extract DFS, the Short-Time Fourier Transform is applied to Hq​(f,t)H\_{q}(f,t):

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Sf​(τ,ω)=∫−∞∞Hq​(f,t)​w​(t−τ)​e−j​ω​t​𝑑t,S\_{f}(\tau,\omega)=\int\_{-\infty}^{\infty}H\_{q}(f,t)w(t-\tau)e^{-j\omega t}dt\ , |  | (7) |

where:
w⁡(t−τ)w(t-\tau): Window function (e.g., Hanning window) to segment the signal.
τ\tau: Time localization.
ω\omega: Frequency in radians, tied to the Doppler shift.
The power spectrogram is then computed:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | DFS=|Sf​(τ,ω)|2=|∫−∞∞Hq​(f,t)​w​(t−τ)​e−j​ω​t​𝑑t|2.\text{DFS}=|S\_{f}(\tau,\omega)|^{2}=\left|\int\_{-\infty}^{\infty}H\_{q}(f,t)w(t-\tau)e^{-j\omega t}dt\right|^{2}\ . |  | (8) |

In this spectrogram:The frequency ω\omega at each time τ\tau corresponds to the Doppler shift fd=ω2​πf\_{d}=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}.fdf\_{d} is proportional to the gesture speed v⁡(t)v(t).Positive frequencies indicate motion toward the receiver, while negative frequencies indicate motion away.This time-frequency representation enables detailed analysis of gesture dynamics.For the Widar3.0 dataset, each DFS file is a 6\*121\*T matrix, where the first dimension represents the 6 receivers, the second dimension represents the 121 frequency segments ranging from [-60, 60] Hz, and the third dimension represents the timestamps with a sampling rate of 1000Hz. ### 3.3 Two-branch Intra-modal Self-attention Learning

Two-Branch Self-attention.
The proposed dual-path spatial attention mechanism processes phase (𝐏x\mathbf{P}\_{x}) and Doppler (𝐃x\mathbf{D}\_{x}) features through independent attention branches. Let fconv(k)f\_{\text{conv}}^{(k)} denote a convolution operation with kernel size k×kk\times k, and BN represent batch normalization. The attention weights are computed as:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | 𝐀p\displaystyle\mathbf{A}\_{p} | =σ⁡(BN​(fconv(7)​(fconv(7)​(𝐏x))));\displaystyle=\sigma\left(\text{BN}\left(f\_{\text{conv}}^{(7)}\left(f\_{\text{conv}}^{(7)}(\mathbf{P}\_{x})\right)\right)\right); | 𝐀d\displaystyle\quad\mathbf{A}\_{d} | =σ⁡(BN​(fconv(7)​(fconv(7)​(𝐃x)))),\displaystyle=\sigma\left(\text{BN}\left(f\_{\text{conv}}^{(7)}\left(f\_{\text{conv}}^{(7)}(\mathbf{D}\_{x})\right)\right)\right), |  | (9) |

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function. The refined features are obtained through:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | 𝐏out\displaystyle\mathbf{P}\_{\text{out}} | =𝐏x⊗𝐀p⊕𝐏x;\displaystyle=\mathbf{P}\_{x}\otimes\mathbf{A}\_{p}\oplus\mathbf{P}\_{x}; | 𝐃out\displaystyle\quad\mathbf{D}\_{\text{out}} | =𝐃x⊗𝐀d⊕𝐃x,\displaystyle=\mathbf{D}\_{x}\otimes\mathbf{A}\_{d}\oplus\mathbf{D}\_{x}, |  | (10) |

where ⊗\otimes is element-wise multiplication, ⊕\oplus is element-wise summation. Each branch maintains independent convolution parameters, with channel dimensions preserved in first convolution (3→33\rightarrow 3) and reduced to single channel (3→13\rightarrow 1) in the second convolution.

Symmetric padding (3 pixels) maintained in all convolutions; No parameter sharing between ϕResNetP\phi\_{\text{ResNet}}^{P} and ϕResNetD\phi\_{\text{ResNet}}^{D}.

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | 𝐗P=ϕResNetP​(𝐏out);𝐗D=ϕResNetD​(𝐃out),\begin{aligned} \mathbf{X}\_{P}&=\phi\_{\text{ResNet}}^{P}(\mathbf{P}\_{\text{out}});&\quad\mathbf{X}\_{D}&=\phi\_{\text{ResNet}}^{D}(\mathbf{D}\_{\text{out}})\end{aligned}, |  | (11) |

where ϕResNetP\phi\_{\text{ResNet}}^{P} and ϕResNetD\phi\_{\text{ResNet}}^{D} denote independent ResNet-18 backbones. The final representation combines features through:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | 𝐗PD=Concat​(𝐗P,𝐗D)∈ℝ1024×7×7.\mathbf{X}\_{\text{PD}}=\text{Concat}(\mathbf{X}\_{P},\mathbf{X}\_{D})\in\mathbb{R}^{1024\times 7\times 7}. |  | (12) |

### 3.4 Cross-modal Synergistic Interaction and Fusion

Cross-modal Interaction. To make the extracted Phase and DFS features interact and merge, we use group normalization to achieve the attention of different channels. The generated attention maps are thresholded to get the strengthened and weakened maps, and then the strengthened and weakened Phase and DFS features are obtained. Based on retaining important features and attenuating minor features  [[43](#bib.bib43)], the feature space redundancy is reduced while utilizing both features.

Separate operation aims to separate those informative feature maps from less informative ones corresponding to the spatial content. We leverage the scaling factors in Group Normalization (GN)  [[44](#bib.bib44)] layers to assess the informative content of different feature maps. To be concrete, given an intermediate feature map XPD∈ℝN×C×H×WX\_{\text{PD}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C\times H\times W}, where NN is the batch axis, CC is the channel axis, HH and WW are the spatial height and width axes. We first standardize the input feature XX by subtracting mean μ\mu and dividing by standard deviation σ\sigma as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Xgn=GN​(𝐗PD)=γ​XPD−μσ2+ϵ+β,X\_{\text{gn}}=\text{GN}(\mathbf{X}\_{\text{PD}})=\gamma\frac{X\_{\text{PD}}-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\epsilon}}+\beta, |  | (13) |

where μ\mu and σ\sigma are the mean and standard deviation of XPDX\_{\text{PD}}, ϵ\epsilon is a small positive constant added for numerical stability, γ\gamma and β\beta are trainable affine transformation parameters.

Noted that we leverage the trainable parameters γ∈ℝC\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{C} in GN layers as a way to measure the variance of spatial pixels for phase and DFS. The richer spatial information reflects more variation in spatial pixels contributing to a larger γ\gamma. The normalized correlation weights Wγ∈ℝCW\_{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} are obtained by equation 14, which indicates the importance of different phase and DFS feature maps.

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Wγ={wi}=γi∑j=1Cγj,i,j=1,2,…,C.W\_{\gamma}=\{w\_{i}\}=\frac{\gamma\_{i}}{\sum\_{j=1}^{C}\gamma\_{j}},\quad i,j=1,2,\dots,C. |  | (14) |

Then the weight values of feature maps reweighted by WγW\_{\gamma} are mapped to the range (0, 1) by the sigmoid function and gated by a threshold. We set those weights above the threshold to 1 to obtain the informative weights W1W\_{1} while setting them to 0 to gain the non-informative weights W2W\_{2} (the threshold is set to 0.5 in the experiments). The whole process of acquiring WW can be expressed as equation ([16](#S3.E16 "In 3.4 Cross-modal Synergistic Interaction and Fusion ‣ 3 Method ‣ Wi-CBR: WiFi-based Cross-domain Behavior Recognition via Multimodal Collaborative Awareness")):

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | W=G​a​t​e​(Sigmoid​(Wγ​(G​N​(XPD)))).W=Gate(\text{Sigmoid}(W\_{\gamma}(GN(X\_{\text{PD}})))). |  | (15) |

We multiply input features XPDX\_{\text{PD}} by W1W\_{1} and W2W\_{2} respectively, yielding two weighted features: the strengthen ones XPDSX\_{\text{PD}}^{S} and less informative ones XPDWX\_{\text{PD}}^{W}.Thus, we completed the interaction between the input phase and DFS features. The attention weights are obtained by learning the variance and bias through group normalization, which is gated to obtain the strengthened and weakened attention maps. Two components obtained are as follows: XPDSX\_{\text{PD}}^{S} has informative and expressive spatial content and is strengthened, while XPDWX\_{\text{PD}}^{W} has little or no information, which is considered redundant and weakened.

Cross-modal Fusion.
We propose a fusion operation to achieve synergistic utilization. An information-rich feature after strengthening is added to a feature with less information after weakening. New features with richer information are generated, i.e., one feature dominates while the other aids. Instead of adding the two components directly, we use a cross-fertilization operation to thoroughly combine the two weighted different information features to enhance the information flow between them. The cross-rendered features Xw1 and Xw2 are then stitched together to obtain a spatially fine feature mapping of Xw.
The whole process of Fusion operation can be expressed as :

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {XPDS=W1⊗XPD,XPDW=W2⊗XPD;YPS\_DW=XPS⊕XDW,YPW\_DS=XPW⊕XDS;Xout=YPS\_DW∪YPW\_DS,\begin{cases}X\_{\text{PD}}^{S}=W\_{1}\otimes X\_{\text{PD}},X\_{\text{PD}}^{W}=W\_{2}\otimes X\_{\text{PD}};\\ Y\_{\text{PS\\_DW}}=X\_{\text{P}}^{S}\oplus X\_{\text{D}}^{W},Y\_{\text{PW\\_DS}}=X\_{\text{P}}^{W}\oplus X\_{\text{D}}^{S};\\ X\_{\text{out}}=Y\_{\text{PS\\_DW}}\cup Y\_{\text{PW\\_DS}},\end{cases} |  | (16) |

where ⊗\otimes is element-wise multiplication, ⊕\oplus is element-wise summation, ∪\cup is concatenation. YPS\_DWY\_{\text{PS\\_DW}} is a phase-dominant DFS-assisted fusion feature, while YPW\_DSY\_{\text{PW\\_DS}} is a phase-assisted DFS-dominant fusion feature. After the Cross-Model Fusion is applied to the intermediate input features XPDX\_{\text{PD}}, not only do we separate the informative features from less informative ones, but also we reconstruct them to enhance the representative features and suppress the redundant features in spatial dimension.

### 3.5 Gestrue Recognition and Contrastive Loss Optimization

Building upon the aforementioned modules, we obtain the Cross-Model Fusion feature representation XoutX\_{\text{out}}.Most existing works directly feed the global representation XoutX\_{\text{out}} into the classifier (i.e., a fully-connected layer with a Softmax) to predict the probability of gestures y^\hat{y}. The model is then trained by minimizing the corresponding loss Lc​eL\_{ce} between the prediction values y^\hat{y} and their ground truths yy.

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | y^=fclassifier​(Xout,Θclassifier),\hat{y}=f\_{\text{classifier}}(X\_{\text{out}};\Theta\_{\text{classifier}}), |  | (17) |

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ℒc​e=ℒc​e​(y,y^)=1M​∑m=1M∑s=1Sym,s​log⁡(y^m,s),\mathcal{L}\_{ce}=\mathcal{L}\_{ce}(y,\hat{y})=\frac{1}{M}\sum\_{m=1}^{M}\sum\_{s=1}^{S}y\_{m,s}\log(\hat{y}\_{m,s}), |  | (18) |

where Θc​l​a​s​s​i​f​i​e​r\Theta\_{classifier} is the learned parameter, Lc​eL\_{ce} is a classification cross-entropy loss, and MM is the number of data samples, SS is the number of gestures.

Contrastive Loss optimizes the objective by learning a distance measure based on multiple positive and negative sample-to-sample pairs. The key idea behind this is to learn an embedding space where similar pairs of samples are close to each other and dissimilar pairs are far apart. Thus, we can obtain an invariant representation across different environments for the same instance, i.e., a domain-independent characterization. We aim to learn generalizable representations by minimizing the following contrast-based objective.For the iith sample extracted feature xix\_{i}:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ℒc​o​n=−1N∑i=1Nloge(xiT​x+)/τe(xiT​x+)/τ+∑e(xiT​x−)/τ,\mathcal{L}\_{con}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum\_{i=1}^{N}\log\frac{e^{(x\_{i}^{T}x\_{+})/\tau}}{e^{(x\_{i}^{T}x\_{+})/\tau}+\sum e^{(x\_{i}^{T}x\_{-})/\tau}}, |  | (19) |

where, the pair (xi,x+)(x\_{i},x\_{+}) represents samples of the same class (positive pair), while (xi,x−)(x\_{i},x\_{-}) denotes samples from different classes (negative pair), with τ\tau serving as the temperature parameter. Several elements can influence the variation patterns of the CSI signal, with varying degrees of effect. For example, a user’s influence on signal patterns is less significant compared to changes in location and orientation. Importantly, positive sample pairs across diverse environments differ, and some may be challenging to match due to substantial data discrepancies. Perfectly aligning all negative samples might limit the model’s ability to generalize. To mitigate this, we utilize class proxies to symbolize each gesture, ideally enhancing resilience across samples from varied settings. Formally, these proxy vectors are defined as the weights of the final fully connected layer in the classifier. To further improve semantic consistency, we implement a proxy-based contrastive loss that utilizes the connections between class proxies and samples to foster robust representations  [[45](#bib.bib45)].
Given the representation xix\_{i} of iith sample , we select its class proxy wcw\_{c} in place of positive samples x+x\_{+} to form proxy-to-sample positive pairs. The contrast loss is incorporated into the overall loss function ℒ\mathcal{L}:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ℒc​o​n=−1N∑i=1Nloge(wcT​x​i)/τe(wcT​xi)/τ+∑k=1,k≠cRe(wkT​xi)/τ;ℒ=ℒc​e+ℒc​o​n,\mathcal{L}\_{con}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum\_{i=1}^{N}\log\frac{e^{(w\_{c}^{T}xi)/\tau}}{e^{(w\_{c}^{T}x\_{i})/\tau}+\sum\_{k=1,k\neq c}^{R}e^{(w\_{k}^{T}x\_{i})/\tau}};\quad\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}\_{ce}+\mathcal{L}\_{con}, |  | (20) |

where wcw\_{c} represents the class proxy of sample ii, RR is the number of classes, and PP is the number of negative pairs. In general, we aim to minimize the following final loss function, where ℒc​e\mathcal{L}\_{ce} is cross-entropy loss, and ℒc​o​n\mathcal{L}\_{con} is the proxy-based contrastive loss. β\beta is trade-off parameter.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Implementation Details

Datasets Setting. To evaluate the effectiveness of our model for cross-domain gesture recognition, we conducted extensive experiments on the Widar 3.0 and XRF55 datasets. For in-domain, cross-location, and orientation evaluations on Widar 3.0, we used 80% of the data for training and 20% for testing with five-fold cross-validation. For cross-location evaluation, one location was used for testing and the remaining four for training. The in-domain and cross-direction evaluations followed a similar approach. For cross-environment evaluation, we used data from three environments, totaling 12,750 samples (17 users × 5 locations × 5 directions × 6 gestures × 5 instances), with training on two environments and testing on the third using triple cross-validation. For XRF55, the cross-environment evaluation involved four scenarios, with quad-fold cross-validation on 6,240 samples.

In our implementation, we used Matlab to preprocess CSI data and generate 224×224 RGB images. After obtaining phase and DFS images, all models were implemented in PyTorch 1.13.1. The network architecture and data dimensions are shown in Fig. [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 CSI Denoising Preprocessing ‣ 3 Method ‣ Wi-CBR: WiFi-based Cross-domain Behavior Recognition via Multimodal Collaborative Awareness"). Wi-CBR employs ResNet-18 [[46](#bib.bib46)] with pre-trained ImageNet weights as the feature extractor, addressing parameter learning challenges due to limited training data [[37](#bib.bib37), [47](#bib.bib47)]. The Cross-Model Interaction module uses 4 groups, with a threshold set at 0.5. The contrast loss weight β\beta and temperature are both set to 0.1. During training, the model is optimized using Adam with a learning rate of 0.001, a batch size of 10, and 30 epochs. We used the same network structure for both the Widar 3.0 and XRF55 datasets, ensuring robustness across datasets. The final fully connected layer is adjusted to 6 or 8 units, corresponding to the number of gestures in each dataset. A random seed of 42 was set for reproducibility.

To analyze recognition accuracy and misclassification rates, we present confusion matrices for test location 1, orientation 1, and environment 3 on Widar 3.0, as shown in Fig. [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Overall Performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Wi-CBR: WiFi-based Cross-domain Behavior Recognition via Multimodal Collaborative Awareness").
In cross-location and cross-orientation tests, “push” and “zigzag” gestures achieve the highest accuracy, while “slide” and “sweep” show the lowest, respectively. In the cross-environment test, “sweep” and “clap” perform best.
Interestingly, “slide” is frequently misclassified as “clap.” This likely stems from similar motion trajectories, as both gestures involve inclined or sliding movements, making them harder to distinguish.

Ablation Study. We evaluate four variants of our model to conduct an ablation study.
Wi-CBR w/o D: Only the CSI ratio phase is used as input data for the model.
Wi-CBR w/o P: Only the DFS image is utilized as input data.
Wi-CBR w/o IF: No interaction, use WiGRUNT  [[37](#bib.bib37)] channel-attention module CRU instead of ours.
Wi-CBR w/o CL: Only use cross-entropy loss.

The results in Tab. [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Overall Performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Wi-CBR: WiFi-based Cross-domain Behavior Recognition via Multimodal Collaborative Awareness") show that input data significantly affects model performance, with phase data and DFS both contributing to recognition accuracy. Phase data provides comprehensive raw information, while DFS has some omissions. Removing our feature interaction and fusion modules consistently reduced model accuracy, highlighting the importance of cross-modal interaction for balancing phase and DFS data. The multimodal fusion module effectively integrates different modal features. Additionally, omitting contrast loss guidance led to a noticeable drop in cross-domain performance, while intra-domain performance remained stable, indicating that contrast loss helps the model focus on gesture-related features rather than environmental noise. Overall, Wi-CBR effectively leverages full CSI raw data and DFS for improved cross-domain performance.

## 5 Conclusion

We propose Wi-CBR, a WiFi-based cross-domain human behavior recognition framework with strong cross-domain performance. It combines model-based and learning-based approaches, leveraging phase data (dynamic path length changes) and DFS data (frequency changes related to gesture speed). By utilizing full data and domain-independent feature guidance, Wi-CBR enhances recognition accuracy. The framework includes a two-branch self-attention module to capture spatio-temporal cues, followed by bi-gating for feature enhancement and suppression. Cross-modal data fusion in both time and frequency domains enables robust behavioral feature extraction, focusing on the behavior itself while minimizing environmental influence.

args.key_excerpts: We propose a multimodal collaborative awareness method for WiFi-based behavior recognition, which exploits two modal cues: phase and DFS. Phase reflects dynamic path length changes, while DFS captures the frequency variations related to gesture movement speed., A two-branch self-attention learning module is developed to capture the spatiotemporal cues within the modality, and a group attention mechanism is designed to mine key group features from the concatenated phase and DFS data., Through a gating mechanism, combined features are divided into PD-strengthen and PD-weaken branches, and collaborative awareness interactions are further performed to improve cross-modal complementarity., Wi-CBR has an average recognition accuracy of 99.54% for in-domain gesture recognition and 98.34%, 96.30%, and 96.57% for cross-location, orientation, and environment, respectively., For the XRF55 dataset, the average recognition accuracy across environments is 66.05%.
args.summary:
This paper presents Wi-CBR, a novel multimodal collaborative awareness method for WiFi-based cross-domain human behavior recognition (HBR). The method combines phase data (reflecting dynamic path length changes) and Doppler Shift (DFS) data (reflecting frequency changes related to gesture movement speed) to improve recognition accuracy across different environments, locations, and orientations.

**Key Technical Components:**
1. A dual-branch self-attention module captures spatial-temporal cues within each modality (phase and DFS)
2. A group attention mechanism applied to concatenated phase and DFS features to mine key group features
3. A gating mechanism divides combined features into PD-strengthen and PD-weaken branches, optimizing information entropy and promoting cross-modal collaborative awareness

**Preprocessing:** Uses CSI-ratio model for denoising (eliminates random phase offsets from commodity WiFi), and STFT for extracting DFS. Phase and DFS matrices are visualized as 224×224 RGB images processed by ResNet-18 backbones.

**Experiments and Results:**
- Tested on two large public datasets: Widar3.0 and XRF55
- Widar3.0 results: 99.54% in-domain, 98.34% cross-location, 96.30% cross-orientation, 96.57% cross-environment (average 97.07%)
- XRF55 results: 66.05% cross-environment
- Outperforms state-of-the-art methods including WiGRUNT (95.28%), Wi-SFDAGR (96.66%), and others
- Ablation studies confirm contributions of both phase and DFS modalities, the interaction fusion module, and contrastive loss

**Loss Function:** Combines cross-entropy loss with proxy-based contrastive loss to learn domain-invariant representations.

**Training:** Adam optimizer, learning rate 0.001, batch size 10, 30 epochs, pre-trained ResNet-18 with ImageNet weights.

# WiFi CSI Human Pose Detection

**See through walls with WiFi.** No cameras. No wearables. Just radio waves.

WiFi DensePose turns commodity WiFi signals into real-time human pose estimation, vital sign monitoring, and presence detection — all without a single pixel of video. By analyzing Channel State Information (CSI) disturbances caused by human movement, the system reconstructs body position, breathing rate, and heartbeat using physics-based signal processing and machine learning.

## 🔬 How It Works

WiFi routers flood every room with radio waves. When a person moves — or even breathes — those waves scatter differently. WiFi DensePose reads that scattering pattern and reconstructs what happened:

```
WiFi Router → radio waves pass through room → hit human body → scatter ↓ ESP32 / WiFi NIC captures 56+ subcarrier amplitudes & phases (CSI) at 20 Hz ↓ Signal Processing cleans noise, removes interference, extracts motion signatures ↓ AI Backbone (RuVector) applies attention, graph algorithms, and compression ↓ Neural Network maps processed signals → 17 body keypoints + vital signs ↓ Output: real-time pose, breathing rate, heart rate, presence, room fingerprint 
```

No training cameras required — the [Self-Learning system (ADR-024)](/euaziel/WiFi-CSI-Human-Pose-Detection/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-024-contrastive-csi-embedding-model.md) bootstraps from raw WiFi data alone. [MERIDIAN (ADR-027)](/euaziel/WiFi-CSI-Human-Pose-Detection/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-027-cross-environment-domain-generalization.md) ensures the model works in any room, not just the one it trained in.

  **🧠 Self-Learning WiFi AI (ADR-024)** — Adaptive recognition, self-optimization, and intelligent anomaly detection

Every WiFi signal that passes through a room creates a unique fingerprint of that space. WiFi-DensePose already reads these fingerprints to track people, but until now it threw away the internal "understanding" after each reading. The Self-Learning WiFi AI captures and preserves that understanding as compact, reusable vectors — and continuously optimizes itself for each new environment.

**What it does in plain terms:**

* Turns any WiFi signal into a 128-number "fingerprint" that uniquely describes what's happening in a room
* Learns entirely on its own from raw WiFi data — no cameras, no labeling, no human supervision needed
* Recognizes rooms, detects intruders, identifies people, and classifies activities using only WiFi
* Runs on an $8 ESP32 chip (the entire model fits in 55 KB of memory)
* Produces both body pose tracking AND environment fingerprints in a single computation

**Key Capabilities**

| What | How it works | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Self-supervised learning** | The model watches WiFi signals and teaches itself what "similar" and "different" look like, without any human-labeled data | Deploy anywhere — just plug in a WiFi sensor and wait 10 minutes |
| **Room identification** | Each room produces a distinct WiFi fingerprint pattern | Know which room someone is in without GPS or beacons |
| **Anomaly detection** | An unexpected person or event creates a fingerprint that doesn't match anything seen before | Automatic intrusion and fall detection as a free byproduct |
| **Person re-identification** | Each person disturbs WiFi in a slightly different way, creating a personal signature | Track individuals across sessions without cameras |
| **Environment adaptation** | MicroLoRA adapters (1,792 parameters per room) fine-tune the model for each new space | Adapts to a new room with minimal data — 93% less than retraining from scratch |
| **Memory preservation** | EWC++ regularization remembers what was learned during pretraining | Switching to a new task doesn't erase prior knowledge |
| **Hard-negative mining** | Training focuses on the most confusing examples to learn faster | Better accuracy with the same amount of training data |

**Architecture**

```
WiFi Signal [56 channels] → Transformer + Graph Neural Network ├→ 128-dim environment fingerprint (for search + identification) └→ 17-joint body pose (for human tracking) 
```

**Quick Start**

```

```

| Mode | What you need | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Self-Supervised | Just raw WiFi data | A model that understands WiFi signal structure |
| Supervised | WiFi data + body pose labels | Full pose tracking + environment fingerprints |
| Cross-Modal | WiFi data + camera footage | Fingerprints aligned with visual understanding |

**Fingerprint Index Types**

| Index | What it stores | Real-world use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `env_fingerprint` | Average room fingerprint | "Is this the kitchen or the bedroom?" |
| `activity_pattern` | Activity boundaries | "Is someone cooking, sleeping, or exercising?" |
| `temporal_baseline` | Normal conditions | "Something unusual just happened in this room" |
| `person_track` | Individual movement signatures | "Person A just entered the living room" |

| --- | --- | --- |

| **Total** | **~55,000** | **55 KB** (of 520 KB available) |

  **🌍 Cross-Environment Generalization (ADR-027 — Project MERIDIAN)** — Train once, deploy in any room without retraining

WiFi pose models trained in one room lose 40-70% accuracy when moved to another — even in the same building. The model memorizes room-specific multipath patterns instead of learning human motion. MERIDIAN forces the network to forget which room it's in while retaining everything about how people move.

**What it does in plain terms:**

* Models trained in Room A work in Room B, C, D — without any retraining or calibration data
* Handles different WiFi hardware (ESP32, Intel 5300, Atheros) with automatic chipset normalization
* Knows where the WiFi transmitters are positioned and compensates for layout differences
* Generates synthetic "virtual rooms" during training so the model sees thousands of environments
* At deployment, adapts to a new room in seconds using a handful of unlabeled WiFi frames

**Key Components**

| What | How it works | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Gradient Reversal Layer** | An adversarial classifier tries to guess which room the signal came from; the main network is trained to fool it | Forces the model to discard room-specific shortcuts |
| **Geometry Encoder (FiLM)** | Transmitter/receiver positions are Fourier-encoded and injected as scale+shift conditioning on every layer | The model knows *where* the hardware is, so it doesn't need to memorize layout |
| **Hardware Normalizer** | Resamples any chipset's CSI to a canonical 56-subcarrier format with standardized amplitude | Intel 5300 and ESP32 data look identical to the model |
| **Virtual Domain Augmentation** | Generates synthetic environments with random room scale, wall reflections, scatterers, and noise profiles | Training sees 1000s of rooms even with data from just 2-3 |
| **Rapid Adaptation (TTT)** | Contrastive test-time training with LoRA weight generation from a few unlabeled frames | Zero-shot deployment — the model self-tunes on arrival |
| **Cross-Domain Evaluator** | Leave-one-out evaluation across all training environments with per-environment PCK/OKS metrics | Proves generalization, not just memorization |

**Architecture**

```
CSI Frame [any chipset] │ ▼ HardwareNormalizer ──→ canonical 56 subcarriers, N(0,1) amplitude │ ▼ CSI Encoder (existing) ──→ latent features │ ├──→ Pose Head ──→ 17-joint pose (environment-invariant) │ ├──→ Gradient Reversal Layer ──→ Domain Classifier (adversarial) │ λ ramps 0→1 via cosine/exponential schedule │ └──→ Geometry Encoder ──→ FiLM conditioning (scale + shift) Fourier positional encoding → DeepSets → per-layer modulation 
```

**Security hardening:**

* Bounded calibration buffer (max 10,000 frames) prevents memory exhaustion
* `adapt()` returns `Result<_, AdaptError>` — no panics on bad input
* Atomic instance counter ensures unique weight initialization across threads
* Division-by-zero guards on all augmentation parameters

See [`docs/adr/ADR-027-cross-environment-domain-generalization.md`](/euaziel/WiFi-CSI-Human-Pose-Detection/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-027-cross-environment-domain-generalization.md) for full architectural details.

## WiFi CSI Human Pose Detection — GitHub Repository Summary

This open-source project (MIT-licensed, by ruvnet/euaziel) enables **human pose estimation, vital sign monitoring, and presence detection through walls using WiFi signals** — without cameras or wearables. It analyzes Channel State Information (CSI) disturbances caused by human movement to reconstruct body position, breathing rate, and heartbeat.

### Key Technical Details

- **Performance**: Rust v2 implementation achieves 810x speedup over Python v1, processing 54,000 frames/sec. Docker image is 132 MB (Rust) or 569 MB (Python). 542+ Rust tests, 1,031 audit tests passed.
- **Capabilities**: Pose estimation (17 keypoints), breathing rate (6-30 BPM), heart rate (40-120 BPM), presence sensing (<1ms latency), through-wall detection up to 5m depth.
- **Hardware**: Requires CSI-capable hardware. Recommended: 3-6x ESP32-S3 nodes (~$54 total) for full functionality. Research NICs (Intel 5300, Atheros) also work. Consumer WiFi only provides RSSI-based presence detection.
- **Signal Processing**: Uses SpotFi phase correction, Hampel outlier rejection, Fresnel zone modeling, FFT peak detection, and 6 SOTA algorithms.
- **AI Architecture**: Transformer + Graph Neural Network processing 56 CSI channels. Self-learning system (ADR-024) uses contrastive learning without labeled data. Cross-environment generalization (ADR-027, Project MERIDIAN) uses adversarial domain adaptation to work in any room without retraining.
- **Model Size**: ~55,000 parameters (55 KB) — runs on ESP32 with 520 KB available memory.
- **Self-Learning (ADR-024)**: Generates 128-dimension environment fingerprints, supports room identification, anomaly detection, person re-identification, and MicroLoRA adaptation (1,792 parameters per room).
- **MERIDIAN (ADR-027)**: Gradient Reversal Layer, Geometry Encoder (FiLM), Hardware Normalizer, Virtual Domain Augmentation, and test-time training for zero-shot deployment across environments.

### Use Cases

WiFi sensing works anywhere WiFi exists. Applications span elderly care (fall detection), healthcare (patient monitoring), retail (occupancy tracking), search & rescue (WiFi-Mat disaster response through rubble), robotics (cobot safety zones), military (through-wall personnel detection), and more.

### Installation

Multiple profiles: `verify` (~5 MB), `python`, `rust`, `browser` (WASM), `iot` (ESP32), `docker`, `field` (disaster response), `full`. One-command Docker setup: `docker pull ruvnet/wifi-densepose:latest`. Rust workspace consists of 15 published crates on crates.io.

### Architecture

The Rust workspace includes 15 crates covering: core types, CSI signal processing, neural inference (ONNX/PyTorch/Candle), vital signs, disaster response, hardware interfaces (ESP32, Intel 5300, Atheros), WiFi scanning, WASM bindings, sensing server, CLI, API, configuration, and database persistence. Integrates with RuVector v2.0.4 for AI signal processing (attention, graph min-cut, sparse solvers, compression).

#### Abstract

The popularity of WiFi devices and the development of WiFi sensing have alerted people to the threat of WiFi sensing-based privacy leakage, especially the privacy of human poses. Existing work on human pose estimation is deployed in indoor scenarios or simple occlusion (e.g., a wooden screen) scenarios, which are less privacy-threatening in attack scenarios. To reveal the risk of leakage of the pose privacy to users from commodity WiFi devices, we propose CSIPose, a privacy-acquisition attack that passively estimates dynamic and static human poses in through-the-wall scenarios. We design a three-branch network based on transfer learning, auto-encoder, and self-attention mechanisms to realize the supervision of video frames over CSI frames to generate human pose skeleton frames. Notably, we design AveCSI, a unified framework for preprocessing and feature extraction of CSI data corresponding to dynamic and static poses. This framework uses the average of CSI measurements to generate CSI frames to mitigate the instability of passively collected CSI data, and utilizes a self-attention mechanism to enhance key features. We evaluate the performance of CSIPose across different room layouts, subjects, devices, subject locations, and device locations. Evaluation results emphasize the generalizability of CSIPose. Finally, we discuss measures to mitigate this attack.

## Abstract

WiFi-based human pose estimation has garnered significant interest in deep learning research. However, due to the varying angles of signal transceivers and the differing sensitivities of signal subcarriers to movement, inaccuracies can arise in WiFi-based human pose estimation. For instance, when a person is within a WiFi field, local changes in one or more channels and directions of structure can be detected. This channel interaction generally involves mutual interference, modifying movement localization, and perception sensitivity. To achieve unambiguous localization and identification, we decompose the properties of the Channel State Information spatial structure and its behavior, demonstrating that dual-view observation—spatial direction and channel sensitivity—is sufficient. Furthermore, we propose a CSI-Channel Spatial Decomposition Strategy (**CSDS**). Specifically, we introduce the Spatial Orientation Attention Module (**SOA**), which employs angle-dependent weighting to mitigate the error induced by signal transceiver pairs with deviated angles relative to the human body. Subsequently, the Spatial Sensitivity Enhancement Module (**SSE**) addresses errors from low-sensitivity signal carriers for motion detection by employing channel decoupling. Applying these two modules enables the model to discern potentially valid human pose information more effectively in WiFi transmission signals. The experimental results on the Wi-Pose public dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of CSDS.

Keywords: 

[human pose estimation](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=human+pose+estimation); [channel state information](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=channel+state+information); [attention mechanism](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=attention+mechanism)

## 1. Introduction

Human pose estimation, which is designed to predict the coordinates of the human skeleton, as depicted in [Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#fig_body_display_electronics-14-00756-f001), is attracting growing attention. With the development of computer vision technology, models like OpenPose [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B1-electronics-14-00756)], AlphaPose [[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B2-electronics-14-00756)], TransPose [[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B3-electronics-14-00756)], VitPose [[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B4-electronics-14-00756)], and Vitaev2 [[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B5-electronics-14-00756)] demonstrate excellent performance and [[6](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B6-electronics-14-00756),[7](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B7-electronics-14-00756),[8](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B8-electronics-14-00756)] are applicable for real-time use. However, due to constraints in image acquisition, these methods exhibit suboptimal performance in special scenarios, such as low-light conditions and occlusion. Additionally, the process of collecting images may raise concerns about privacy violations.

![Image 14: Electronics 14 00756 g001](https://www.mdpi.com/electronics/electronics-14-00756/article_deploy/html/images/electronics-14-00756-g001-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#fig_body_display_electronics-14-00756-f001)

Sensor-based human pose estimation methods [[9](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B9-electronics-14-00756),[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B10-electronics-14-00756),[11](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B11-electronics-14-00756),[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B12-electronics-14-00756),[13](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B13-electronics-14-00756),[14](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B14-electronics-14-00756)] have emerged as viable alternatives. These methods leverage propagated signals between sensors for human pose estimation, thereby circumventing the need for light and addressing privacy concerns without requiring image capture. In particular, WiFi-based methods can be implemented using a standard home router, offering both cost-effectiveness and broad applicability. Models like PerUnet [[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B15-electronics-14-00756)], GoPose [[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B16-electronics-14-00756)], Wi-Mose [[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B17-electronics-14-00756)] and [[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B17-electronics-14-00756),[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B18-electronics-14-00756),[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B19-electronics-14-00756),[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B20-electronics-14-00756),[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B21-electronics-14-00756),[22](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B22-electronics-14-00756)] have verified the feasibility of WiFi-based human pose estimation.

However, WiFi-based methods encounter certain limitations. Specifically, multi-antenna routers are employed for data collection, and the signal transceiver pairs have varying angles relative to the human body. The angular deviations in the signal transceiver pair data can result in prediction inaccuracies. Furthermore, at the subcarrier level of Channel State Information (**CSI**) data [[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B23-electronics-14-00756)], there is the problem of different subcarriers having different sensitivities to human movements. If all subcarriers are processed with the same weight, it will cause a large error in the human pose estimation results.

This article proposes a CSI-Channel Spatial Decomposition Strategy (**CSDS**), designed for WiFi-based 2D single human pose estimation. The model incorporates the Spatial Orientation Attention Module (**SOA**) and the Spatial Sensitivity Enhancement Module (**SSE**), which utilize attentional mechanisms to mitigate the noise inherent in CSI data. Concretely, the SOA employs a spatial self-attention mechanism to prioritize signal transceivers with optimal angles, thereby reducing interference from those exhibiting angular deviations. The SSE targets subcarriers more responsive to movement, employing a channel attention mechanism to lessen the noise contribution from low-sensitive carriers. We strategically position the modules based on their characteristics and parameter counts to optimize the model’s parameter efficiency and performance. Furthermore, the experimental results on the public dataset Wi-Pose demonstrate that the CSDS attains state-of-the-art performance, suggesting its effectiveness in WiFi-based 2D single human pose estimation.

The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

*   We propose a CSI-Channel Spatial Decomposition Strategy (**CSDS**), which incorporates a Spatial Orientation Attention Module (**SOA**) and Spatial Sensitivity Enhancement Module (**SSE**) to address the problem of signal transceiver angle differences and CSI carrier sensitivity to motion in WiFi-based human pose estimation. 
*   Specifically, the Spatial Orientation Attention Module employs a spatial attention mechanism to diminish the influence of signal transceiver pairs that are not spatially aligned with the human body, thereby reducing the associated prediction bias. The Spatial Sensitivity Enhancement Module utilizes a channel attention mechanism to allocate greater weight to carriers within the CSI that exhibit heightened sensitivity to the human body’s movements, mitigating the impact of errors caused by low-sensitive carriers. 
*   The proposed CSDS achieves state-of-the-art results on the public dataset Wi-Pose, suggesting its effectiveness in WiFi-based 2D single human pose estimation. 

## 2. Related Works

### 2.1. Image-Based Human Pose Estimation

The rapid development of computer vision has led to the emergence of many excellent image-based human pose estimation models. OpenPose [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B1-electronics-14-00756)], utilizing Part Affinity Fields (**PAFs**), demonstrates robust tracking of facial expressions, torso, limbs, and fingers. Nakano et al. [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B24-electronics-14-00756)] evaluated OpenPose with multi-camera setups, highlighting its effectiveness in multi-person scenarios. Dabral et al. [[25](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B25-electronics-14-00756)] proposed anatomically inspired loss functions and a temporal network for weakly-supervised 3D human pose estimation from single images, achieving state-of-the-art improvements on Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP while running at 30 FPS. Neff et al. [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B26-electronics-14-00756)] introduced EfficientHRNet, a lightweight multi-person pose estimator designed for real-time performance on resource-constrained devices, which achieves competitive accuracy while significantly reducing model size and computation. Yang et al. proposed TransPose [[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B3-electronics-14-00756)], introducing Transformer for human pose estimation. Xu et al. further proposed VitPose [[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B4-electronics-14-00756)], which incorporates advanced vision transformer (ViT) [[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B27-electronics-14-00756)] into the model and was found to achieve the highest accuracy of 81.1 AP in the MS COCO dataset. Li et al. [[28](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B28-electronics-14-00756)] proposed GaitFormer, combining 2D keypoint estimation, spatio-temporal networks, and self-attention for precise and affordable gait analysis, outperforming traditional multi-camera systems.

Despite the high accuracy of image-based human pose estimation, there are unavoidable drawbacks such that it is difficult to achieve excellent accuracy under the conditions of occlusion and low light. These methods may also face social problems such as privacy concerns. Therefore, it is still necessary to find appropriate methods to solve these problems.

### 2.2. WiFi-Based Human Pose Estimation

Recently, WiFi-based human pose estimation has been developed, which has attracted great interest. Wang et al. proposed a fully convolutional network (**FCN**) [[29](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B29-electronics-14-00756)], termed WiSPPN [[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B17-electronics-14-00756)], which can estimate 2D single human pose based on WiFi signals. Wang et al. [[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B20-electronics-14-00756)] further introduced a U-shaped network which first performs body segmentation and 2D pose estimation taking 1D WiFi signals as input. Ren et al. proposed GoPose [[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B16-electronics-14-00756)], which leverages the 2D AoA spectrum of signals reflected from the human body to predict 3D human pose even in unfamiliar surroundings. Zhou et al. proposed PerUnet [[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B15-electronics-14-00756)], introducing an attention mechanism into 2D WiFi-based human pose estimation, which consists of a U-shaped backbone and Performer. It also proposed the attention-based denoising (**ABD**) method to overcome the traditional filter’s disadvantages and extract pose features from CSI effectively. Chen et al. [[30](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B30-electronics-14-00756)] integrated static spatial and dynamic frequency information from CSI signals and employed an evolving attention module to focus on relevant feature channels. Zhou et al. [[31](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B31-electronics-14-00756)] introduced a WiFi-based IoT-enabled human pose estimation scheme for metaverse avatar simulation, addressing privacy and illumination challenges in smart homes. Zhou et al. [[32](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B32-electronics-14-00756)] proposed MetaFi++ by leveraging a Transformer-based architecture (**WPFormer**) to map WiFi channel state information to human pose landmarks. Furthermore, Zhou et al. [[33](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B33-electronics-14-00756)] proposed AdaPose and Mapping Consistency Loss, which enables reliable application of WiFi-based pose estimation in smart cities. Nguyen et al. [[34](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B34-electronics-14-00756)] proposed a framework combined with a Denoiser based on an autoencoder and an Estimator using SDy-CNN, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on the MM-Fi dataset.

Although WiFi-based pose estimation has good performance, the aforementioned works remain insufficient with respect to network structure and effective denoising methods. Due to this, this paper is based on WiFi CSI characteristics to further improve the performance of WiFi-based 2D single human pose estimation.

## 3. Methods

### 3.1. CSI

Channel State Information (**CSI**) [[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B23-electronics-14-00756)] characterizes how wireless signals propagate from the transmitter to the receiver at certain carrier frequencies, which can be extracted from the signal using a commodity WiFi device that is equipped with a network interface card (**NIC**) [[35](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B35-electronics-14-00756)]. For each subcarrier, the propagation process of the signal can be modeled

$$
y = \mathbf{H} x + \mathbf{n} ,
$$

(1) 

 where y is the received signal, x is the transmitted signal, $\mathbf{n}$ is the noise vector, and $\mathbf{H}$ is the CSI matrix of the subcarrier.

In wireless communication, each entry in the CSI matrix represents the Channel Frequency Response (**CFR**) for a particular subcarrier frequency. CFR is dynamic and is influenced by both the dynamic and static components of the surrounding environment. Consequently, the CSI matrix can be modeled

$$
H \left(\right. f : t \left.\right) = \sum_{i}^{n} a_{i} \left(\right. t \left.\right) e^{- j 2 \pi f \tau_{i} \left(\right. t \left.\right)} ,
$$

(2) 

 Among these, $a_{i} \left(\right. t \left.\right)$, signifying the amplitude attenuation factor, $\tau_{i} \left(\right. t \left.\right)$, representing the propagation delay, and the carrier frequency, f, serve as foundational elements in channel characterization.

### 3.2. Cross-Modal Network

The experiments in this paper employ a supervised learning approach, where the training process relies on CSI data as input and human joint coordinates as labels. However, the direct training prediction of human joint points from raw CSI data proves to be infeasible. Consequently, manual label creation becomes imperative. In this paper, we utilize teacher–student networks [[36](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B36-electronics-14-00756),[37](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B37-electronics-14-00756)] to conduct network training, as illustrated in [Figure 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#fig_body_display_electronics-14-00756-f002).

![Image 15: Electronics 14 00756 g002](https://www.mdpi.com/electronics/electronics-14-00756/article_deploy/html/images/electronics-14-00756-g002-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#fig_body_display_electronics-14-00756-f002)

**Figure 2.** Based on the image part of the Wi-Pose dataset, the teacher network utilizes the AlphaPose tool to extract the human pose information to supervise the student network’s learning process. The student network CSDS takes the CSI segment part of the Wi-Pose dataset as input and outputs the human body’s joint points to match supervision labels provided by the teacher networks. The CSDS keeps learning and optimizing itself until it achieves WiFi-based human pose estimation. 

The teacher network employs the AlphaPose tool, known for its exceptional proficiency in image-based human pose estimation, to extract human body joint coordinates from corresponding image data collected alongside the CSI data. These derived coordinates serve as labels for the model training process. Subsequently, the student network CSDS is trained to learn from the provided input data CSI to extract the human pose information. The CSDS keeps learning and optimizing itself until it achieves CSI-based pose estimation.

### 3.3. CSI-Channel Spatial Decomposition Strategy

#### 3.3.1. Data Preprocessing

The Wi-Pose dataset input data for the CSDS comprises CSI data with a resolution of $150 \times 3 \times 3$, where $3 \times 3$ indicates nine sets of signals from three pairs of signal transceivers and 150 represents the five sets of CSI segments in 30 subcarriers. However, this initial input resolution is inadequate for the multilayered Unet-like architecture. Therefore, we upsample the input resolution to $150 \times 64 \times 64$.

#### 3.3.2. Encoder and Decoder

As depicted in [Figure 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#fig_body_display_electronics-14-00756-f003), we employ a U-shaped architecture [[38](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B38-electronics-14-00756)] as the backbone network in the CSDS. The U-shaped architecture was originally proposed for a semantic segment with a symmetric structure, and excels in feature extraction in the encoder and feature recovery in the decoder, as well as having the ability to combine low-high features in the skip connections. In this paper, we use a multi-layer encoder to extract CSI pose features, a decoder to restore the specific pose information, and skip connections to ensure the perception of details, which efficiently perform the cross-modal task confirmed by the experimental proofs.

![Image 16: Electronics 14 00756 g003](https://www.mdpi.com/electronics/electronics-14-00756/article_deploy/html/images/electronics-14-00756-g003-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#fig_body_display_electronics-14-00756-f003)

**Figure 3.** Overview of the CSDS. The CSDS comprises an encoder-decoder U-shaped backbone and two attention-based modules. The SSE module is introduced to assign weights to channels, drawing inspiration from channel attention ECA. The SOA module not only incorporates the SSE channel attention module but also includes spatial attention similar to ViT. The input of the CSDS is CSI and the output is the pose estimation, which includes the coordinates of 18 skeleton key points. 

The following is specific to the U-shaped backbone implementation in the CSDS. In the encoder, each layer is connected to the next deeper layer using a convolutional layer and downsampling function that doubles the number of channels in the resolution and halves the height and width. In the decoder, the connection between each layer and the shallower layer requires the assistance of the shallower encoder, using a convolutional layer, providing a concatenating and upsampling function, which results in the opposite effect of the encoder. The encoder and decoder processes can be modeled

$$
e n_{i + 1} = D o w n \left(\right. A C \left(\right. B N \left(\right. C o n v \left(\right. e n_{i} \left.\right) \left.\right) \left.\right) \left.\right) ,
$$

(3) 

$$
d e_{i - 1} = A C \left(\right. B N \left(\right. C o n v \left(\right. U P \left(\right. d e_{i} \left.\right) \oplus S k i p \left(\right. e n_{i - 1} \left.\right) \left.\right) \left.\right) \left.\right) ,
$$

(4) 

 where $d e_{i}$ and $e n_{i}$ denote the output of layer i of the decoder and encoder, $C o n v \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denotes a convolutional layer with convolutional kernel $3 \times 3$, step 1, and padding 1, $B N \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denotes the normalization layer, $A C \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denotes the activation layer, $D o w n \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ and $U P \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denote the downsampling and upsampling function, and $S k i p \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denotes the skip connections.

#### 3.3.3. Spatial Sensitivity Enhancement Module

As depicted in [[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B15-electronics-14-00756)], different subcarriers within CSI exhibit varying sensitivities to different actions. Consequently, weighting subcarriers with more sensitivity to actions becomes essential. In the Wi-Pose dataset, the resolution of the original input data of CSI is $150 \times 3 \times 3$, of which the third dimension 150 represents $30 \times 5$, i.e., the number of carriers × the amount of time. In this paper, we introduce the Spatial Sensitivity Enhancement Module (**SSE**) in the third dimension to give more weight to the more sensitive carriers. The SSE is designed for the skip connections of the U-shaped architecture and is based on ECA [[39](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B39-electronics-14-00756)], which offers channel attention that precisely aligns with CSI data in WiFi-based human pose estimation. The application of these channel weights serves to accentuate carriers exhibiting heightened sensitivity to specific actions, thereby effectively suppressing noise. The SSE process can be modeled

$$
Y = S i g \left(\right. C o n v_{1 \times 3} \left(\right. G A P \left(\right. X \left.\right) \left.\right) \left.\right) \bigotimes X ,
$$

(5) 

 where $G A P \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denotes the global average pooling function, which simplifies computation and retains global information, $C o n v_{1 \times 3} \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denotes a convolutional layer with convolutional kernel $1 \times 3$, step 1 and padding $0 \times 1$, $S i g \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denotes the Sigmoid function, and ⊗ denotes the elements multiplication.

The SSE exhibits independence from the input resolution and ensures constancy in both input and output resolutions. Moreover, the SSE operates efficiently with a modest parameter requirement. The advantage of the SSE lies in its alignment with the inherent characteristics of CSI carriers through the application of channel attention. Consequently, the SSE is employed across each skip connection in the U-shaped backbone to augment the model’s responsiveness to diverse actions.

#### 3.3.4. Spatial Orientation Attention Module

As depicted in [Figure 4](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#fig_body_display_electronics-14-00756-f004), each of the transceiver pairs has utility in human pose estimation in the Wi-Pose dataset, which represents a dimension of $150 \times 1 \times 1$ and can theoretically predict human poses. However, in practice, each antenna transceiver pair has a slight difference in angle because of the equipment itself. Therefore, it seems reasonable to assign different weight values to different transceiver signals. In this paper, we introduce the Spatial Orientation Attention Module (**SOA**), based on the spatial attention mechanism applied to the $H \times W$ dimensions. The SOA comprises spatial attention ViT [[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#B19-electronics-14-00756)] and channel attention ECA. This enhancement improves the network’s ability to perceive and process data, contributing to better human pose estimation performance. The SOA process can be modeled

$$
Y = S E E \left(\right. T r a n s \left(\right. P o s \left(\right. P a t c h \left(\right. X \left.\right) \left.\right) \left.\right) \left.\right) ,
$$

(6) 

 where $P a t c h \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denotes the patch embedding layer, $P o s \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denotes the positional embedding layer, $T r a n s \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denotes multiple consecutive Transformer layers, and $S E E \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denotes an SSE module.

![Image 17: Electronics 14 00756 g004](https://www.mdpi.com/electronics/electronics-14-00756/article_deploy/html/images/electronics-14-00756-g004-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/4/756#fig_body_display_electronics-14-00756-f004)

**Figure 4.** (**a**) represents the input data CSI of Wi-Pose. The first and second dimensions of CSI together constitute nine parameters which demonstrates the amplitudes of different transceiver pairs at the same time and carrier. (**b**,**c**) Indicate the similarity of the sensitive parts of (**a**) corresponding CSI segments, which are all effective in the estimation of human pose. 

ViT in the SOA focuses on capturing global information and establishing long-distance connections, while convolutional functions excel at capturing local information. In principle, the SOA may be better suited for deeper skip connections in a U-shaped structure, given that shallow skip connections inherently possess larger feature dimensions. args.key_excerpts: We propose a CSI-Channel Spatial Decomposition Strategy (CSDS), which incorporates a Spatial Orientation Attention Module (SOA) and Spatial Sensitivity Enhancement Module (SSE) to address the problem of signal transceiver angle differences and CSI carrier sensitivity to motion in WiFi-based human pose estimation., The Spatial Orientation Attention Module employs a spatial attention mechanism to diminish the influence of signal transceiver pairs that are not spatially aligned with the human body, thereby reducing the associated prediction bias., The Spatial Sensitivity Enhancement Module utilizes a channel attention mechanism to allocate greater weight to carriers within the CSI that exhibit heightened sensitivity to the human body's movements, mitigating the impact of errors caused by low-sensitive carriers., The proposed CSDS achieves state-of-the-art results on the public dataset Wi-Pose, suggesting its effectiveness in WiFi-based 2D single human pose estimation.
args.summary:
This is a research article published in *Electronics* (2025, Volume 14, Issue 4, Article 756) titled "CSI-Channel Spatial Decomposition for WiFi-Based Human Pose Estimation" by Jie Deng, Kaiqi Chen, Pengsen Jing, Guannan Dong, Min Yang, Aichun Zhu, and Yifeng Li from Nanjing Tech University, China.

The paper addresses inaccuracies in WiFi-based human pose estimation caused by varying angles of signal transceiver pairs and differing sensitivities of signal subcarriers to movement. The authors propose a **CSI-Channel Spatial Decomposition Strategy (CSDS)** that incorporates two attention-based modules:

1. **Spatial Orientation Attention Module (SOA)**: Uses angle-dependent weighting (spatial self-attention) to mitigate errors from signal transceiver pairs with deviated angles relative to the human body.
2. **Spatial Sensitivity Enhancement Module (SSE)**: Uses channel attention (inspired by ECA) to address errors from low-sensitivity signal carriers for motion detection by employing channel decoupling.

The model uses a U-shaped encoder-decoder backbone with cross-modal teacher-student network training (AlphaPose as teacher, CSDS as student). Input is CSI data (150×3×3 resolution, upsampled to 150×64×64), and output is coordinates of 18 skeleton key points for 2D single human pose estimation.

Experiments on the public Wi-Pose dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of CSDS, achieving state-of-the-art results. The method overcomes limitations of image-based approaches (low-light, occlusion, privacy concerns) by using standard WiFi routers, offering cost-effective and privacy-preserving human pose estimation.

FCUP iii 3D Human Pose Estimation using WiFi CSI data Resumo O principal objetivo da Estimativa da Pose Humana em 3D é prever a posição das articu-lações do corpo usando dados de sensores, permitindo que os computadores analisem o movimento humano para uso em casos como cuidados de saúde ou vigilância. Tra-dicionalmente, as câmaras têm sido a escolha preferida para este tipo de tarefa, mas esta abordagem tem os seus próprios problemas, tais como oclusões, má iluminação e questões de privacidade, que dificultam a sua implementação. Com o objetivo de superar esses desafios, abordagens baseadas em Informação do Estado do Canal (IEC), que po-dem detetar as mudanças no sinal WiFi causadas por movimentos humanos, começaram a ganhar força. Devido ao facto de os routers WiFi serem dispositivos comuns, as solu-ções baseadas em IEC tornaram-se mais atraentes, pois podem lidar com as questões mencionadas anteriormente e oferecer uma solução económica. No entanto, ainda não é possível obter uma estimativa tão precisa da pose humana com IEC como com dados de imagem. Uma vez que atividades que envolvem múltiplas pessoas ou objetos, bem como a necessidade de lidar com os efeitos do desvanecimento e interferência multipath, são alguns dos problemas que os métodos baseados em IEC ainda enfrentam.
Portanto, o objetivo desta tese é contribuir para a pesquisa atual neste campo e propor uma nova solução para uma estimativa mais precisa da pose humana 3D usando dados IEC como entrada. Assim, vários estudos de ablação foram realizados com diferentes arquiteturas, técnicas de regularização, como batch normalization e dropout, número de camadas e mecanismos de atenção. A partir desses estudos, foi possível alcançar uma solução melhor combinando uma CNN com uma LSTM, aplicando batch normalization, duas camadas de dropout com uma taxa de 0.2, 6 camadas LSTM e um mecanismo de atenção com 4 cabeças de atenção e uma dimensão de modelo de 64.
Em seguida, foi realizado um estudo comparando diferentes modelos de aprendizagem profunda para reconhecimento de imagens, como InceptionV3, ResNet-18, GoogLeNet, utilizando espectrogramas criados com base nos dados IEC. No entanto, o modelo com melhor desempenho com espectrogramas não foi capaz de superar o modelo com melhor desempenho com dados IEC, apresentando um desempenho 0.212 pior para o limiar mais restrito em comparação com o resultado do CNN+LSTM usando dados IEC.
Assim, a melhor configuração de modelo alcançada foi o modelo CNN+LSTM mencio-nado, utilizando os dados IEC brutos como entrada. A comparação deste modelo com o estado da arte revelou que esta abordagem é melhor para a maioria dos limiares, sendo FCUP iv 3D Human Pose Estimation using WiFi CSI data apenas ligeiramente inferior para o limiar mais restritivo, com uma diferença de 0.047.
Palavras-chave: Estimativa de pose 3D, Informação de Estado do Canal (IEC), Visão Computacional, Aprendizagem de Máquina FCUP v 3D Human Pose Estimation using WiFi CSI data Abstract 3D Human Pose Estimation’s main objective is to predict the position of body joints using data from sensors, allowing computers to analyse human movement for use cases like healthcare or surveillance. Traditionally, cameras have been the primary choice for this kind of task, but this kind of approach has its own problems, such as occlusions, poor light-ing, and privacy concerns, that hinder their implementation. In order to overcome those challenges, approaches based on Channel State Information (CSI), which can detect the changes in the WiFi signal caused by human movements, started gaining traction. Due to WiFi routers being common devices, CSI-based solutions became more appealing as they can handle the previously mentioned issues and offer a cost-effective solution. How-ever, it is not yet possible to obtain as accurate a human pose estimates with CSI as with image data. Since activities involving several people or objects, as well as handling the effects of multi-path fading and interference, are some of the problems that CSI-based methods still face.
Therefore, the objective of this thesis is to contribute to the current research in this field and propose a new solution for a more accurate estimation of the 3D Human pose using CSI data as input. Hence, several ablation studies were performed with different architectures, regularisation techniques such as batch normalisation and dropout, number of layers and attention mechanisms. Out of these studies, it was possible to achieve a greater solution by combining a CNN with a LSTM, employing batch normalisation, two layers of dropout with a rate of 0.2, 6 LSTM layers, and an attention mechanism with 4 attention heads and a model dimension of 64.
Then, a study comparing different image recognition deep learning models, such as In-ceptionV3, ResNet-18, GoogLeNet, was performed using spectrograms created based on the CSI data. However, the best performing model using spectrograms, which was InceptionV3, was not able to overcome the best performing model using CSI data, giv-ing a performance 0.212 worse for the stricter threshold compared to the result of the CNN+LSTM using CSI data.
Thus, the best model configuration achieved was the mentioned CNN+LSTM model using the raw CSI data as input. Comparing this model with the state-of-the-art revealed that this approach is better for most thresholds, being only slightly worse for the most restrictive threshold, with a difference of 0.047.

Introduction This chapter provides the context and explains the motivation that guided this thesis. Fol-lowing that, the research questions are discussed, and the goals are presented. Finally, this chapter concludes with a summary of the thesis’s structure along with a short descrip-tion of each chapter.
1.1.
Context and Motivation Human pose estimation is a computer vision task focused on detecting and estimating the positions of human body parts, such as arms, knees, and shoulders. The output is usually a set of keypoints that are connected to create a skeleton-like representation of a human.
This task is typically handled by camera-based methods. However, these techniques have limitations in certain environmental conditions, such as poor lighting, occlusion, or when privacy is a concern [1, 2].
Researchers have explored multiple solutions, and one of those solutions is using WiFi Channel State Information (CSI). It measures small variations in wireless signals as they propagate between the transmitter and the receiver. When an individual moves through the environment, the WiFi signal is reflected and scattered when in contact with the hu-man body. These variations in the signal carry information about the body position and movement, allowing algorithms to reconstruct the poses without the need for cameras.
Compared to camera-based methods, WiFi CSI offers some benefits. It is not affected by poor lighting and can work through visual obstructions like walls. It also handles privacy concerns, since it does not capture human identifiable information, making it less intrusive in sensitive cases such as healthcare or smart home systems.
1.2.

2.1.1 Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) is a digital modulation technique used in communication systems. It improves data transmission efficiency and robust-ness, specially in environments with multipath propagation and interference.
It splits high-speed data streams into multiple lower-speed sub-streams, which are trans-mitted simultaneously over different frequencies known as subcarriers. Each subcarrier is orthogonal to the others, meaning their cross-correlation is zero, minimizing interference and maximizing spectral efficiency.
Its ability to transmit data easily and reliably over various channels makes it a vital com-ponent in wireless communication technologies [3].
2.1.2 Channel State Information WiFi CSI provides detailed information about the state of a wireless channel. It captures the amplitude and phase of the signal across multiple subcarriers, providing a more de-tailed view of how a signal propagates through a wireless environment.
It’s derived from the OFDM technology used in modern CSI standards such as Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.11n, 802.11ac, and 802.11ax. It addresses problems where the distribution of each layer’s input changes during training, which can slow down learning and require careful parameter initialization. By normalizing layer inputs, batch normalization allows higher learning rates, reduces sensitivity to initialization, and in some cases, can reduce the need for other regularization techniques like dropout.

3.1.
Human Pose Estimation Human pose estimation went through significant changes over the decades. Initial efforts in the field were focused on the development of methods for tracking and analysing simple movements using elementary image processing techniques [9]. These systems often relied on marker-based approaches, where physical markers were fixed onto the subject’s body and subsequently tracked. As technology progressed, more markerless approaches began to emerge, using complex algorithms to identify and contextualize human poses directly from video footage [10, 11].
The integration of depth sensors, like Microsoft Kinect [12], has led to major advances in HPE. These sensors made it feasible to keep track of body movements in real-time without being intrusive, which increased their accessibility and range of use. However, there were still issues to take into account, like occlusion and accuracy [13].
Computer vision algorithms and machine learning approaches started gaining promi-nence, allowing systems to learn and infer human poses from visual data. Systems based on rules are used to provide a way towards more flexible and data-driven approaches, that have increased robustness and accuracy in estimating different poses in a variety of environments [14].
The introduction of WiFi CSI data has given pose estimation a new dimension. Since WiFi CSI data has distinct characteristics, it has some advantages compared to images for pose estimation. While objects can look distorted in images, as cameras rely on what is in their field-of-view as well as on the lighting and backgrounds; WiFi CSI data uses the electromagnetic spectrum to transmit and receive information in the radio frequency range. This makes it less disturbed by obstacles and changes in light. In addition, it has FCUP 12 3D Human Pose Estimation using WiFi CSI data the ability to capture even small changes, such as faint motions, that could be missed in images. Also, it ensures confidentiality because it doesn’t capture visual details [1].

However, they still had some limitations, preprocessing requirements and computational complexity remain notable considerations in implementing CNN-based approaches.
Person-In-Wifi [17] added U-Net to the CNN architecture, to address challenges like capturing long-term dependencies. This approach demonstrated promising results in ex-tracting spatial features across different scales, but may increase computational costs and require large amounts of labelled data for training.
WiLISensing [18] used a CNN along with Transfer Learning to recognize activities in a position without training or with very few training samples. This method made a good trade-off between performance and quantity of training data.

Attention mechanisms transform the processing of CSI data by enabling mod-els to selectively focus on salient spatial and temporal features crucial for understand-ing human movement dynamics [1]. These mechanisms dynamically allocate attention across different regions of the CSI data, allowing models to distinguish subtle nuances in pose variations with unprecedented precision and adaptability.
Each approach presents its own set of challenges and considerations, requiring care-ful optimization and trade-off assessment. This is a Master's thesis by João Pedro Martins Rocha at the University of Porto (2025) on 3D Human Pose Estimation using WiFi CSI (Channel State Information) data. The thesis addresses limitations of traditional camera-based pose estimation methods (occlusions, poor lighting, privacy concerns) by proposing a WiFi CSI-based approach.

**Key Contributions:**
- Extensive ablation studies were performed comparing different architectures, regularization techniques, and attention mechanisms
- The best configuration combined a CNN with LSTM, using batch normalization, two dropout layers (rate 0.2), 6 LSTM layers, and an attention mechanism with 4 heads and model dimension of 64
- Raw CSI data outperformed spectrogram-based approaches (InceptionV3, ResNet-18, GoogLeNet)
- The best model (CNN+LSTM with raw CSI) achieved performance comparable to state-of-the-art, being better for most thresholds and only slightly worse (0.047 difference) for the most restrictive threshold

**Background:** WiFi CSI captures amplitude and phase of signals across multiple subcarriers. When humans move, WiFi signals are reflected/scattered, and these variations carry information about body position. The thesis covers OFDM, machine learning concepts (CNN, LSTM, RNN, batch normalization, dropout, attention mechanisms), and surveys existing approaches like CSI-Former, Wi-Pose, Person-In-WiFi, WiPose, and others.

**Experimental Setup:** Used the Wi-Pose dataset (12 volunteers, 12 actions, ~166,600 data points, 80-20 train-test split). CSI data format: 5×30×3×3. Evaluation metric: Percentage of Correct Keypoints (PCK). Spectrogram-based comparison used image recognition models (InceptionV3, ResNet-18, GoogLeNet) but these underperformed compared to raw CSI input.

**Conclusion:** The CNN+LSTM model using raw CSI data provides a cost-effective, privacy-preserving alternative to camera-based systems for 3D human pose estimation, with results competitive with the state-of-the-art.

### Abstract

Wi-Fi signals, in contrast to cameras, offer privacy protection and occlusion resilience for some practical scenarios such as smart homes, elderly care, and virtual reality. Recent years have seen remarkable progress in the estimation of single-person 2D pose, single-person 3D pose, and multi-person 2D pose. This paper takes a step forward by introducing \system, a pioneering Wi-Fi system that accomplishes multi-person 3D pose estimation. Person-in-WiFi 3D has two main updates. Firstly, it has a greater number of Wi-Fi devices to enhance the capability for capturing spatial reflections from multiple individuals. Secondly, it leverages the Transformer for end-to-end estimation. Compared to its predecessor, Person-in-WiFi 3D is storage-efficient and fast. We deployed a proof-of-concept system in 4mx3.5m areas and collected a dataset of over 97K frames with seven volunteers. Person-in-WiFi 3D attains 3D joint localization errors of 91.7mm (1-person), 108.1mm (2-person), and 125.3mm (3-person), comparable to cameras and millimeter-wave radars.
