### 2.2. TRANS-CNN Model Training

#### 2.2.1. Preprocessing of Training Data

When analyzing the collected point cloud data, it is found that the number of frames in each sample data and the number of target points in each frame are not the same, while the input of the model requires that the data format retains strictly consistent dimensions. The sample point cloud data are normalized in a matrix with 30 frames by 45 target points. Each point cloud datum has 5 features: x, y, range, Doppler, and azimuth. The frame cycle is 100 ms. If the sample data have a smaller matrix, the rest of the data matrix is padded with zeros; otherwise, sub-sampling is performed. Finally, the sample point cloud data represented as a 3D matrix with 30 frames by 45 points by 5 features are obtained.

#### 2.2.2. TRANS-CNN Model

In 2017, the attention mechanism was first noticed and applied in Transformer [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#B26-sensors-24-01800)]. Today, the attention mechanism has been widely used in NLP, CV, and other fields [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#B27-sensors-24-01800)] and has achieved great success. However, for gesture recognition using point cloud data in this paper, the structure of the Transformer model is very complex and slow in computation. In contrast, this paper only employs the attention mechanism, reducing the complexity of the Transformer model by half, from the original O(n × d 2) + O(m × d 2) to O(n × d 2), where n is the length of the input sequence, m is the length of the output sequence, and d is the dimensionality of the heads. Additionally, multi-head self-attention mechanisms are good at time sequential data and the lack of the spatial features in modeling. Adding one-dimensional convolutional networks strengthens the model’s attention with spatial features by using the point cloud data. The network structure of the TRANS-CNN model is shown in [Figure 9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f009). This part reviews the TRANS-CNN model.

*   Attention Module

The structure of the attention module network in this paper is mainly improved based on the Transformer encoder network. It is divided into two pieces: temporal position encoding and the computation of dependencies between sequence targets.

The workflow of the time sequence position coding part is as follows: Firstly, the three-dimensional mixed feature tensor (30 × 45 × 5) is distributed and flattened in the time dimension through the Time Distributed function to ensure that all the data of each time frame participate in the calculation of the attention mechanism. Then, the Positional Encoding function is used to add nonlinear encoding values to the sequence using the standard position encoding method [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#B26-sensors-24-01800)] which is used in our model, so that the model can better learn the relative relationship between different positions. Finally, it is copied and normalized by (7) 

$$
\overset{\sim}{X} = \frac{X_{i} - \bar{X}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{X}^{2} + K}}
$$

 where $\overset{\sim}{X}$ is the data after normalization, $X_{i}$ is the feature of the _i_ th position of each frame, $\bar{X}$ is the mean of $X_{i}$, $\sigma_{X}^{2}$ is the standard deviation of $X_{i}$, and $K$ is a constant.

Utilizing the attention mechanism based on scaled dot-product as shown in [Figure 9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f009)b, continuous learning and computing the interdependence between different positions of target points in the target sequence are carried out. The variable A is duplicated and assigned to the query vector _Q_, the key vector _K_, and the value vector _V_, so as to realize the self-attention mechanism. The distinctiveness between different gestures is adequately extracted by (8) 

$$
h_{i} = soft max \left(\right. \frac{Q \times K^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}} \left.\right) \times V
$$

 where $h_{i}$ is the output of the _i_ th attention header, and $d_{k}$ is the length of _K_.

Single-head attention has some limitations in extracting gesture features, and it is difficult to fully capture the gesture features in the sample data [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#B37-sensors-24-01800)]. In contrast, in the multi-head attention mechanism, the _Q_, _K_, and _V_ of each sub-network of the attention head are independent of each other, and different feature expressions can be learned in different subspaces. Therefore, this paper proposes a multi-head self-attention mechanism to concatenate the results of sub-networks of these single attention heads. Subsequently, a linear layer continuously learns the dependencies between different targets. The learned weight matrix is utilized to map the multi-head self-attention output to the input data’s dimensions. Including the multi-head attention mechanism in the model effectively improves the expressive power of the model. (9) 

$$
M H = M u l t i H e a d \left(\right. Q , K , V \left.\right) = C o n c a t \left(\right. h_{1} , h_{2} , \hdots , h_{i} \left.\right) \times W
$$

 where $W$ is the weight matrix learned by the linear layer, $M H = M u l t i H e a d \left(\right. Q , K , V \left.\right)$ is the output of the attention module, and $C o n c a t \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ is the connection function.

*   Serialization of 1D Convolution Modules

In the process of multi-head self-attention computation, the focus is on the dependencies between targets at different positions within a sequence, but less attention is paid to the dependencies between different sequences. Therefore, after the attention module, this paper introduces a one-dimensional convolutional network and constructs a serial one-dimensional convolutional module, the structure of which is shown in [Figure 9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f009)c. It is used to capture the dependencies between different sequences.

A one-dimensional convolution operation is performed for each frame of data output from the attention module. The process utilizes Equation (14) to extract features between sequences in different time spaces using appropriate step sizes and convolution kernels. Subsequently, the results are input into an activation function for nonlinear transformation, and the extracted features are fed into an average pooling layer for down-sampling. Next, the down-sampled results are inputted into the next one-dimensional convolutional layer to perform the same feature extraction operation. (10) 

$$
x_{i , j}^{n} = f \left(\right. \underset{\begin{matrix}i \in 30 \\ j \in 225\end{matrix}}{\sum} x_{i , j}^{n - 1} \times w_{i , j}^{n} + b_{i , j}^{n} \left.\right) \\ y_{i , j} = D o w n \left(\right. x_{i , j - 1} \left.\right)
$$

 where $f \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ is the activation function (PReLU), $x_{i , j}$ is the input data and the output data, $i , j$ is the position of the target point, $n$ is the first convolutional layer, $w^{n}$ is the weight matrix of the convolutional layer, $b$ is the bias, $D o w n \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ is the average pooling function, and $y_{i , j}$ is the pooled feature.

The output of the sequential one-dimensional convolutional module undergoes normalization through a one-dimensional convolutional layer and a regularization layer. Subsequently, a residual connection is employed to fuse the output with the input of the sequential one-dimensional convolutional module. Finally, the gesture is recognized by the global average pooling and a fully connected layer (Softmax).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769)3. Experimental Result

### 3.1. Radar Configuration

The IWR1642 mmWave radar from TI was used in this experiment, transmitting FMCW through time-division multiplexing mode (TDM-MIMO). The parameter configurations of the radar are detailed in [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-t001). The distance resolution of the target was obtained from the calculations to be 0.039 m, and the radial velocity resolution was obtained to be 0.125 m/s.

The experimental platform also includes a computer with an I9-12900H processor, an RTX3060 (6G) graphics card, and 16GDDR5 RAM. The TRANS-CNN model was built using the TensorFlow-gpu 2.7.0 and Keras 2.7.0 frameworks.

### 3.2. Data Acquisition and Training Data Collection

Before collecting the data, we investigated the gesture habits of 20 students in the lab. We counted the palm shapes they used when performing gestures, the range of motion of the gestures, and the trajectory of each gesture. We found that all 20 students used the two palm shapes as in [Figure 8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f008) to perform gestures, and the range of motion of their gestures were different, and the trajectories of the same gesture were not the precisely the same. Therefore, when we collected data, we stipulated that the radar was placed horizontally, and the gesture movement range was completed within 30~85 cm (±10 cm) in the radar boresight direction and −65~65 cm in the horizontal direction. At the same time, we collected data through different hand shapes with varying trajectories of motion of the same gesture. As an example of the wipe gesture, the gesture trajectory is not strictly in boresight and can be deviated by 5–10° to the left and right when collecting data. An example of the test setup and the palm shapes for gesture is shown in [Figure 10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f010).

To demonstrate the concept of our gesture recognition system, ten typical gesture movements are defined in our tests, including wipe up (up), wipe down (down), wipe to the left (left), wipe to the right (right), rotating clockwise (CW), rotating counterclockwise (CCW), drawing a hook (√), drawing an X, drawing a Z, and drawing an S. Five volunteers (3 men and 2 women) are invited to participate in the data collection. A total of 10,000 sets of sample data are collected for 5 participants, 10 gestures, 2 palm shapes, and 100 groups for each palm shape. Each dataset contains five significant features, resulting in a multi-dimensional point cloud dataset. A specific example of a gesture action and its corresponding multi-frame cumulative point cloud is shown in [Figure 11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f011). The colors from light to dark represent the movement direction of the gesture.

### 3.3. Recognition Results and Evaluation

The input data of the model are uniformly processed as 30 × 45 × 5, and the Epoch is set to 200. The Early Stopping function is used, and the model is developed to stop training and save the best model when the loss value of the model is no longer decreasing within 25 consecutive Epochs on the test set. The loss function uses the categorical cross-entropy function, which is widely used in multi-objective classification applications. The Adam optimizer is selected, and the learning rate was set to be dynamically adjustable. If the loss value is not decreasing within 10 Epochs on the test set, the learning rate is reduced to 20% of the current learning rate. The initial learning rate was set to 0.001. The data-splitting ratio is 70:30, which means 70% of the data is for training and 30% is for testing. All models in the experiment were trained using the above parameter settings.

To investigate the effect of multiple attention heads (Num_heads) on the model performance, 1, 4, 8, 16, and 32 attention heads were selected for the experiment, the default Batch_size was used to train the model, and the model accuracy was obtained to be 85.4%, 91.8%, 92.43%, 97.91%, and 95.83%, respectively, as shown in [Figure 12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f012)a. It can be seen that the model accuracy achieves the maximum when the Num_heads is 16.

After setting Num_heads to 16, the effect of Batch_size on model performance is further explored; in the experiment, 8, 16, 32, and 64 are chosen to train the model, respectively, and the model accuracies are obtained as 97.02%, 98.48%, 98.1%, 97.50%, as shown in [Figure 12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f012)b. Among them, the highest model accuracy is obtained when the Batch_size is 16.

While the Num_heads and Batch_size values are set to 16, the curves of accuracy and loss values are shown in [Figure 13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f013). During training, using the early stopping strategy, the model stops training at 109 Epochs, at which point we consider the model converged. It is clear from the curve that the model’s accuracy converges at about 98.5%. We test multiple n values, and the results show that the model’s accuracy is optimal when n is set to 25 (early stopping strategy: stop training when the loss value of the model on the test set is not decreasing within n consecutive Epochs; at this time, the model is considered to have reached convergence).

To evaluate the performance of the TRANS-CNN model, 1500 samples are collected again—150 samples for each gesture—and the confusion matrix is generated using the validation set simultaneously. The performance of the model is evaluated using precision, F1-score, recall, and the confusion matrix. Precision evaluates the model’s classification accuracy on the overall data, recall is used to assess the model’s ability to recognize positive samples, the F1-score integrates the relationship between precision and recall, and the confusion matrix visualizes the model’s classification effectiveness across different categories. The specific results are shown in [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-t002). The average recognition accuracy of the ten gestures reaches 98.4%. The precision, F1-score, and recall of each gesture are statistically analyzed in [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-t002). Prec (precision), Recall, F1-score (F1), and Acc (accuracy) are calculated as follows: (11) 

$$
P r e c = \frac{T P}{T P + F P}
$$

 (12) 

$$
R e c a l l = \frac{T P}{T P + F N}
$$

 (13) 

$$
F 1 = 2 \cdot \frac{P r e c \cdot R e c a l l}{P r e c + R e c a l l}
$$

 (14) 

$$
A c c = \frac{T P + T N}{T P + T N + F P + F N}
$$

 where _TP_ represents the number of instances where Class A is correctly identified as Class A, _TN_ represents the number of instances where Class B is correctly identified as Class B, _FP_ represents the number of instances where Class B is incorrectly identified as Class A, and _FN_ represents the number of instances where Class A is incorrectly identified as Class B.

#### Validating Models with Public Datasets

The TRANS-CNN model is trained using the point cloud dataset disclosed by Piotr Grobelny and Adam Narbudowicz in IEEE [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#B38-sensors-24-01800)], and the curves on the test set are plotted as shown in [Figure 14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f014). The TRANS-CNN model achieves an accuracy of about 98% in gesture recognition on this dataset, and the experimental results show that the TRANS-CNN model has good generalization ability.

### 3.4. Comparison of Different Gesture Recognition Approaches

#### 3.4.1. TRANS-CNN Compared with Other Models

[Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-t003) compares the TRANS-CNN model proposed in this paper with four models that use micro-Doppler images as input, including the Tesla model, Self-Attention, 2DCNN-Transformer, 8HBi-GRU, Dense-Net-CBAM, and VGG16. Ref. [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#B18-sensors-24-01800)] uses optical flow to track the interest points in gesture videos and stores the tracked gesture motion as images for model input. Although the accuracy reaches 99%, the data processing is complicated, the data volume is large, and it cannot avoid the influence of occlusion and illumination changes. In contrast, this paper collects gesture information using radar, avoiding the impact of occlusion and illumination. Using point clouds as the model input simplifies data processing and reduces data volume. Compared to the Self-Attention model in Ref. [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#B39-sensors-24-01800)], our TRANS-CNN model adds a one-dimensional convolutional network after the attention mechanism, fully considering the correlation and differences between sequences, resulting in a 3.7% increase in accuracy. Compared to Ref. [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#B30-sensors-24-01800)]’s use of a 2D CNN network combined with a Transformer, our TRANS-CNN model reduces the complexity by half by removing the decoder and feedforward network parts of the Transformer and optimizing the 2D-CNN to a 1D-CNN network, while the gesture recognition accuracy increased by 0.5%. Compared to Ref. [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#B40-sensors-24-01800)]’s 8HBi-GRU model, the TRANS-CNN model uses point clouds as input data. When the quality of the gesture trajectory is not as strong as the micro-Doppler image, the gesture recognition accuracy is improved by 0.3%, and gesture recognition can be completed within 1 s. Compared to the DenseNet-CBAM model designed in Ref. [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#B32-sensors-24-01800)], which has an average accuracy of 99.03%, it does not fully utilize attention mechanisms to calculate the internal correlation of the sequence. Compared to the TRANS-CNN model in this paper, the robustness and generalization ability of the DenseNet-CBAM model is weaker, and the use of micro-Doppler images as input data involves more data processing, making it difficult to achieve real-time gesture recognition. Compared to the Tesla model in Ref. [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#B34-sensors-24-01800)], the TRANS-CNN model combines multi-head self-attention mechanisms with one-dimensional convolutional networks to fully extract the global and local information of temporal sequence data and increase the attention between sequences, leading to a 1% increase in gesture recognition accuracy in an office environment.

In contrast, the TRANS-CNN model in this paper uses point cloud data as input. In comparison to micro-Doppler images, even with a lower quality trajectory and less gesture information carried, the recognition accuracy of the gesture can still reach 98.5% when the point cloud is sparse. Gesture recognition using point cloud data can be completed within 1 s, significantly improving the real-time performance of the gesture recognition system. Additionally, including attention mechanisms in the model enhances its robustness and generalization ability.

#### 3.4.2. Evaluation of Recognition on Simple Radar Sensor

Using the mmWave Radar ADT6101-4P with 2Tx2Rx developed in our lab shown in [Figure 15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f015), the data acquisition was carried out for the training and testing of the model. The radar parameter configuration is detailed in [Table 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-t004). The distance resolution of the target is calculated to be 0.1 m, and the radial velocity resolution is 0.28 m/s. In our test, the azimuth effective angle of the radar is about ±50°, and the elevation effective angle of the radar is about ±15° due to the four patches of the radar we developed in our lab. The hand motion range is from 30 to 85 cm (±10 cm) in boresight and from −65 to 65 cm in azimuth.

Due to the frame cycle of 100 ms, a fast hand motion is not allowed in our data capture. This limitation could be improved by increasing the frame cycle to 50 ms, and a real-time application is possible. For research purposes, a moderate hand motion is expected.

In this experiment, two volunteers were invited to perform data acquisition for four gestures, up, down, left, and right, with 120 groups for each gesture, totaling 480 groups of point cloud data. Subsequently, the dataset splitting ratio is 70:30 for TRANS-CNN model training and testing. The model converges quickly, and the specific test results are listed in [Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-t003). Using the ADT6101 radar for gesture recognition, it remains above 97%. The results indicate that the TRANS-CNN model can achieve significant performance on different radar devices.

To more comprehensively evaluate the model’s performance on different devices, the accuracy (Acc) variation curves of the IWR1642 and ADT6101 radar data are compared on the test set (see [Figure 16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f016) for details). The results show that the model exhibits high accuracy on both radars.

The confusion matrix for recognizing four gestures using the ADT6101 radar on the testing set is depicted in [Figure 17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769#sensors-24-01800-f017). The confusion matrix illustrates that the recognition accuracy for both “up” and “down” gestures surpass 97%, while “left” and “right” gestures also approach 97%. Based on the actual gesture recognition performance, the TRANS-CNN model performs the gesture recognition task well in either radar.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10974769)4. Conclusions

In this paper, the TRANS-CNN model constructed by using point clouds as training data is proposed to solve the problems of high redundancy of information in micro-Doppler maps, insufficient feature extraction, and large amounts of data, which significantly improves the speed of gesture recognition and the possibility of model deployment. The gesture features are fully extracted using the multi-head self-attention mechanism and one-dimensional convolutional network to realize ten gestures. The robustness and generalization ability of the model is improved. Regarding to effectiveness, real-time, generalization ability, and gesture recognition accuracy, our proposed TRANS-CNN gesture recognition is better performed than other gesture recognition approaches. In the experiments, the proposed gesture recognition is evaluated on the benchmarking TI radar sensor, and it is also adapted to our lab-designed radar sensor, which is configured with the simple 2Tx2Rx antenna layout. The results show that our approach has potential applications in modern human–computer interaction. In our subsequent research, we consider implementing the TRANS-CNN model proposed in this paper in an embedded system. Another research direction is to reduce the frame cycle so that a faster hand gesture recognition is possible.

args.summary:
This scientific paper from Sensors (Basel), published March 11, 2024, proposes a TRANS-CNN-based gesture recognition system using mmWave radar point cloud data rather than traditional micro-Doppler maps. The key innovation is using point cloud features (reducing data size from 2-3 MB per gesture to under 15 KB) combined with a TRANS-CNN model that integrates multi-head self-attention mechanisms with 1D convolutional networks to extract both global and local features from gesture data.

The system works in two steps: (1) point cloud estimation via 3D-FFT and peak grouping, and (2) TRANS-CNN model training for gesture classification. Ten gestures (up, down, left, right, clockwise, counterclockwise, √, X, Z, S) were tested.

Using the TI IWR1642 radar (76-81 GHz, 2Tx4Rx), the system achieved 98.5% accuracy. With a simpler lab-developed 2Tx2Rx radar sensor (ADT6101-4P), accuracy reached 97.1%. The model was trained on 10,000 samples from 5 volunteers, with 30-frame sequences of 45 target points × 5 features (x, y, range, Doppler, azimuth). Optimal performance was achieved with 16 attention heads and batch size of 16, with convergence at ~109 epochs.

The approach addresses limitations of micro-Doppler map-based methods (high data redundancy, large data volume) and camera-based systems (privacy concerns, light sensitivity, occlusion issues). Gesture recognition is completed within 1 second, enabling real-time performance. Validation on a public dataset confirmed ~98% accuracy, demonstrating good generalization ability.

## Abstract

[Gesture recognition](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/gesture-recognition) has found versatile applications in natural human–computer interaction (HCI). Compared with traditional camera-based or wearable sensors-based solutions, gesture recognition using the [millimeter wave](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/millimeter-wave) (mmWave) radar has attracted growing attention for its characteristics of contact-free, privacy-preserving and less environment-dependence. Recently, most of studies adopted one of the Range Doppler Image (RDI), Range Angle Image (RAI), Doppler Angle Image (DAI) or Micro-Doppler [Spectrogram](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/physics-and-astronomy/spectrogram) extracted from the raw radar signal as the input of a [deep neural network](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/deep-neural-network) to realize gesture recognition. However, the effectiveness of these four inputs in gesture recognition has attracted little attention so far. Moreover, the lack of large amounts of labeled data restricts the performance of traditional supervised learning network. In this paper, we first conducted extensive experiments to compare the effectiveness of these four inputs in the gesture recognition, respectively. Then we proposed a semi-supervised leaning framework by utilizing few labeled data in the source domain and large amounts of [unlabeled data](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/unlabeled-data) in the target domain. Specially, we combine the ∏-model and some specific [data augmentation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/data-augmentation) tricks on the [mmWave](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/millimeter-wave) signal to realize the domain-independent gesture recognition. Extensive experiments on a public mmWave gesture dataset demonstrate the superior effectiveness of the proposed system.

;

## Introduction

Gesture recognition has recently attracted increased attention in the field of human–computer interaction (HCI) from both industrial and research communities with the development of several applications using the Internet of Things (IoT) scenarios (Li et al., 2018, Tan et al., 2020). For instance, the smart home system enables users to automatically play music by snapping their fingers, or drawing their curtains with simple hand gestures (Guo et al., 2019, Lai and Yanushkevich, 2018, Liu et al., 2020).

Traditional methods for gesture recognition usually employ camera-based (Gkioxari et al., 2018, Narayana et al., 2018, Oudah et al., 2020, Wang et al., 2017) or wearable sensor-based (Jung et al., 2015, Wu and Jafari, 2018, Yuan et al., 2020, Zhu and Sheng, 2011) solutions. Although these conventional methods yield good performances by utilizing deep learning networks, some specific conditions limit their real-world applicational potential. For example, in camera-based solutions, the rooms must be equipped with multiple cameras to obtain high-quality videos at different angles, which is usually expressive. Besides, it has strict illumination intensity requirements. Finally, users of this technology expressed concerns about personal privacy. The wearable solutions could also make users uncomfortable when wearing these contact sensors.

Considering the shortcomings and drawbacks of these traditional methods, researchers have proposed using wireless signals for gesture recognition due to their advantageous characteristics, such as contactless operation, privacy protection and less light-dependence. Among them, some researchers generally employed Wi-Fi signals to realize gesture recognitions (Abdelnasser et al., 2018, Abdelnasser et al., 2015, Tan and Yang, 2016, Zhang et al., 2021). However, due to the relatively higher wave lengths and shorter-range resolutions of Wi-Fi signals, it is generally difficult to capture fine-grained gesture information. Furthermore, these signals are affected by the surrounding environments, different users, and room layouts. Compared to Wi-Fi signal-based gesture recognition, the millimeter wave (mmWave)-based solution received more attention for its superior performance with a much higher frequency band. On the one hand, the mmWave radar provides more subtle motion information because of its high range and angle resolution, contributing to recognizing gestures. On the other hand, with the development of advanced manufacturing and fabrication, individuals can buy commercialized, miniaturized, radar-on-chip mmWave radars, such as Google Soli and Texas Instruments' (TI) AWR/IWR sensors, at low cost, which is helpful for academic research and commercial applications. By transforming the raw mmWave signal into Range Doppler Image (RDI), Range Angle Image (RAI), Doppler Angle Image (DAI), Micro-Doppler Spectrogram, for example, and combining these inputs with deep learning network, several researches have achieved significantly high gesture recognition accuracies (Liu et al., 2020, Liu et al., 2021, Palipana et al., 2021, Patra et al., 2018, Wang et al., 2016, Zhang et al., 2018).

Although a lot of progress has been made using the mmWave wave signal for gesture recognition, some essential problems still need to be discussed and solved.
*   1)To solve the challenges associated with mmWave radar-based gesture recognition, the aforementioned radar heatmaps (RDI, RAI, DAI, and Micro-Doppler Spectrogram) are most used for gesture classification. However, different researchers have used different heatmaps for gesture recognition. Nonetheless, critical areas such as the impact of these heatmaps on recognition accuracy, the distinctions and correlations between different heatmaps, and the most effective heatmap for raw mmWave gesture signal processing have not been comprehensively investigated. 
*   2)With the advancement in the computing resources, deep learning models have received widespread adoption for latent feature extraction. However, most researchers still adopt traditional supervised deep learning networks for gesture recognition, largely limited by the amount of labeled data (Caruana and Niculescu-Mizil, 2006, Liu, 2011, Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana, 2005). Nonetheless, in mmWave signal-based gesture recognition studies, it is usually difficult to obtain massively labeled data for practical deployments. Because mmWave signals propagate differently under different scenarios, such as environment setup and relative locations. For instance, different users making the same gestures at different anchor locations in different rooms yield different data domains. While it is easier to obtain a few labeled data from one domain and large amounts of unlabeled data from several other domains, the key challenge lies in utilizing these datasets to realize generalizability in gesture recognition. 

Motivated by the challenges above, 1) we introduce a standard procedure for transforming raw mmWave signals into the RDI, RAI, DAI, and Micro-Doppler Spectrogram and investigate the theoretical differences and correlations between these four types of heatmaps. Next, we run numerous experiments to compare and evaluate the effectiveness of these four heatmaps for gesture recognition. 2) Secondly, we adopt the semi-supervised learning (SSL) framework to design a robust and generalized gesture recognition system by combining a few labeled data in one domain with large amounts of unlabeled data in several other domains (Ouali et al., 2020, Reddy et al., 2018, Van Engelen and Hoos, 2020). Specifically, as shown in Fig. 1, we combined the ∏-model (Laine & Aila, 2016) and some specific data augmentation techniques for the mmWave radar signal. On the one hand, the ∏-model improves the model's regularization consistency by slightly perturbating the input. On the other hand, these specific data augmentation techniques colud simulate labeled data in different domains.

The proposed semi-supervised gesture recognition system has excellent performance under cross-domain conditions with a small number of labeled datasets, as determined by a comprehensive investigation of the four heatmaps' efficiency for gesture recognition under various conditions. Under the cross-user condition, the proposed method achieved an average accuracy of 98.59% when seven out of 25 users were labeled in the gesture samples. Under the cross-location condition, it obtained an average accuracy of 96.72%, which is nearly 10% higher than in the basic deep learning model when only 1/6th of the data is labeled (from only 1 location), and 5/6th is unlabeled (from the other 4 locations). It also obtained an average accuracy of 97.79% under cross-environmental conditions where only data from one environment is labeled, and the data from the other five environments are unlabeled. Particularly for the evaluation in Office Room B, where only 11.6% of the data is labeled, the model achieved an accuracy of 97.39%, a nearly 4% improvement over the basic deep learning model.

The following is a summary of the main contributions of this paper:
*   1)We investigate and assess the theoretical and experimental efficiency of several heatmaps (RAI, RDI, DAI, and Micro-Doppler Spectrogram) for gesture recognition. 
*   2)We develop an end-to-end semi-supervised gesture recognition system by combining the ∏-model with mmWave signal-specific data augmentation techniques. 
*   3)We conduct extensive experiments using a public mmWave gesture dataset. Even when the ratio of labeled to unlabeled data approaches 1:8, our framework achieves impressive performance. 

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, relavant work in mmWave sensing and SSL is discussed. Section 3 describes the FMCW radar signal processing method. Section 4 outlines the approach used in this study. The experimental findings and evaluations of the proposed framework are presented in Section 5. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper.

This hybrid 3D–2D network design effectively extracts features from the 3D TRD representation, thereby avoiding oversized features from full-sized 3D networks and the information loss of 2D networks on 2D representations. Finally, a homogeneous gated fusion network was designed to fuse the three sets of 2D features. The proposed method was evaluated on the UGRS, MIMOGR, and mmWRWD datasets. The experimental results for all datasets demonstrate that the proposed POMEN significantly and consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art models in both 2D and 3D representations.

args.key_excerpts: Gesture recognition has found versatile applications in natural human–computer interaction (HCI)., Compared with traditional camera-based or wearable sensors-based solutions, gesture recognition using the millimeter wave (mmWave) radar has attracted growing attention for its characteristics of contact-free, privacy-preserving and less environment-dependence., Under the cross-user condition, the proposed method achieved an average accuracy of 98.59% when seven out of 25 users were labeled in the gesture samples., Under the cross-location condition, it obtained an average accuracy of 96.72%, which is nearly 10% higher than in the basic deep learning model when only 1/6th of the data is labeled (from only 1 location), and 5/6th is unlabeled (from the other 4 locations).
args.summary:
This is a research article published in Expert Systems with Applications (Volume 213, Part B, March 1, 2023) by Elsevier, authored by Baiju Yan, Peng Wang, Lidong Du, Xianxiang Chen, Zhen Fang, and Yirong Wu. The paper presents "mmGesture," a semi-supervised gesture recognition system using mmWave radar.

**Key Contributions:**
1. The authors systematically compared four types of radar heatmaps (Range Doppler Image - RDI, Range Angle Image - RAI, Doppler Angle Image - DAI, and Micro-Doppler Spectrogram) for gesture recognition effectiveness — a topic that had received little attention.
2. They proposed a semi-supervised learning framework combining the ∏-model with mmWave-specific data augmentation techniques to enable domain-independent gesture recognition using few labeled data and large amounts of unlabeled data.
3. Extensive experiments on a public mmWave gesture dataset (25 volunteers, 6 indoor environments, 5 locations, 6 common gestures) demonstrated superior performance.

**Performance Results:**
- Cross-user condition: 98.59% average accuracy (7 of 25 users labeled)
- Cross-location condition: 96.72% average accuracy (only 1/6 labeled, 5/6 unlabeled) — nearly 10% higher than basic deep learning
- Cross-environmental condition: 97.79% average accuracy (data from one environment labeled, five others unlabeled)
- Office Room B evaluation: 97.39% accuracy with only 11.6% labeled data — nearly 4% improvement over basic model

The paper addresses key limitations of traditional gesture recognition methods (camera-based and wearable sensor-based) by using mmWave radar, which offers contact-free operation, privacy preservation, and less environment-dependence. The proposed system performs well even when the ratio of labeled to unlabeled data approaches 1:8.

## Abstract

A millimeter-wave radar is widely accepted by the public due to its low susceptibility to interference, such as changes in light, and the protection of personal privacy. With the development of the deep learning theory, the deep learning method has been dominant in the millimeter-wave radar field, which usually uses convolutional neural networks for feature extraction. In recent years, transformer networks have also been highly valued by researchers due to their parallel processing capabilities and long-distance dependency modeling capabilities. However, traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers each have their limitations: CNNs usually overlook the global features of images and vision transformers may neglect local image continuity, and both of them may impede gesture recognition performance. In addition, whether CNN or transformer, their implementation is hindered by the scarcity of public radar gesture datasets. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a new recognition method using a local pyramid visual transformer (LPVT) based on millimeter-wave radar. LPVT can capture global and local features in dynamic gesture spectrograms, ultimately improving the recognition ability of gestures. In this paper, we mainly carried out the following two tasks: building the corresponding datasets and executing gesture recognition. First, we constructed a gesture dataset for training. In this stage, we use a 77 GHz radar to collect the echo signals of gestures and preprocess them to build a dataset. Second, we propose the LPVT network specifically designed for gesture recognition tasks. By integrating local sensing into the globally focused transformer, we improve its capacity to capture both global and local features in dynamic gesture spectrograms. The experimental results using the dataset we constructed show that the proposed LPVT network achieved a gesture recognition accuracy of 92.2%, which exceeds the performance of other networks.

## 1. Introduction

With the development of artificial intelligence, gesture recognition technology is used in many fields such as intelligent transportation, healthcare, and entertainment. At present, traditional gesture recognition techniques primarily utilize both contact-based and non-contact devices to recognize gestures. Contact devices are costly and inconvenient to carry, limiting their practical applications [[1](#B1-remotesensing-16-04602),[2](#B2-remotesensing-16-04602)]. In contrast, there are many applications of contactless devices, such as cameras [[3](#B3-remotesensing-16-04602)], Wi-Fi [[4](#B4-remotesensing-16-04602)], radar [[5](#B5-remotesensing-16-04602),[6](#B6-remotesensing-16-04602)], and other devices used for data collection. However, cameras usually have the potential to violate personal privacy. In addition, it is susceptible to adverse environmental influences. Similarly, Wi-Fi also has some limitations, such as signal attenuation and electromagnetic interference, which can reduce its recognition accuracy. Furthermore, if there is a large delay in the network, the recognition efficiency will decrease. Millimeter-wave radar offers several benefits over traditional sensors, including higher distance resolution and higher angle resolution, better resistance to interference, a more compact design, enhanced privacy, and reliable performance in all weather conditions. Especially for small gestures, millimeter-wave radar can provide high-resolution images that can capture the subtle movements and details of gestures. This high resolution enables millimeter-wave radar to have high precision in gesture recognition.

Recently, the rapid advancement of deep learning algorithms has led to them dominating the field of millimeter-wave radar gesture recognition. In particular, a convolutional neural network (CNN) [[7](#B7-remotesensing-16-04602),[8](#B8-remotesensing-16-04602),[9](#B9-remotesensing-16-04602),[10](#B10-remotesensing-16-04602),[11](#B11-remotesensing-16-04602),[12](#B12-remotesensing-16-04602)] acts as the mainstream network for gesture recognition. For instance, Kim et al. [[7](#B7-remotesensing-16-04602)] derived the Doppler spectrum of radar signals and used the Doppler spectrum image as the input data to a CNN for gesture recognition research. Du et al. [[8](#B8-remotesensing-16-04602)] merged the information of micro-Doppler features and instantaneous angles to accomplish millimeter-wave radar gesture recognition using a CNN. However, while a single CNN is effective at extracting features from static data, it encounters challenges such as the inability to obtain global information. To address these limitations, Zhang et al. [[12](#B12-remotesensing-16-04602)] introduced a novel model. This model uses a portion of ResNet18 and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to build a new network for gesture recognition and uses the Soli dataset [[13](#B13-remotesensing-16-04602)] to demonstrate its performance. Zhao et al. [[14](#B14-remotesensing-16-04602)] investigated a gesture separation network to separate double-target gestures into two single-target gestures, applying the CNN and LSTM models for recognition. Zhang et al. [[2](#B2-remotesensing-16-04602)] combined an end-to-end 3D-CNN and LSTM neural network to recognize eight kinds of dynamic gestures. These methods obtain better accuracy compared to a single CNN algorithm. The combination of LSTM and CNN in a hybrid network effectively captures both the static and temporal features of the gesture target, leading to enhanced recognition accuracy.

While the abovementioned deep neural networks have seen some success in millimeter-wave radar gesture recognition, they also have notable shortcomings. For example, CNNs lack a global receptive field, which can lead to unsatisfactory recognition performance. Similarly, LSTM cannot be parallelized and is computationally inefficient. Different from CNN and LSTM, transformer networks [[15](#B15-remotesensing-16-04602),[16](#B16-remotesensing-16-04602),[17](#B17-remotesensing-16-04602),[18](#B18-remotesensing-16-04602),[19](#B19-remotesensing-16-04602),[20](#B20-remotesensing-16-04602),[21](#B21-remotesensing-16-04602),[22](#B22-remotesensing-16-04602)] can obtain a global receptive field during the feature extraction stage and possess parallel computing capabilities, which are suitable for solving the aforementioned problems. For instance, K. Kehelella et al. demonstrated high accuracy in a millimeter-wave radar gesture recognition task by employing a vision transformer (ViT) [[20](#B20-remotesensing-16-04602)]. However, ViT has certain disadvantages. It overlooks the continuity of the image and can only produce a feature map of a single size. In addition, it is computationally intensive. The Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT) [[22](#B22-remotesensing-16-04602),[23](#B23-remotesensing-16-04602)] enhances the ViT architecture by utilizing a pyramid design, which decreases computational demands while simultaneously improving model performance. Additionally, its feature maps can produce different effects at different scales. Feature maps of different scales can also be applied to different tasks simultaneously. Nonetheless, both PVT and ViT did not fully extract local information from the image, neglecting the local continuity present in the image. To help extract local features for the PVT, Li et al. introduced locality into the feedforward network of ViT by studying the mechanism of locality [[24](#B24-remotesensing-16-04602)]; however, it inevitably increased network complexity and slowed down the inference speed of the network. Chen et al. [[25](#B25-remotesensing-16-04602)] proposed a region-to-local method based on a vision transformer, which enhances the network’s attention to the interior of each region. However, it abandons the traditional global self-attention structure and does not have patch embedding structures at each layer, which reduces the efficiency of image processing.

The abovementioned methods conducted a large number of experiments, which promoted the development of gesture recognition in the field of millimeter-wave radar. However, the traditional neural networks used in the aforementioned studies all have certain limitations. CNNs do not consider global characteristics during the training process of data. PVT and ViT usually focus on global features but overlook the importance of local features. In addition, they also have a great demand for data volume. Although the application of millimeter-wave radar is becoming increasingly widespread, the existing publicly available dynamic gesture datasets of millimeter-wave radars are very limited. This poses significant challenges for methods based on transformers.

To tackle the aforementioned challenges, this paper proposes a local pyramid visual transformer (LPVT) network for millimeter-wave radar gesture recognition. Compared to the neural network mentioned above, LPVT not only retains the ability of PVT to process global information, but also improves the feedforward neural network in PVT to have the ability to process local information. Additionally, this paper also proposes a large-sized millimeter-wave radar dataset for gesture recognition, which resolves the problem of lacking training data in the transformer network. During the construction of the dataset, the radar echo signals are collected using a 77 GHz millimeter-wave radar. Following the digital decoding of the raw echo signals, the data undergo radar signal processing to produce micro-Doppler time spectrograms that correspond to the gestures. The gesture dataset collected by the millimeter-wave radar has been created and prepared for the subsequent recognition process. In the next stage, although the PVT model performs well in processing global information, it has shortcomings in locality, which may lead to insufficient information interaction within the image and unclear differentiation in subtle actions. Therefore, in order to improve the network’s ability to extract local information, we have made improvements to the PVT network. Feedforward neural networks are an important part of feature extraction, so we have added a mechanism here that can extract local information. In this way, the LPVT can focus on extracting local information while retaining the original extracted global information. Furthermore, we introduced the DropKey [[26](#B26-remotesensing-16-04602)] algorithm in LPVT to prevent overfitting and other limitations during the training process of the network. This article provides a detailed description of the network based on the paper [[27](#B27-remotesensing-16-04602)], and verifies the accuracy of the proposed module through ablation experiments. Compared with traditional deep networks, the proposed network can extract and recognize dynamic gesture features more efficiently, and thus better recognition results can be achieved.

The main contributions of this article can be reflected in the following points:

(1).
:   We construct a novel millimeter-wave radar gesture recognition (MWRGR) dataset. Due to the limited availability of publicly available datasets, this article uses the data collected by ourselves for training and recognition. In particular, the model of the millimeter-wave radar was AWR1642, and we used DCA1000EVM for data recording. A total of 12 volunteers were collected in this experiment, with each person collecting six identical gestures. The dataset was constructed by preprocessing the radar echo signals.

(2).
:   We propose a hybrid global and local information-aware gesture recognition network. The LPVT network captures both global and local image information, greatly enhancing gesture recognition performance.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: [Section 2](#sec2-remotesensing-16-04602) presents the proposed method for gesture recognition using millimeter-wave radar, which is based on LPVT. [Section 3](#sec3-remotesensing-16-04602) presents and analyzes the experimental results based on the self-built dataset. Finally, [Section 4](#sec4-remotesensing-16-04602) concludes this paper.

### 2.1. Constructing the MWRGR Dataset

The limited availability of public radar gesture recognition datasets hinders the advancement of gesture recognition technologies. Consequently, we constructed the MWRGR dataset support for gesture recognition. The millimeter-wave radar we used is AWR1642, which can support frequencies from 76 to 81 GHz and provide three times more accurate sensing than other radars with minimal usage space. The DCA1000EVM acquisition card is fully compatible with this model of radar for data collection. We meticulously collected six distinct gestures: wave, pinch, click, clap, circle, and swipe; each of them is a common hand movement that can be detected and recognized using a millimeter-wave radar. Here, to ensure the generalization and robustness of our dataset, we carefully selected a diverse group of 12 participants, varying in body types, to participate in the data acquisition process. This approach aimed to capture a wide range of movement patterns and physical characteristics, thereby enhancing the adaptability of our recognition system. Each participant was instructed to repeat each action 30 times, ensuring consistency and reliability in the data. A comprehensive dataset containing 2160 samples was created by multiplying the number of participants, the number of repetitions per gesture, and the total number of gestures. The actual radar gesture echo acquisition scene is displayed in [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-f002). As shown in [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-f002), it can be seen that the setup where participants performed the gestures was under controlled conditions, ensuring accurate and consistent data collection. The millimeter-wave radar and data acquisition card were connected to a portable power bank, which enabled data acquisition in different scenarios. During the data collection process, the distance between the hand and the millimeter-wave radar was controlled between 20 and 30 cm. This meticulous data collection process laid the foundation for the development and training of our LPVT network, facilitating its ability to accurately recognize and distinguish between different gestures.

After collecting the echo data of the gesture, we processed it according to [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-f004). As shown in [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-f004), firstly, AWR1642 uses two transmitting antennas and four receiving antennas. From these receiving antennas, we extracted and analyzed the echoes of each gesture action, obtaining original data. Next, we combined the data from the four channels in a noncoherent manner. This method accumulates the amplitude information of the signal without considering the phase information of the signal. Then, we used a static clutter filtering module to remove static variables during the signal acquisition process while retaining dynamic variables containing gesture action information. Thirdly, a single frame was captured and then analyzed using a range FFT, which involved applying a fast Fourier transform to the column vectors of the collected data. Next, we applied the Doppler FFT to the outcome generated by the range FFT. This can obtain Doppler frequencies at different frames. Finally, we projected each frame onto the velocity dimension to generate the micro-Doppler time spectrogram.

### 2.2. LPVT Network

The proposed LPVT network has the ability to capture local information of images, as well as the ability of PVT to process global information. This greatly improves network performance. The architecture of the suggested LPVT network is illustrated in [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-f006).

![Remotesensing 16 04602 g006](/remotesensing/remotesensing-16-04602/article_deploy/html/images/remotesensing-16-04602-g006-550.jpg)

**Figure 6.**
LPVT network structural diagram.

As shown in [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-f006), the network architecture proposed in this paper adopts a pyramid structure, which is strategically designed to efficiently reduce computational complexity and maintain high performance. This pyramid structure primarily comprises four distinct stages, each contributing to the hierarchical processing of the input data. Within each stage, a key component is the overlapping patch embedding module. This module innovatively combines the information of each individual patch with its immediate upper, lower, left, and right adjacent patches. This integration step is crucial as it allows the network to initially capture and represent the local information of the image, enhancing its ability to understand the spatial relationships within the data. Then, in the patch embedding process, a position-encoding module is introduced. Given the inherent parallelization of the transformer operations, it becomes imperative to encode the positional information of the patches. This positional encoding is essential to ensure that the network can differentiate between patches located at different spatial positions, thereby preserving the structural integrity of the image and facilitating accurate recognition and classification.

[Figure 7](#fig_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-f007) shows the structure diagram of the LPVT encoder. As shown in [Figure 7](#fig_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-f007), the transformer encoder primarily comprises a spatial reduction attention (SRA) layer and a local feedforward network [[28](#B28-remotesensing-16-04602)]. The SRA layer enables the network to concurrently focus on information from various representational subspaces, enhancing its ability to capture more comprehensive details. In addition, the SRA layer reduces the number of key and value pairs in the attention layer compared to the multi-head attention layer of ViT, which greatly reduces the amount of computation. The output through SRA goes through a normalization layer before entering the local feedforward layer. The local feedforward network integrates locality into the system, enhancing the capture of detailed and continuous features within the feature map.

![Remotesensing 16 04602 g007](/remotesensing/remotesensing-16-04602/article_deploy/html/images/remotesensing-16-04602-g007-550.jpg)

**Figure 7.**

[Figure 8](#fig_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-f008)a,b, respectively, show the local receptive field in CNN and the global receptive field in a transformer. As shown in [Figure 8](#fig_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-f008), the CNN convolution operation only aggregates local domain information, while the global self-attention mechanism carried by the transformer fuses the global information of the image. To ensure that the network emphasizes local continuity within the image while maintaining a broad global receptive field, we strategically integrated local features into the feedforward network of the transformer encoder, as shown in [Figure 9](#fig_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-f009). It allowed for a balanced focus on both local and global information.

At the end of each neural network, there is usually a mechanism to prevent overfitting. Dropout, a technique widely employed in neural network training, serves as a potent method for bolstering the generalization capabilities of these models. By randomly deactivating (dropping out) a subset of neurons during the training phase, dropout effectively mitigates the limitation of coadaptation among neurons, where neurons become overly reliant on specific patterns in the training data. This reduction in coadaptation helps guard against overfitting, thereby enhancing the model’s robustness and ability to generalize to unseen data. However, when applied to vision transformers (ViTs), dropout encounters several challenges. One significant limitation is the potential loss of critical information during the prediction phase. During training, the random dropout of neurons introduces variability, but during inference, the model utilizes all neurons, leading to potential discrepancies and slight instability in the output results. Furthermore, dropout does not adequately account for the inherent structured nature of the input patch grid in ViT. This structured information is crucial for capturing spatial relationships and contextual cues within the image, and its neglect can undermine performance and limit the generalization capabilities of ViTs.

To address the limitations with dropout, we replaced the dropout algorithm with the DropKey algorithm, which produces a more seamless attention weight matrix that promotes the focus of the model on global features while also mitigating the overfitting limitation commonly encountered in ViT.

The traditional PVTv2 network stacks multiple attention layers to gradually learn high-dimensional features. Usually, shallow layers extract low-dimensional visual features, while deep layers aim to extract rough but complex information in the modeling space. Therefore, DropKey sets a lower drop probability for deep layers to avoid losing important information about the target object. Specifically, DropKey does not perform random drops with a fixed probability at each layer, but gradually reduces the probability of drops as the number of layers increases.

## 3. Experimental Results

### 3.1. Experimental Configuration

At present, there is a limited number of publicly available datasets for millimeter-wave radar-based dynamic gesture recognition, which poses a challenge for developing millimeter-wave radar gesture recognition systems. Hence, we built the MWRGR dataset for millimeter-wave radar dynamic gesture recognitions. This dataset was participated in by 12 volunteers, with each volunteer performing six sets of actions. These actions include circling, clicking, waving, swiping, clapping, and pinching. For data consistency, each action was repeated 30 times. Finally, a gesture micro-Doppler spectrogram dataset containing 2160 was constructed. The data of 10 volunteers was used for network training, while the data of the remaining two volunteers was used for testing the proposed method.

All the experiments were conducted with the same configuration during the training stage and transfer learning was not introduced in this paper. The specific configuration was as follows: the number of epochs was 100, the optimizer was Adam, and the initial learning rate was 1 × 10−5. Due to its fast convergence and easy parameter tuning ability, we chose to use Adam [[29](#B29-remotesensing-16-04602),[30](#B30-remotesensing-16-04602),[31](#B31-remotesensing-16-04602)] for the optimizer. During the experiment, we could see that the experimental results tended to stabilize when the number of epochs exceeded 100. Therefore, we set the epoch count to 100 to avoid unexpected situations. We used the Adam optimizer to update the gradient. The Adam optimizer could achieve fast convergence of the model, with low computational cost and fewer hyperparameters. In addition, we compared the learning rates of various sizes and found that when the learning rate was too low, it resulted in slow convergence or even vanishing gradients [[32](#B32-remotesensing-16-04602)]. When the learning rate was too high, it could easily lead to unstable model training or exploding gradients [[33](#B33-remotesensing-16-04602)]. Based on the above reasons, we have included the final test accuracy and loss at different learning rates, as shown in [Table 2](#table_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-t002). From [Table 2](#table_body_display_remotesensing-16-04602-t002), we can conclude that the learning rate of 1 × 10−5 can both minimize the loss and achieve the highest accuracy. The experimental platform was a personal computer with NVIDIA RTX 2080Ti GPU and Inter (R) Xeon (R) Silver 4210 CPU on the Ubuntu 18.04 Linux system. The deep learning framework was Pytorch 1. 2.

## 4. Discussion

From the experiments in [Section 3](#sec3-remotesensing-16-04602), it is obvious that the proposed LPVT is superior to the state-of-the-art methods. This is mainly based on the following reasons: Firstly, compared to typical convolutional networks, this method effectively utilizes both global and local information. Secondly, the pyramid structure of the feature extraction module effectively improves the performance of the model by integrating multi-scale information. Therefore, due to the lack of sufficient data in gesture recognition tasks, the proposed method may be more suitable for millimeter-wave radar gesture recognition tasks. The experimental results on our dataset further demonstrate the excellent performance of the proposed LPVT network.

Based on the above advantages, the method proposed in this paper can be applied to various gesture recognition scenarios. By integrating millimeter-wave radar and the proposed network into one system, safe interaction between drivers and cars in intelligent driving can be achieved. In the field of smart homes, the proposed technology can be used for smart lighting, smart home appliance control, and so on. Users can control the on/off of lights, adjust brightness, or operate household appliances such as televisions and air conditioners through simple gestures, achieving a more intelligent and convenient home life. This technology not only improves the convenience of home life, but also enhances user experience and interactivity. Moreover, in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) applications, the proposed method can be applied to control game characters, browse virtual scenes, etc. through gestures, improving immersion and interactivity.

Although the proposed method has obtained some good performance in the millimeter-wave radar gesture recognition tasks, it also has some limitations.

(1)
:   The proposed method is only applicable to the Doppler image of millimeter-wave radar. The proposed method includes the preprocessing of millimeter-wave radar data. This is a necessary imaging process for the millimeter-wave radar systems used in computer vision. Therefore, it is impossible to extend the proposed method to other fields. Its application is limited.

(2)
:   The proposed method has not been verified using a large-scale dataset. The dataset used in this article was collected and created using AWR1642. Although millimeter-wave radar applications are becoming increasingly widespread, there is currently no publicly available large-scale micro-Doppler gesture dataset. Therefore, we have not yet validated the proposed method using large-scale datasets.

(3)
:   The potential for the proposed method to be extended to other tasks in the field of millimeter-wave radar has not yet been verified.

Based on the above analysis, the proposed method may have limitations, as it is only applicable to the field of millimeter-wave radar gesture recognition. Furthermore, based on the aforementioned limitations, we will further improve the proposed method.

## 5. Conclusions

At present, the integration of millimeter-wave radars with deep learning technologies is gaining significant traction within the research community. Despite its promising potential, the development of this field has faced challenges due to the inherently limited data volume collected by millimeter-wave radars and the difficulty in fully exploiting the rich information contained within these data. To address these limitations, this article introduces an innovative recognition method that leverages the LPVT (Local Pyramid Vision Transformer) network. Our proposed approach encompasses two crucial stages: dataset creation and network development. During the initial stage, we meticulously gathered gesture echoes using the AWR1642 radar to compile a comprehensive dataset. This dataset served as the foundation for training and evaluating our model. In the subsequent stage, we enhanced the traditional PVT (Pyramid Vision Transformer) network by incorporating mechanisms to process local features, thereby preserving its unique characteristics while augmenting its capacity for image feature extraction. This proposed LPVT method exhibits superior accuracy compared to conventional deep learning networks.

args.summary:
This scientific paper (Remote Sens. 2024, 16(23), 4602) presents a Local Pyramid Vision Transformer (LPVT) network for millimeter-wave radar gesture recognition, published on December 7, 2024, in MDPI Remote Sensing. The research addresses limitations in both CNNs (which overlook global features) and vision transformers (which neglect local image continuity) for gesture recognition.

**Key Contributions:**
1. **MWRGR Dataset Construction:** Using a 77 GHz AWR1642 radar and DCA1000EVM acquisition card, the authors collected echo signals from 12 volunteers performing 6 gestures (wave, pinch, click, clap, circle, swipe), each repeated 30 times, creating 2,160 samples total. The radar signals were preprocessed through range FFT and Doppler FFT to generate micro-Doppler time spectrograms.

2. **LPVT Network:** The proposed network adopts a pyramid structure with four stages, integrating overlapping patch embedding (for local feature capture), Spatial Reduction Attention (SRA) for global awareness, and a local feedforward network using 1×1 and 3×3 depth-wise convolutions instead of fully connected layers. The DropKey algorithm replaces traditional dropout to prevent overfitting.

**Results:** The LPVT achieved 92.2% recognition accuracy on the self-built dataset, outperforming LSTM, ResNet18/50, Swin Transformer, ViT, and PVTv2. Ablation experiments showed the local feedforward structure and DropKey contributed 4.1% improvement over the base network. The confusion matrix revealed some difficulty distinguishing between similar subtle gestures (click vs. pinch).

**Limitations noted:** The method is only applicable to millimeter-wave radar Doppler images, has not been validated on large-scale public datasets, and its extension to other radar tasks remains unverified. Potential applications include intelligent driving, smart homes, and VR/AR systems.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484)Abstract

Automatic fall detection plays a significant role in monitoring the health of senior citizens. In particular, millimeter-wave radar sensors are relevant for human pose recognition in an indoor environment due to their advantages of privacy protection, low hardware cost, and wide range of working conditions. However, low-quality point clouds from 4D radar diminish the reliability of fall detection. To improve the detection accuracy, conventional methods utilize more costly hardware. In this study, we propose a model that can provide high-quality three-dimensional point cloud images of the human body at a low cost. To improve the accuracy and effectiveness of fall detection, a system that extracts distribution features through small radar antenna arrays is developed. The proposed system achieved 99.1% and 98.9% accuracy on test datasets pertaining to new subjects and new environments, respectively.

**Keywords:**radar, fall detection, machine learning

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484)1. Introduction

According to a report from the World Health Organization, approximately 28–35% of older adults fall each year, leading to serious injury or death [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B1-sensors-24-00648)]. Therefore, intelligently detecting falls in indoor conditions can reduce the risk of the elderly injuring themselves.

Various technologies have been adopted to detect falls. Existing fall detection methods require wearable sensors [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B2-sensors-24-00648)]. Accelerometers have been widely used in wearable methods, and a velocity threshold can be set to detect fall events [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B3-sensors-24-00648),[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B4-sensors-24-00648)]; however, these may be forgotten because of their inconvenience. Vision-based methods eliminate the need to wear something, but they are costly, sensitive to the lighting conditions, and invade privacy [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B5-sensors-24-00648),[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B6-sensors-24-00648)]. Recently, radar sensors have become more popular in fall detection system due to the advantages compared with other sensing technologies: (a) convenience over wearable technologies [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B7-sensors-24-00648)]; (b) high sensitivity to motion compared to depth sensors in complex living environments and weak lighting conditions; (c) privacy compliance over vision sensors [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B8-sensors-24-00648)]; and (d) low hardware cost compared with other sensors [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B9-sensors-24-00648)]. Typical radars for human fall detection are continuous wave (CW) radars and frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) radars. A CW radar signal was converted into the time–frequency domain and extracted artificial features for detecting a falling person [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B10-sensors-24-00648),[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B11-sensors-24-00648)]. Doppler-time signatures recorded in the CW signals were used for the training of a machine learning algorithm [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B12-sensors-24-00648)]. However, CW radar can only provide velocity information. Due to the lack of information richness, actions with similar postures, such as sitting and squatting, may lead to inaccuracies. A better choice is to use an FMCW radar, which can simultaneously provide the range, Doppler, and angle information of the targets and also high sensitivity to motion [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B13-sensors-24-00648)].

Traditionally, researchers have explored serval methods based on FMCW radars, which range from 57–85 GHz [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B14-sensors-24-00648)]. The Doppler information could describe the velocity attribute of a motion; thus, the range-Doppler map has been widely used in FMCW radar-based fall detection methods proposed in the literature [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B15-sensors-24-00648),[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B16-sensors-24-00648),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B17-sensors-24-00648),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B18-sensors-24-00648)]. The Doppler-time map, including time information, was directly used as a feature to detect fall events [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B18-sensors-24-00648)]. Many studies on FMCW radar-based fall detection rely on the time–frequency characteristics of the FMCW radar return signal, including the frequency magnitude, frequency ratio, and the duration of the motion [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B19-sensors-24-00648)]. However, similar to CW radar-based methods, these methods cannot provide spatial information, and similar motions may lead to inaccuracies. Micro-Doppler and spatial information have been used to achieve high accuracy, proving that deep learning methods are superior to traditional artificial feature extraction methods [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B20-sensors-24-00648)]. An FMCW radio has been used to obtain the 3D position information of the human body and heatmaps in both horizontal and vertical directions [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B17-sensors-24-00648)]. However, there is still a problem in combining 3D location information: achieving high angular resolution using radars with large antenna arrays.

To utilize 3D spatial information, recent innovations in human activity detection have explored point clouds from radar [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B21-sensors-24-00648),[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B22-sensors-24-00648),[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B23-sensors-24-00648)], in which each point contains a 3D position in space. However, in contrast to LiDAR and camera sensors, there are two main challenges in these studies: (1) the point clouds generated by mmWave radar are usually sparse and of low resolution, and (2) the point clouds include many ghost points caused by the multipath effect. As a result, the classification accuracy and reliability may be negatively affected. To address these challenges, several methods have been designed for use in conjunction with high-resolution radars. 12Txs-16Rxs antenna arrays have been used to generate high-quality point clouds [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B22-sensors-24-00648)]. Hawkeye generated 2D depth images using radar intensity maps obtained from SAR scans [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B23-sensors-24-00648)]. However, although large antenna arrays and SAR technologies can improve the resolution, they are still very slow and may not be practical in many applications that require a short response time and low-cost hardware. In addition, sparsity-related methods and deep learning-based methods have been used for point clouds’ quality enhancement [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B24-sensors-24-00648)]. Some sparsity-related methods, such as K-mean [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B25-sensors-24-00648)] and density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) algorithm [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B26-sensors-24-00648)], have been used to cluster firstly to remove outliers in the point clouds. However, these technologies could not adequately remove a sufficient number of outlier points. In recent studies, a few deep learning-based methods have been developed based on PointNet [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B27-sensors-24-00648)]. After learning a mapping from the noisy input, they can automatically generate a set of clean points. Inspired by the PointNet, PCN combined a permutation invariant and non-convolutional feature extractor to complete a point cloud from a partial input, and then used a refinement block to denoise the prediction to produce the final point cloud [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B28-sensors-24-00648)]. GPDNet was applicable to denoise point clouds based on graph-convolutional layers [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B29-sensors-24-00648)]. However, most of these methods used LiDAR or other sensor applications and extracted pointwise features. Hence, they may not be efficient for radar-based point clouds because of their very low resolution.

In this study, we propose an FMCW radar-based fall detection method that investigates 3D point clouds while operating at 24 GHz. These systems have not been studied well owing to hardware limitations. First, we obtained raw point clouds from the radar. We then designed a new model to transform the raw points into high-quality point clouds that are closer to the ground truth. Next, we estimated the distribution parameters in the point clouds for classification.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:(1)We propose an efficient fall detection system that uses a small, low-cost radar. As shown in [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f001), the novel framework is primarily composed of three parts: point cloud enhancement (PCE) for point cloud quality improvement, a feature extractor for human pose parameter extraction, and a classifier for classifying normal events and fall events;(2)A PCE model is introduced to transform low-quality point clouds into high-quality point clouds and to reconstruct the shape of the point clouds using the shape of human body. A novel 3D point-box hybrid regression loss function based on pointwise and 3D bounding box features is proposed as a substitute for the traditional loss function;(3)Our system works on sparse and noisy raw radar data without using expensive hardware or synthetic aperture radar (SAR) scans.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. [Section 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sec2-sensors-24-00648) provides an overview of the radar system and signal processing flow. In [Section 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sec3-sensors-24-00648), the details of the proposed method are presented. The results are discussed in [Section 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sec4-sensors-24-00648). Finally, [Section 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sec5-sensors-24-00648) concludes this study.
