## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484)2. Radar System Design

An FMCW radar is often used to estimate the range and velocity of a target using its radio frequency signals. Each transmitted signal $s \left(t\right)$ is a chirp signal, the analytical expression [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B30-sensors-24-00648)] of which is (1)

$$
s \left(t\right) = exp ⁡ \left(j 2 \pi \left(f_{0} t + \frac{1}{2} K t^{2}\right)\right)
$$

 where $f_{0}$ denotes the carrier frequency, and $K$ is the chirp constant.

Referring to the Boulic model [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B31-sensors-24-00648)], the echo from the _i_ th human body part is a time-delayed vision of the transmitted signal, and the received baseband signal can be expressed as (2)

$$
S_{i} \left(t\right) = exp ⁡ \left(j 2 \pi f_{0} \left(t - \frac{2 R_{i}}{c}\right)\right)
$$

 where $R_{i}$ is the distance between the $i^{t h}$ ellipsoidal center and the radar, and $c$ is the speed of light. The echo from the entire human body can be expressed as (3)

$$
S_{a l l} \left(t\right) = \sum_{i = 1}^{M} \eta_{i} S_{i} \left(t\right)
$$

 where $\eta_{i}$ is the attenuation coefficient, which is governed by the radar cross section for different body regions, and M is the number of scattering points of human body parts.

As shown in [Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f002), the raw data from each channel generated a 3D data cube. FMCW radar signal processing started with the sampled echoes that were transferred to the range-Doppler matrix [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B32-sensors-24-00648)]. First, the range of the fast Fourier transform (FFT) assisted in estimating the range of the targets, and the second FFT determined the Doppler frequency. The moving target indicator distinguished the targets from the background. For more reliable detection, a constant false alarm rate was used to detect the targets against the background noise. A direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation algorithm was used to estimate the angle of the target.

For angle estimation, both 3D FFT and the multiple signal classification (MUSIC) algorithm [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B33-sensors-24-00648)] are popular methods. Compared with the MUSIC algorithm, 3D FFT has computing efficiency, but the resolution of 3D FFT is not sufficient for detecting closely spaced points. To obtain a better image of the human body and low computing cost, based on TDM-MIMO antenna arrays in [Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f003), after we obtained eight virtual receiver samples, a 3D FFT was used to obtain the azimuth angle $\theta_{a z}$, and the MUSIC algorithm was used to estimate the elevation angle $\theta_{e l}$. The output spherical coordinates were converted into Cartesian coordinates using transfer matrix T:(4)

$$
\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \left(c o s \theta\right)_{t} & \left(s i n \theta\right)_{t} \\ 0 & \left(- s i n \theta\right)_{t} & \left(c o s \theta\right)_{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} R \left(c o s \theta\right)_{e l} \left(s i n \theta\right)_{a z} \\ R \left(c o s \theta\right)_{e l} \left(c o s \theta\right)_{a z} \\ R \left(s i n \theta\right)_{e l} \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ h \end{bmatrix}
$$

 where $R$ is the distance between the $t a r g e t$ and the radar. After the transformation, we obtained the position values $\left[\right. x , y , z \left]\right.$ of each point in each frame in Cartesian coordinates.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484)3. Proposed Method

The point clouds detected from the range-Doppler map are sensitive to the environment. [Figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f004) shows different point distributions generated in different indoor environments, in which obstacles cause severe multipath interference and affect the performance of fall detection systems in new environments.

Therefore, we propose a fall detection method based on a PCE model. A flowchart of the proposed method is presented in [Figure 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f005). The flow of proposed method consists of four steps: (1) to satisfy the input of the PCE model, the number of point clouds of a motion pattern could be extended to fixed number; (2) after raw point clouds from the radar in pre-processing, PCE model removes noise points and generates high-quality point clouds; (3) these point clouds are then fed into the feature extractor for human pose parameter extraction; (4) a lightweight classifier is used for classifying normal and fall events. In this section, the functionality of each component is described. More detailed descriptions are as follows.

### 3.1. Pre-Processing

The motion window accumulates _L_ frames of the point cloud from the radar, where _L_ is determined by the length of an action such as walking, squatting, and falling. For each action pattern, we extracted the 3D vectors of $\left[x , y , z\right]$ for each point in every frame. In each frame, the number of radar point clouds was random owing to the nature of the FMCW radar measurement. To satisfy the input of the PCE model, zero padding was used for data oversampling. Thus, the number of point clouds can be extended to a fixed number. We obtained the motion pattern (5)

$$
\mathbf{\mathit{X}} = \left{\left{\mathbf{\mathit{x}}_{m}^{i}\right}_{m = 1}^{M}\right}_{l = 1}^{L}
$$

 where _l_ is the frame index of the motion, _M_ is the number of points from radar in each frame, and $p_{m}^{l}$ is the $m^{t h}$ point in the $l^{t h}$ frame, which is a vector of $\left[x_{m}^{l} , y_{m}^{l} , z_{m}^{l}\right] .$

Simultaneously, the Azure Kinect was used as a reference sensor because of its high precision in extracting human skeletal keypoints. Ignoring some inessential points, the desired 27 skeletal keypoints returned from Azure Kinect were also accompanied by a radar time stamp in system time and served to label the ground truth in the training process.

### 3.2. PCE Model

Although point clouds have already been obtained from range-Doppler maps, the resulting points are still low-resolution, very noisy, and affect the classification accuracy and reliability. In addition, it is unnecessary for a fall detection system to increase the computational cost of reconstructing each point. Thus, to improve the quality of these point clouds and increase classification reliability, we propose a PCE model that aims to minimize the difference between the shapes of the radar point clouds and the ground truth. An overview of the proposed PCE architecture is shown in [Figure 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f006).

#### 3.2.1. Encoder

The encoder is responsible for extracting global features from incomplete point clouds. As shown in [Figure 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f006), the encoder comprises three consecutive gate recurrent units (GRU) [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B34-sensors-24-00648)] followed by a dense layer. Using GRU mechanisms in a machine learning network is a relatively new time-series architecture compared with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memories (LSTMs). GRUs can retain long-term dependencies and are also faster for training compared with traditional LSTMs because there are fewer gates to update. As shown in [Figure 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f006), the units of the three GRU layers are 32, 32, and 16. The input data $\mathbf{\mathit{X}}^{\mathbf{\mathit{R}} \mathbf{\mathit{P}}} = \left{\mathbf{\mathit{x}}_{1}^{\mathbf{\mathit{R}} \mathbf{\mathit{P}}} , \mathbf{\mathit{x}}_{2}^{\mathbf{\mathit{R}} \mathbf{\mathit{P}}} , \ldots \mathbf{\mathit{x}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{N}}}^{\mathbf{\mathit{R}} \mathbf{\mathit{P}}}\right}$ are first reconstructed by the hidden parts, and the output of the encoder is a series of vectors $\left{\mathbf{\mathit{h}}_{1} , \mathbf{\mathit{h}}_{2} , \ldots \mathbf{\mathit{h}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{b}}}\right}$. Thus, the encoder process is given by (6)

$$
\mathbf{\mathit{h}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{b}}} = G R U \left(\mathbf{\mathit{W}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{e}} , \mathbf{\mathit{b}}} \mathbf{\mathit{X}}^{R P} + \mathbf{\mathit{b}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{e}} , \mathbf{\mathit{b}}}\right)
$$

 where $\mathbf{\mathit{W}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{e}} , \mathbf{\mathit{b}}}$ and $\mathbf{\mathit{b}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{e}} , \mathbf{\mathit{b}}}$ are the encoder weight matrix and bias vector for the _bth_ node (_b_ = 1, 2, …_B_).

#### 3.2.2. Decoder

The decoder consists of three consecutive GRUs followed by a dense layer. The units of the three GRU layers are 32. The output from the GRU is (7)

$$
\mathbf{\mathit{u}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{i}}} = G R U \left(\mathbf{\mathit{W}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{d}} , \mathbf{\mathit{b}}} \mathbf{\mathit{w}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{i}}} + \mathbf{\mathit{b}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{d}} , \mathbf{\mathit{b}}}\right)
$$

 where $\mathbf{\mathit{W}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{d}} , \mathbf{\mathit{b}}}$ and $\mathbf{\mathit{b}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{d}} , \mathbf{\mathit{b}}}$ are the decoder weight matrix and bias vector for the _bth_ node (_b_ = 1, 2…_B_), and _**wi**_ is the input layer of the decoder. The recovered point clouds $\hat{\mathbf{\mathit{X}}}$ through the dense layer is obtained via (8)

$$
\hat{\mathbf{\mathit{X}}} = \mathbf{\mathit{W}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{d}}} \mathbf{\mathit{u}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{i}}} + \mathbf{\mathit{b}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{d}}}
$$

 where $\mathbf{\mathit{W}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{d}}}$ and $\mathbf{\mathit{b}}_{\mathbf{\mathit{d}}}$ are the weights and biases of the output layer, respectively. After the sampling layer, an enhanced point cloud $\mathbf{\mathit{X}}^{\mathbf{\mathit{E}} \mathbf{\mathit{P}}}$ is obtained.

#### 3.2.3. Loss Function

A simple method for extracting pointwise features in 3D space is supervised by the mean squared error (MSE). However, directly supervising the pointwise features of point clouds may not utilize 3D receptive field information. The observations in [Figure 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f007) indicate that the change in the 3D receptive field bounding box of a falling human body is different from that of a walking human body. Specifically, changes in the bounding box of a human body are related to its pose. Therefore, we not only consider pointwise features but also detect fall events by characterizing the uniqueness of bounding box changes for such poses.

To use the bounding box of the radar point clouds for fall detection, the position and shape of the predicted box should be closely related to the corresponding ground truth. In this manner, we propose a 3D point-box hybrid regression loss to reduce the error between the predicted radar bounding box and ground truth. Previous studies [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B35-sensors-24-00648),[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B36-sensors-24-00648)] found intersection over union (IoU) loss and generalized IoU functions for 2D boxes using only the width and height of the boxes without considering the direction of the boxes. In addition, it is difficult to provide a specific formula describing the intersection between two 3D bounding boxes because a variety of cases must be considered. Some previous studies projected a 3D bounding box onto two 2D bounding boxes, but this did not increase the accuracy because of lack of direction [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B37-sensors-24-00648)].

In this study, because most of the measured human motion states were symmetrical along the x-axis (as shown in [Figure 8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f008)), a 3D bounding box was obtained based on the 2D rotated IoU by multiplying the length along the x-axis. As shown in [Figure 9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f009), the intersection of the predicted box and ground truth included a variety of polygons, which was the sum of the areas of all the triangles. Therefore, the 3D IoU can be expressed as (9)

$$
\left(I o U\right)_{3 D} = \frac{\left(A r e a\right)_{O L} \cdot x_{O L}}{\left(A r e a\right)_{r} \cdot x_{r} + \left(A r e a\right)_{G T} \cdot x_{G T} - \left(A r e a\right)_{O L} \cdot x_{O L}}
$$

 where $\left(A r e a\right)_{O L}$ is the area of overlap between the two boxes; $\left(A r e a\right)_{r}$ and $\left(A r e a\right)_{G T}$ are the areas of the predicted box from radar and ground truth, respectively; $x_{O L}$ is the overlap on the x-axis; and $x_{r}$ and $x_{G T}$ are the lengths of the predicted box and ground truth along the x-axis, respectively.

Additionally, an accurate center [$x_{c e n t e r}$, $y_{c e n t e r}$, $z_{c e n t e r} \left]\right.$ is a prerequisite for predicting an accurate bounding box. An accurate width along the y-axis and an accurate height along the z-axis also contribute to maximizing the fall detection accuracy. Based on the above observations, the box-based loss function is expressed as (10)

$$
\left(L o s s\right)_{b o x} = \left(L o s s\right)_{\left(I o U\right)_{3 D}} + \left(L o s s\right)_{\left(c e n t e r\right)_{d i s}} + \left(L o s s\right)_{l i n e} \\ = 1 - \left(I o U\right)_{3 D} + \frac{d^{2} \left(b^{r} , b^{G T}\right)}{\left(l^{e}\right)^{2} + \left(w^{e}\right)^{2} + \left(h^{e}\right)^{2}} \\ + \frac{d^{2} \left(w^{r} , w^{G T}\right)}{\left(w^{e}\right)^{2}} + \frac{d^{2} \left(h^{r} , h^{G T}\right)}{\left(h^{e}\right)^{2}}
$$

 where $b^{r}$ and $b^{G T}$ are the center positions of the predicted box and ground truth box, respectively; $l^{e}$, $w^{e}$, and $h^{e}$ are the length, width, and height of the enclosing box, respectively; $l^{r}$, $w^{r}$, and $h^{r}$ are the length, width, and height of the predicted box, respectively; and $l^{G T}$, $w^{G T}$, and $h^{G T}$ are the length, width, and height of the ground truth box, respectively.

In summary, the 3D point-box hybrid regression loss consisted of a 3D bounding box IoU loss and a pointwise loss, which can be described as (11)

$$
\left(L o s s\right)_{H y L o s s} = \left(L o s s\right)_{p o i n t} + \left(L o s s\right)_{b o x}
$$

 where $\left(L o s s\right)_{p o i n t}$ is the position loss of the points for optimizing the IoU of the human body and the ground reflection points.

### 3.3. Feature Extraction

We used a lightweight CNN for classification. The architecture of the lightweight CNN is shown in [Figure 10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f010). The CNN included an input layer sequence, one convolution layer, one dense layer, and a softmax layer. The feature parameters from one frame included $\left[\right. x_{c e n t e r}$, $y_{c e n t e r}$, $z_{c e n t e r} , w , l , h , \theta \left]\right.$, and L frames of $7 \times 1$ feature parameters were first subjected to the convolution layer. The convolution layer captured the movement features, consisting of eight hidden neurons with a kernel size of eight. The convolution layer employed rectified linear units as activation functions for the hidden layers. The $L \times 7 \times 8$ output from the convolution layer was fed into the dense layer. The softmax function was used in the final dense layer for classification.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484)4. Implementation and Evaluation

### 4.1. Setup and Data Collection

We used the 24 GHz mmWave FMCW radar from ICLegend Micro for data collection. The radar sensor had two transmitting antennas and four receiving antenna channels. The radar parameter configurations are listed in [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-t001).

To evaluate the proposed system, we set up the experiments and collected data in two different indoor environments. The experimental setup is shown in [Figure 11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f011). Room A, shown in [Figure 11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f011)b, was a relatively empty office, and room B, shown in [Figure 11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f011)c, was a bedroom where obstacles caused severe multipath and motion interference. The elevation field of view (FOV) of the Kinect sensor is 135 degrees, and the elevation FOV of the radar is 90 degrees. To capture more of a scene, the radar and Kinect sensors were both mounted at heights of 1.3 m. We collected 17,600 frames of data from 13 subjects performing fall and non-fall actions. The participants were aged between 20 and 30 years, and their heights were between 165 and 177 cm.

Furthermore, we divided these frames into three datasets:

Dataset0. This dataset included 10,860 frames from five participants who performed the experiments in room A. After data argumentation, including shifting, rotating, and adding noise points, the dataset included 13,560 frames.

Dataset1. This dataset included 3040 frames from four participants who performed the experiments in room A.

Dataset2. This dataset included 3700 frames from four participants who performed the experiments in room B.

For each dataset, the motion included falling backward and falling forward, sitting on a chair, jumping, walking, or squatting. The ratio of the number of fall samples to non-fall samples was 1:2.

### 4.2. Evaluation

In this section, we present the experimental results of the proposed model in a fall detection system. All algorithms were realized based on Python code. The computation platform used was a laptop with a 2.60 GHz Intel(R) Core (TM) i7-10750H CPU.

#### 4.2.1. Point Cloud Quality

Before training the proposed PCE model, the 3D radar data and ground truth skeletal points from the Azure Kinect were extracted, as described in Section IV. Then, L frames of data from the radar were combined sequentially to obtain a 3D tensor ($L \times M \times 3$). We then evaluated the PCE model for $L = \left{1,2 , \ldots 10\right}$ by generating 10 distinct datasets, $\left(D a t a s e t 0\right)_{i}$, $\left(D a t a s e t 1\right)_{i}$ and $\left(D a t a s e t 2\right)_{i}$, where $i$$\in \left{1,2 , \ldots 10\right}$ is the frame index. The proposed PCE model $M_{i}$ was trained on $\left(D a t a s e t 0\right)_{i}$, and the trained PCE model $M_{i}$ was subjected to $\left(D a t a s e t 1\right)_{i}$ and $\left(D a t a s e t 2\right)_{i}$, which did not participate in the training. [Figure 12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f012) shows predicted points. We selected two frames of each motion for comparison against the ground truth. In addition, because of the nature of the FMCW radar measurement, an exact and complete match of [_x_, _y_, _z_] between the predicted and ground truth keypoints was simply unrealistic; therefore, finding a method for evaluating the predicted results was crucial.

To evaluate the quality of the point clouds, we calculated the average 3D IoU for every L frame scenario across the f test samples in the dataset according to the formula $\left(3 D I o U\right)_{i} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j = 1}^{N} \left(3 D I o U\right)_{i j}$, $\forall i \in \left{1,2 , \ldots 10\right}$. The average 3D IoU results for all L frames from Dataset1 and Dataset2 are outlined in [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-t002) and [Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-t003), respectively. In the 10th frame, the average 3D IoU is lower than that in the other frames. The reason for this result was that sometimes the number of points was too small because the motion may have already been completed in advance. We also compared the raw point clouds from the radar and the DBSCAN method, which is the most popular method for removing outliers and improving the quality of point clouds. The proposed method outperformed the other methods. In addition, the PCE with the proposed HyLoss function outperformed the traditional MSE loss function.

Furthermore, we computed the centroids of the coordinates of the point clouds. For accuracy, the centroids of the coordinates of the predicted point clouds were compared with the centroids of the coordinates of the ground truth labels by calculating the mean absolute error (MAE) in the x-, y-, and z-coordinates. The centroid of the coordinates was $\left(\right. \frac{m a x \left(x\right) + min ⁡ \left(\right. x \left.\right)}{2} , \frac{m a x \left(y\right) + min ⁡ \left(\right. y \left.\right)}{2} , \frac{m a x \left(z\right) + min ⁡ \left(\right. z \left.\right)}{2} \left.\right)$. The average MAEs for all L frames tested in Dataset1 and Dataset2 are shown in [Figure 13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f013). We also compared the raw point clouds from the radar, DBSCAN, and PCE models using the traditional MSE loss function instead of the proposed HyLoss. The average MAE of the predicted method was comparable to that of the other methods. In other words, the localization of the centroid from the PCE model was the closest to the ground truth. In addition, we computed the average MAE of the width, depth, and height of the bounding box along the x-, y-, and z-axis. As shown in [Figure 14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f014), the width, depth, and height of the predicted bounding box were significantly lower than those of the other methods for both Dataset1 and Dataset2. This result indicates that the PCE model with the proposed HyLoss offers a better image of the human body for a wide range of people and environments.

#### 4.2.2. Classification for Fall Detection

In terms of fall detection, the predicted high-quality point clouds of Dataset0, Dataset1, and Dataset2 were fed into the feature extractor to obtain the human pose parameters. The lightweight CNN shown in [Figure 9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f009) was used to classify normal and fall events. Dataset0 was used to train the lightweight CNN classifier, Dataset1 was used for validation with new people, and Dataset2 was used for validation with new people and new environments. Neither Dataset1 nor Dataset2 were involved in the entire training process. To validate the choice of PCE architecture parameters, we compared the average actuary, recall, and F1 of the PCE model with various parameters. The results are summarized in [Table 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-t004). Every encoder is denoted by E, and every decoder is denoted by D. For example, the proposed PCE model can be described as raw+32E+32E+16E+32D. Clearly, the proposed architecture is suitable. In addition, a comparison of the PCE with the traditional MSE loss function revealed that the accuracy, recall, and F1 score of the proposed HyLoss function outperformed those of the traditional function, which shows that the proposed HyLoss function improves the fall detection system.

The purpose of PCE is to improve the reliability of the classification during fall detection tasks. Therefore, we compared the performance of the PCE classification reliability (instead of position errors or IoU) with existing point cloud models. First, the predicted points are shown in [Figure 9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-f009). The results are listed in [Table 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-t005). The accuracy of the raw points and DBSCAN method for Dataset0 were higher than 0.98 because the test data included some people in the training set. The accuracy of the raw points (baseline) and DBSCAN method for Dataset1 and Dataset2 were lower than 0.8 because the raw data from the radar detection contained many invalid points from new test data, and DBSCAN could not adequately remove a sufficient number of outlier points. However, the performance of the proposed method exhibited no obvious changes for any of the three datasets. This means that the point clouds predicted by the PCE could improve the performance of classification when new people and environments are involved. For computing the complexity analysis, the proposed method had 0.017 million parameters, which was a much smaller number than that of the other methods. The floating-point operations (FLOPs) associated with the proposed method was 0.303M, which was also lower than that of the other methods. In addition, the fall detection system achieved high accuracy and required less response time. For the response times of all the competing methods, we ran them on the same platform. Because all of them required the same computing time for feature extraction and classification, we only calculated the computing time of PCE on a single sample at a time. Although the accuracy was not favorable for new people and environments, the response time of the proposed method was shorter than that of the others. In summary, our work balances accuracy and speed.

However, fall detection based on radar currently uses different data formats, such as time-frequency maps and range-Doppler maps, and there is no public fall detection dataset for radar. It is difficult to find a baseline for a fall detection system; therefore, we compared the reported performance with that of other studies. As shown in [Table 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-t006), the proposed system achieves better performance for new people and environments. Although the performances of studies [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B22-sensors-24-00648),[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B40-sensors-24-00648)] was above 0.9, they were tested only on the same people and in the same environment. The performance of these studies may vary for new people and environments in a way similar to the results of the DBSCAN method shown in [Table 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-t005). In addition, although CW radar has lower cost, the accuracy of the proposed FMCW fall detection system was 0.989, which was higher than the CW radar system [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B41-sensors-24-00648),[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B42-sensors-24-00648)]. Moreover, even though the 77 GHz 3T4R radar has a higher resolution than our sensor, the proposed fall detection system could still outperform it [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#B22-sensors-24-00648)].

To investigate the potential of our fall detection system for real-time implementation, we evaluated the computational time of one sample for all the steps in our work. As shown in [Table 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484#sensors-24-00648-t007), although the computing time for the PCE and classification was 20.349 ms in total, the signal processing cost a significant amount of time because, in this study, we used the super-resolution algorithm MUSIC for DOA, which is considered to be the bottleneck of real-time fall detection systems. However, further research is required to design a system with lower computing costs for real-time detection and mobile devices. Furthermore, it is difficult to collect samples when real falls start among older adults. The limitations of the sample size may cause potential biases. In the future, we will improve our experiment and test it with large-scale experiments in more practical environments and with more subjects.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10820484)5. Conclusions

This study demonstrated a fall detection system based on the 3D point clouds of a 24 GHz FMCW radar. Unlike other conventional methods that utilize more costly hardware to improve detection accuracy, we used a low-cost small radar antenna array operating at 24 GHz to maintain high accuracy. By applying the PCE model to a fall detection system, we improved the quality of the point clouds and also the system performance, especially the accuracy, sensitivity, and generalization ability for new users and environments. As a result of our efforts to reduce computing costs in signal processing, the proposed method has the potential for widespread applications in monitoring the health of the elderly in an indoor environment without considering privacy protection.

args.summary: This scientific paper presents a fall detection system for elderly health monitoring using a 24 GHz FMCW radar with a small, low-cost antenna array. The authors—Tingxuan Liang, Ruizhi Liu, Lei Yang, Yue Lin, C.-J. Richard Shi, and Hongtao Xu from Fudan University, ICLegend Micro, and the University of Washington—propose a Point Cloud Enhancement (PCE) model that transforms low-quality, noisy radar point clouds into high-quality 3D point clouds resembling human body shapes. The system uses a novel 3D point-box hybrid regression loss function (HyLoss) combining pointwise and bounding box features. After PCE, a lightweight CNN classifier extracts human pose parameters (center, width, length, height, angle) to distinguish falls from normal activities (walking, sitting, jumping, squatting). Experiments using 17,600 frames from 13 subjects in two environments (empty office and cluttered bedroom) achieved 99.1% accuracy on new subjects and 98.9% accuracy on new subjects in new environments—outperforming raw point clouds and DBSCAN-based methods. The model has only 0.017 million parameters and 0.303M FLOPs, with total computing time of 20.349 ms per sample. The MUSIC algorithm for DOA estimation was identified as the computational bottleneck for real-time implementation. The paper concludes that the system offers high accuracy, sensitivity, and generalization ability for new users and environments without requiring expensive hardware or sacrificing privacy protection.

## Abstract

Propelled by advancements in deep learning technology, autonomous driving has undergone rapid development in recent years. Object sensing, as the core technology of autonomous vehicles, is undergoing a transformation from traditional single-modal sensing to multi-modal sensing, aiming to perceive environmental information in a robust, accurate, and real-time manner to adapt to increasingly complex application scenes. This paper aims to offer a comprehensive guide for radar-camera fusion, focusing on the object detection task. Firstly, detailed explanations are provided regarding the characteristics, principles, data processing methods, and representations of radar and camera data. Secondly, we analyze the evaluation metrics of object detection via a group-independent form and summarize existing radar-camera fusion datasets. Thirdly, we comprehensively review and analyze key issues in radar-camera fusion across five hierarchies (_why_, _what_, _where_, _when_, and _how_ to fuse). Fourthly, we discuss and anticipate potential challenges and emerging research directions from the view of the robustness, accuracy, and real-time performance for object detection.

## 1 Introduction

Traffic safety is a global challenge. According to the Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023 (WHO [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR176 "WHO (2023) Global status report on road safety 2023. World Health Organization")), road accidents cause about 1.19 million deaths annually worldwide. They are the 12th leading cause of death overall, and the leading cause of death among people aged 5-29 years. More than half of the victims are vulnerable road users–pedestrians, cyclists, and motorcyclists–with the burden especially high in low- and middle-income countries.

While road safety garners considerable attention, it remains a consistently prominent subject that is extensively researched (He et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR62 "He Y, Ma L, Jiang Z et al (2021) Vi-eye: Semantic-based 3d point cloud registration for infrastructure-assisted autonomous driving. In: Proc. of ACM MobiCom, pp 573–586"); Shi et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR149 "Shi S, Cui J, Jiang Z et al (2022) Vips: Real-time perception fusion for infrastructure-assisted autonomous driving. In: Proc. of ACM MobiCom, pp 133–146")). In recent years, significant advancements have been made by both the scientific community and the market in this field, particularly with regard to the advancement of autonomous driving technology (Barbosa and Osório [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR5 "Barbosa FM, Osório FS (2023) Camera-radar perception for autonomous vehicles and adas: Concepts, datasets and metrics. 
                  arXiv:2303.04302
                  
                "); Dong et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR37 "Dong X, Zhuang B, Mao Y et al (2021) Radar camera fusion via representation learning in autonomous driving. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 1672–1681")). Autonomous driving holds immense potential to mitigate traffic congestion and enhance driving safety. Perception acts akin to the human eyes in autonomous driving, forming the foundation for critical functions, especially with the object detection ability (Deng et al. [2022a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR30 "Deng K, Zhao D, Han Q et al (2022) Geryon: edge assisted real-time and robust object detection on drones via mmwave radar and camera fusion. Proc of ACM IMWUT 6(3):1–27"), [b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR31 "Deng K, Zhao D, Han Q et al (2022b) Global-local feature enhancement network for robust object detection using mmwave radar and camera. In: Proc. of IEEE ICASSP, pp 4708–4712")). To enhance the driving system’s accuracy and robustness, autonomous vehicles incorporate various sensors, leveraging their complementary strengths for object detection. Nevertheless, the selection of sensors and the method for fusing data from different sources pose complex challenges that necessitate additional research.

Cameras are extensively employed in autonomous driving for object detection due to their ability to capture rich object texture information (Beery et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR6 "Beery S, Wu G, Rathod V et al (2020) Context r-cnn: Long term temporal context for per-camera object detection. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 13075–13085"); Chapel and Bouwmans [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR19 "Chapel MN, Bouwmans T (2020) Moving objects detection with a moving camera: a comprehensive review. Comput Sci Rev 38:100310")). LiDARs measure the distance to surrounding objects by calculating the time difference between the emission and reception of a laser beam (Tian et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR159 "Tian H, Chen Y, Dai J et al (2021) Unsupervised object detection with lidar clues. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 5962–5972"); Peri et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR134 "Peri N, Li M, Wilson B et al (2023) An empirical analysis of range for 3d object detection. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 4074–4083")). Note that emitting a greater number of laser beams leads to a clearer three-dimensional representation of the object. Radars, as an emerging sensing modality, can surmount challenging conditions and have been extensively employed in autonomous driving and intelligent transportation systems (Dong et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR36 "Dong X, Wang P, Zhang P et al (2020) Probabilistic oriented object detection in automotive radar. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR Workshops, pp 102–103"); Wang et al. [2021b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR168 "Wang Y, Jiang Z, Gao X et al (2021b) Rodnet: Radar object detection using cross-modal supervision. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 504–513")). However, various sensors will have corresponding shortcomings, rendering them challenging to apply in complex traffic scenes. Therefore, multi-sensor fusion has emerged as a trend to achieve accurate and robust object detection.

To this end, we conduct a detailed comparative analysis of three mainstream sensors, represented through a 6-D radar chart. It should be noted that the radar chart in Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#Fig1) presents a qualitative comparison, where each axis is normalized to a common scale to highlight relative strengths and weaknesses rather than absolute quantitative values. From Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#Fig1) we observe that: (i) while LiDAR and camera have their distinct advantages, they share a common drawback–sensitivity to adverse weather conditions (e.g., foggy weather, poor illumination), which greatly limits their sensing range and ability; in contrast, radar exhibits robust performance under adverse weather conditions and offers a comparable field-of-view to LiDAR; (ii) camera and LiDAR serve as visual sensors, but the former is superior to the latter in terms of price and classification ability; (iii) in general, camera- and radar-based object detection methods entail lower computational overhead compared to LiDAR-based methods; the main reason is that a LiDAR frame typically comprises hundreds of thousands of points, resulting in higher model computational complexity. This motivates researchers to increasingly focus on fusing radar and camera for object detection.

To our knowledge, while radar technology has been extensively utilized in autonomous driving, there has been limited research conducted on radar and camera fusion (Jin et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR72 "Jin S, Wang P, Boufounos P et al (2023) Spatial-domain object detection under mimo-fmcw automotive radar interference. In: Proc. of IEEE ICASSP, pp 1–5"); Jiang et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR71 "Jiang T, Zhuang L, An Q et al (2022) T-rodnet: transformer for vehicular millimeter-wave radar object detection. IEEE TIM 72:1–12")). The main reasons are that: (i) the quality of radar data is not high, such as low resolution, sparseness, disorder, and simple feature representation; (ii) it is insufficient for radar-camera fusion datasets to be applied to autonomous driving, which poses a challenge to the robustness of vehicles on real-world roads; (iii) current LiDAR-based models exhibit poor transferability to radar point clouds due to inherent differences in point cloud characteristics between sensors. Furthermore, while the radar cross section (RCS) indicates the object’s reflection intensity, it is susceptible to various influences and cannot independently serve as a reliable basis for object classification. Even if multi-frame compositing is adopted to improve the density of point clouds, it can cause high latency to vehicle systems (Yuance et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR203 "Yuance C, Ding H, Han D et al (2023) mmyodar: Lightweight and robust object detection using mmwave signals. In: Proc. of IEEE SECON, pp 151–159")). In summary, it is important to fuse radar and camera for accurate and robust object detection in autonomous driving, but it remains challenging to deploy in practice.

### 1.1 Comparison with existing studies

Prior works (Wang et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR163 "Wang K, Zhou T, Li X et al (2022) Performance and challenges of 3d object detection methods in complex scenes for autonomous driving. IEEE TITS 8(2):1699–1716"), [2023b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR165 "Wang L, Zhang X, Song Z et al (2023b) Multi-modal 3d object detection in autonomous driving: A survey and taxonomy. IEEE TIV"); Cui et al. [2021b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR29 "Cui Y, Chen R, Chu W et al (2021) Deep learning for image and point cloud fusion in autonomous driving: a review. IEEE TITS 23(2):722–739")) on sensor fusion has mainly focused on combining LiDAR and camera data, or on broader multi-sensor setups involving LiDAR, radar, and cameras. Among these, LiDAR-camera fusion dominates. For instance, Huang et al. ([2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR63 "Huang K, Shi B, Li X et al (2022) Multi-modal sensor fusion for auto driving perception: A survey. 
                  arXiv:2202.02703
                  
                ")) and Cui et al. ([2021b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR29 "Cui Y, Chen R, Chu W et al (2021) Deep learning for image and point cloud fusion in autonomous driving: a review. IEEE TITS 23(2):722–739")) analyze model architectures specifically for this pairing, with only limited attention to radar-camera fusion.

Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#Tab1) outlines how our study compares with prior work. In contrast to Feng et al. ([2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR45 "Feng D, Haase-Schütz C, Rosenbaum L et al (2020) Deep multi-modal object detection and semantic segmentation for autonomous driving: datasets, methods, and challenges. IEEE TITS 22(3):1341–1360")); Ravindran et al. ([2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR140 "Ravindran R, Santora MJ, Jamali MM (2020) Multi-object detection and tracking, based on dnn, for autonomous vehicles: a review. IEEE JSEN 21(5):5668–5677")); Barbosa and Osório ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR5 "Barbosa FM, Osório FS (2023) Camera-radar perception for autonomous vehicles and adas: Concepts, datasets and metrics. 
                  arXiv:2303.04302
                  
                ")), and Singh ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR153 "Singh A (2023) Vision-radar fusion for robotics bev detections: A survey. In: Proc. of IEEE IV, pp 1–7")) (out-of-domain reference), we offer a more detailed treatment of sensor data processing and representation, including preprocessing and input formats used in detection models. Compared with Yao et al. ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR199 "Yao S, Guan R, Huang X et al (2023) Radar-camera fusion for object detection and semantic segmentation in autonomous driving: A comprehensive review. IEEE TIV")), our contributions include: (i) summarizing a wider range of datasets, which supports further development in radar-camera fusion; (ii) organizing evaluation metrics by detection category and conducting evaluations for improved clarity; and (iii) exploring challenges and new directions based on real-world testing.

### 1.2 Contributions

After analyzing the studies above, it’s evident that radar-camera fusion has received scant attention, making it challenging for researchers, particularly newcomers, to gain a comprehensive understanding of this rapidly evolving research domain. Our work aims to bridge this gap by conducting a comprehensive study of existing works on radar-camera fusion in autonomous driving. Our contributions are summarized below:

*   To our knowledge, this marks the inaugural comprehensive study concentrating on the object detection of radar-camera fusion within autonomous driving; meanwhile, we meticulously elucidate the characteristics and operational principles of radar and camera sensors, along with delineating the benefits derived from their fusion.

*   We focus on the data processing & representation of radar and camera, followed by dividing the performance evaluation metrics for object detection in a group-independent form.

*   We present a comprehensive study of radar-camera fusion datasets and models from 2019 to 2025, delving deeply into the critical inquiries of “_why_, _what_, _where_, _when_, and _how_ to fuse.”

*   We concentrate on analyzing the primary technical obstacles encountered in radar-camera fusion and presenting competitive solutions; meanwhile, we also further explore potential emerging research directions in the future.

## 2 Background

To ensure the safe and reliable operation of autonomous vehicles, it is crucial to have robust sensing of the surrounding environment, which is usually achieved using various sensors. We provide a detailed description of radar and camera sensors and their working principles, followed by demonstrating the necessity of radar-camera fusion. Moreover, the vehicle sensing module utilizes data from radar and camera to comprehend the surrounding environment, thus guiding the focus of our work towards object detection and the associated representative algorithms.

### 2.1 Sensor descriptions

_1) Radar_. Radar (radio detection and ranging) measures an object’s range, angle, and velocity using radio frequency (RF) waves (Iovescu and Rao [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR67 "Iovescu C, Rao S (2017) The fundamentals of millimeter wave sensors. TI pp 1–8"); Liu et al. [2023a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR100 "Liu F, Zheng L, Cui Y et al (2023) Seventy years of radar and communications: the road from separation to integration. IEEE SPM 40(5):106–121")). Unlike passive sensors such as cameras, radar actively emits modulated RF signals and processes the reflected signals to extract object information. The frequency band of the modulated RF signals varies depending on the radar applications, reflecting the diverse carrier frequencies inherent in electromagnetic waves. For example, the 60-64 GHz radar is predominantly suited for indoor applications (Meng et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR118 "Meng Z, Fu S, Yan J et al (2020) Gait recognition for co-existing multiple people using millimeter wave sensing. In: Proc. of AAAI, pp 849–856"); Park et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR133 "Park JK, Park JH, Kim KT (2023) Multipath signal mitigation for indoor localization based on mimo fmcw radar system. IEEE IoTJ")), as it experiences significant energy loss caused by atmospheric attenuation. Conversely, the 76-84 GHz radar is designed for automotive applications (Sun et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR157 "Sun S, Petropulu AP, Poor HV (2020) Mimo radar for advanced driver-assistance systems and autonomous driving: advantages and challenges. IEEE SPM 37(4):98–117"); Li et al. [2022b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR87 "Li P, Wang P, Berntorp K et al (2022b) Exploiting temporal relations on radar perception for autonomous driving. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 17071–17080")), including advanced driver-assistance systems. The primary advantage of radar lies in its compact RF component size and antenna design attributable to its high carrier frequency. Additionally, radar can deliver a substantial signal bandwidth of up to 4 GHz, resulting in a range resolution of up to 3.75 cm. Specifically, the range resolution formula used is:

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta R = \frac{c}{{2B}}, \end{aligned}$$

 (1) 

where _c_ is the speed of light (3 \(\times \)\(10^{8}\) m/s) and _B_ is the radar signal bandwidth. For _B_ = 4 GHz = 4 \(\times \)\(10^{9}\) Hz, \(\Delta R = \frac{{3 \times {{10}^8}}}{{2 \times 4 \times {{10}^9}}} \approx 3.75 cm\).

Working principle of cameras

Figure [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#Fig2) depicts the hardware architecture of a standard frequency modulated continuous wave (FMCW) radar with quadrature receiver. The voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) initiates the sweeping of the linear frequency modulated (LFM) signal, commonly referred to as the chirp signal, which is then amplified by an RF power amplifier (PA) to enhance the transmitting power. The transmitted LFM signal (transmitters, TX antennas), is subsequently propagated through free space by the antennas. Upon encountering objects (e.g., vehicles, pedestrians), the echoes are reflected back to the receivers (RX antennas). The low noise amplifier (LNA) enhances the strength of the received signal while minimally impacting its signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Subsequently, the received echoes are directed to the quadrature mixer, where both the in-phase and quadrature components of these echoes are combined with the local reference of the transmitting linear frequency modulation (LFM) signal, prior to being processed through the anti-aliasing filter (AAF). The analog-to-digital converter (ADC) transforms the filtered signal from analog to digital domain. Finally, the digital signal processor (DSP) executes standard radar signal processing techniques to ascertain the range, angle, and velocity of objects within the environment. Note that in recent years, with the advancement of related technologies, 4D radar has gradually begun to emerge (Paek et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR128 "Paek DH, Kong SH, Wijaya KT (2022) K-radar: 4d radar object detection for autonomous driving in various weather conditions. Proc of NIPS 35:3819–3829"); Lu et al. [2023a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR108 "Lu S, Zhuo G, Xiong L et al (2023a) Efficient deep-learning 4d automotive radar odometry method. IEEE TIV")), with its antennas arranged horizontally and vertically to measure the elevation information of objects.

Framework of a typical radar-camera fusion

Apart from measuring the distance, Doppler velocity, and azimuth angle of objects, radar’s electromagnetic waves also possess strong penetrability. For example, they experience minimal atmospheric attenuation under adverse weather conditions, such as rain, snow, and fog, enabling radar to conduct all-weather operations effectively. Nevertheless, radar still has several limitations: (i) low angular resolution. It is difficult to distinguish multiple objects that are close together; (ii) data sparsity. Typically, pedestrians are represented by only a few data points, while vehicles may have slightly more, yet still limited, points. Consequently, outlining objects and extracting geometric information becomes challenging; (iii) weak sensing ability against static objects. In practical scenes, static objects are often filtered out; the main reason is that the filtering operation can eliminate most noise and minimize the impact of non-objects.

_2) Camera_. A typical camera consists of a lens, an image sensor, an image signal processor (ISP), and I/O interfaces (contributors [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR26 "contributors W (2023) Image sensor – wikipedia, the free encyclopedia. 
                  https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Image sensor&oldid=1146373856
                  
                ")). As shown in Fig. [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#Fig3), the lens projects the optical image produced by vehicles or pedestrians onto the sensor surface, where it undergoes photoelectric conversion into an analog electrical signal. Following noise elimination, this signal is digitized through analog-to-digital (A/D) conversion to form a digital image signal, followed by sending to the DSP chip for further processing. Besides RGB cameras, modern cameras are also equipped with infrared lighting, enabling them to sense even in low-light conditions (Liu et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR101 "Liu J, Fan X, Huang Z et al (2022) Target-aware dual adversarial learning and a multi-scenario multi-modality benchmark to fuse infrared and visible for object detection. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 5802–5811"); Tu et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR161 "Tu Z, Ma Y, Li Z et al (2022) Rgbt salient object detection: A large-scale dataset and benchmark. IEEE TMM")). Additionally, gated cameras exhibit strong sensing capabilities under adverse weather conditions (Julca-Aguilar et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR74 "Julca-Aguilar F, Taylor J, Bijelic M et al (2021) Gated3d: Monocular 3d object detection from temporal illumination cues. In: Proc. of IEEE ICCV, pp 2938–2948"); Marathe et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR114 "Marathe A, Jain P, Walambe R et al (2022) Restorex-ai: A contrastive approach towards guiding image restoration via explainable ai systems. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 3030–3039")), but they do not provide color information.

Cameras are capable of capturing detailed texture information of objects, including their appearance, color, and shape. Utilizing this data, neural network models can be trained to detect various objects, such as vehicles, pedestrians, and traffic signs. Note that cameras are passive sensors, which rely on incident light for object data collection. Adverse lighting conditions, such as poor illumination and extreme weathers, can significantly degrade the quality of image data, thereby impacting object detection performance. Furthermore, the image data lacks distance information of objects, which further demonstrates its limitations in autonomous driving.

### 2.2 The necessity of radar-camera fusion

The specific strengths of each sensor motivate multi-level fusion strategies: radar’s Doppler estimates stabilize object tracking and motion sensing, while camera features sharpen spatial localization and disambiguate categories that radar cannot distinguish reliably (Li et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR90 "Li Y, Padmanabhan A, Zhao P et al (2020) Reducto: On-camera filtering for resource-efficient real-time video analytics. In: Proc. of ACM SIGCOMM, pp 359–376"); Ahuja et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR1 "Ahuja K, Jiang Y, Goel M et al (2021) Vid2doppler: Synthesizing doppler radar data from videos for training privacy-preserving activity recognition. In: Proc. of CHI, pp 1–10")). Instead of relying on either sensor’s limited view, combining modalities enables more comprehensive environmental understanding. From a technical view, this fusion allows for enhanced bounding box refinement (via camera) and motion tracking (via radar). For instance, radar-based velocity estimates can guide proposal generation, while camera data helps refine semantic classification, which has contributed to their widespread adoption in autonomous driving. As shown in Fig. [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#Fig4), we provide a typical radar-camera fusion framework. First, a deep learning model is used to extract object features from radar and camera frames, obtaining information such as object semantics, location, and index. Based on this, the data of the two modalities are aligned to facilitate the fusion of subsequent modules. Second, the features extracted from the radar and camera are concatenated and fused to obtain the final detection results, which can be used for various downstream tasks.

In summary, radar and camera provide mutually reinforcing information: radar supplies reliable measurements of range and velocity, while camera vision enriches perception with semantic and textural detail. This makes their fusion particularly effective for robust autonomous driving perception. Even if one of the sensors fails, the other sensor can continue to operate to ensure the safe operation of the autonomous driving system. Meanwhile, low-cost sensors can also reduce R&D costs and market prices, ultimately benefiting users, particularly those in low and middle-income countries. Therefore, it is necessary to fuse radar and camera for object detection for autonomous driving.

### 2.3 Object detection

The object detection task entails detecting a specific object within an image or a point cloud, pinpointing its position, and classifying its category. Typically, researchers employ a rectangular or cubic bounding box to encapsulate the identified object. For objects marked by rectangular bounding boxes, they are generally representations of 2D sensing data (e.g., camera). Due to the absence of depth information in 2D object detection, the rectangular bounding box is denoted as (_x_, _y_, _h_, _w_, _C_), where (_x_, _y_) represents the 2D box’s center, _h_ and _w_ represent the box’s height and width, respectively, and _C_ represents the category of objects. In contrast, the cube bounding box primarily corresponds to 3D sensing data (e.g., radar), and the detection outcomes are articulated as (_x_, _y_, _z_, _h_, _w_, _l_, \(\alpha \), _C_), where (_x_, _y_, z) represents the 3D box’s center, _h_, _w_, _l_ represent the box’s height, width, and length, respectively, \(\alpha \) represents the orientation of objects.

Object detection is extensively employed in autonomous driving to detect vehicles, pedestrians, traffic signs, and other objects in the surrounding environment (Zhou et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR215 "Zhou D, Fang J, Song X et al (2020) Joint 3d instance segmentation and object detection for autonomous driving. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 1839–1849"); Wu et al. [2023a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR179 "Wu H, Wen C, Li W et al (2023a) Transformation-equivariant 3d object detection for autonomous driving. In: Proc. of AAAI, pp 2795–2802"); Chen et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR21 "Chen L, Lin S, Lu X et al (2021) Deep neural network based vehicle and pedestrian detection for autonomous driving: a survey. IEEE TITS 22(6):3234–3246"); Boukerche and Hou [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR10 "Boukerche A, Hou Z (2021) Object detection using deep learning methods in traffic scenarios. ACM CSUR 54(2):1–35"); Gray et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR56 "Gray N, Moraes M, Bian J et al (2023) Glare: A dataset for traffic sign detection in sun glare. IEEE TITS")). Given the classification of bounding boxes outlined above, we will summarize the relevant algorithms for different sensing modalities.

*   _1) Camera-only Algorithms_. Depending on the training paradigm, camera-only detection algorithms can be categorized into two-stage and one-stage. Two-stage algorithms segment the object detection task into two phases: (i) employing region proposal network (RPN) to produce candidate region proposals for each object, and (ii) refining these proposals to determine the object’s classification and precise position. The more representative algorithms are R-CNN (Girshick et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR52 "Girshick R, Donahue J, Darrell T et al. (2014) Rich feature hierarchies for accurate object detection and semantic segmentation. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 580–587")), Fast R-CNN (Girshick [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR51 "Girshick R (2015) Fast r-cnn. In: Proc. of IEEE ICCV, pp 1440–1448")), Faster R-CNN (Ren et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR143 "Ren S, He K, Girshick R et al (2015) Faster r-cnn: Towards real-time object detection with region proposal networks. Proc of NIPS 28")), SPPNet (He et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR60 "He K, Zhang X, Ren S et al (2015) Spatial pyramid pooling in deep convolutional networks for visual recognition. IEEE TPAMI 37(9):1904–1916")), and FPN (Lin et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR97 "Lin TY, Dollár P, Girshick R et al (2017) Feature pyramid networks for object detection. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 2117–2125")). Experimental results demonstrate that these algorithms exhibit remarkably low precision and recall rates. However, their detection speed is sluggish, rendering them unsuitable for real-time detection scenes (e.g., autonomous driving). In contrast, One-stage algorithms do not have RPN and directly predict bounding boxes for objects along with the probabilities of classifications within these boxes. Consequently, one-stage algorithms typically exhibit faster detection speeds, but they may have lower precision and recall rates compared to two-stage algorithms. The more representative algorithms are YOLO series models (Redmon and Farhadi [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR142 "Redmon J, Farhadi A (2018) Yolov3: An incremental improvement. 
                  arXiv:1804.02767
                  
                "); Bochkovskiy et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR9 "Bochkovskiy A, Wang CY, Liao HYM (2020) Yolov4: Optimal speed and accuracy of object detection. 
                  arXiv:2004.10934
                  
                "); Glenn et al. [2022a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR53 "Glenn J, Alex S, Jirka Borovec ea (2022a) ultralytics/yolov5. 
                  https://github.com/ultralytics/yolov5
                  
                "); Li et al. [2022a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR83 "Li C, Li L, Jiang H et al (2022a) Yolov6: A single-stage object detection framework for industrial applications. 
                  arXiv:2209.02976
                  
                "); Wang et al. [2023a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR162 "Wang CY, Bochkovskiy A, Liao HYM (2023a) Yolov7: Trainable bag-of-freebies sets new state-of-the-art for real-time object detectors. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 7464–7475"); Glenn et al. [2022b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR54 "Glenn J, Chaurasia A, Laughing ea (2022b) Yolo by ultralytics. 
                  https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics
                  
                ")), and SSD (Liu et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR104 "Liu W, Anguelov D, Erhan D et al (2016) Ssd: Single shot multibox detector. In: Proc. of Springer ECCV, pp 21–37")). Moreover, with the advancement of technology, both two-stage and one-stage detectors are poised to enhance detection outcomes by refining them at predefined anchors. Nevertheless, this anchor-based detectors are constrained by factors, such as anchor size, number, and aspect ratio. Therefore, some works (Zhang et al. [2021b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR207 "Zhang H, Wang Y, Dayoub F et al (2021b) Varifocalnet: An iou-aware dense object detector. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 8514–8523"); Duan et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR40 "Duan K, Bai S, Xie L et al (2023) Centernet++ for object detection. IEEE TPAMI")) have introduced anchor-free detectors to enable networks to autonomously learn the position and shape of anchors, thus circumventing the limitations associated with predefined anchors. Anchor-free object detectors can be categorized into two main types: (i) dense prediction, which involves densely predicting the position relative to the anchor. Examples include Varifocalnet (Zhang et al. [2021b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR207 "Zhang H, Wang Y, Dayoub F et al (2021b) Varifocalnet: An iou-aware dense object detector. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 8514–8523")), Hrformer (Yuan et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR202 "Yuan Y, Fu R, Huang L et al (2021) Hrformer: High-resolution transformer for dense prediction. 
                  arXiv:2110.09408
                  
                ")), NAS-FCOS (Wang et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR166 "Wang N, Gao Y, Chen H et al (2020) Nas-fcos: Fast neural architecture search for object detection. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 11943–11951")), Tiny FCOS (Xu et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR193 "Xu X, Liang W, Zhao J et al (2021) Tiny fcos: A lightweight anchor-free object detection algorithm for mobile scenarios. MOBILE NETW APPL pp 1–11")), and Align-DETR (Cai et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR13 "Cai Z, Liu S, Wang G et al (2023) Align-detr: Improving detr with simple iou-aware bce loss. 
                  arXiv:2304.07527
                  
                "); ii) key point detection, which focuses on detecting key points of objects. Examples include Objectbox (Zand et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR204 "Zand M, Etemad A, Greenspan M (2022) Objectbox: From centers to boxes for anchor-free object detection. In: Proc. of Springer ECCV, pp 390–406")), Cornernet-lite (Law et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR81 "Law H, Teng Y, Russakovsky O et al (2019) Cornernet-lite: Efficient keypoint based object detection. 
                  arXiv:1904.08900

IEEE TPAMI")), RepPoints (Yang et al. [2023c](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR170 "Wang Y, Du H, Cheng Z et al (2023c) Krrnet: Keypoint relational regression network for bottom-up anchor-free object detection. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR16 "Carion N, Massa F, Synnaeve G et al (2020) End-to-end object detection with transformers. In: Proc. of Springer ECCV, pp 213–229")), Vivit (Arnab et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR3 "Arnab A, Dehghani M, Heigold G et al (2021) Vivit: A video vision transformer. In: Proc. of IEEE ICCV, pp 6836–6846")), and Trackformer (Meinhardt et al. In: Proc. of IEEE CVPR, pp 8844–8854")). In addition, some recent works have merged convolutional neural networks (CNN) with Transformer to leverage their respective advantages for object detection. Representative algorithms include EdgeVit (Pan et al. *   _2) Radar-only Algorithms._ The active sensing capabilities of radar have rendered it a staple in autonomous driving applications. Distinguishing itself from camera data, radar data is employed in object detection within existing works, predominantly utilizing two data formats: spectrum data and 3D point clouds (Yang et al. [2020b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-025-00302-0#ref-CR196 "Yang X, Liu J, Chen Y et al (2020b) Mu-id: Multi-user identification through gaits using millimeter wave radios. In: Proc. of IEEE INFOCOM, pp 2589–2598"); Zhang et al. IEEE COMST")). Spectral data, akin to an image, encompasses both Doppler and range information. Camera-based algorithms discussed earlier can be modified to accommodate this data type. Nonetheless, spectral data solely represents the 2D information of objects and falls short in adequately supporting autonomous driving tasks. In contrast, 3D point clouds are preferred by researchers due to their ability to encapsulate essential information, such as distance, velocity, and reflection intensity of objects. However, this disparity in data types may render the aforementioned image-based algorithms potentially ineffective. Therefore, some works have been proposed specifically to apply the characteristics of point clouds for object detection, i.e., 3D object detection. Some representative algorithms are RDOGMOD (Diehl et al. IEEE TIV")), and GTR-Net (Meyer et al. This is a Springer Nature open-access review paper titled "Advances in object detection for autonomous driving using mmwave radar and camera: A comprehensive survey," published on November 20, 2025, in the Journal of King Saud University Computer and Information Sciences (Volume 37, Article 328). The paper provides a comprehensive survey of radar-camera fusion for object detection in autonomous driving, covering the period from 2019 to 2025. Key authors include Kaikai Deng, Ling Xing, Honghai Wu, Huahong Ma, Yue Ling, and Jianping Gao.

**Main Contributions:**
1. First comprehensive study focused specifically on radar-camera fusion for object detection in autonomous driving.
2. Detailed explanation of radar and camera sensor characteristics, principles, data processing methods, and representations.
3. Analysis of evaluation metrics for object detection in a group-independent form, with a summary of existing radar-camera fusion datasets.
4. Comprehensive review of key issues in radar-camera fusion across five hierarchies: why, what, where, when, and how to fuse.
5. Discussion of challenges and emerging research directions regarding robustness, accuracy, and real-time performance.

**Key Technical Points:**
- Road accidents cause ~1.19 million deaths annually worldwide (WHO 2023).
- Three mainstream sensors compared: Camera (rich texture info, low cost, poor in adverse weather), LiDAR (good 3D, expensive, sensitive to weather), Radar (all-weather, good range/velocity, low resolution, sparse data).
- Radar offers advantages: anti-adverse-weather ability, comparable field-of-view to LiDAR, lower computational overhead, and lower cost.
- Radar limitations: low angular resolution, data sparsity, weak sensing against static objects.
- FMCW radar can achieve range resolution up to 3.75 cm with 4 GHz bandwidth.
- Object detection categorized into camera-only algorithms (two-stage like R-CNN/Faster R-CNN, one-stage like YOLO/SSD, anchor-free, and attention-based methods) and radar-only algorithms (using spectrum data or 3D point clouds).
- 4D radar is emerging with antennas arranged horizontally and vertically to measure elevation information.
- The paper identifies insufficient radar-camera fusion datasets, poor transferability of LiDAR models to radar, and radar data quality issues as key challenges.
