5 EXPERIMENTS 5.1 Testbeds 5.1.1 VICON System. In this paper, we use the VICON motion capture system [1] to generate ground truth 3D human pose for model training. The VICON system is shown in Figure 5(c), and it consists of 21 VICON Vantage cameras which emit and receive in-frared light. During the pose data collection, 27 high precision pearl markers are placed on each subject to represent the joint points of the subject. Figure 5(a) shows the positions of these markers on the subject. Since these markers are covered with highly reflective materials, the infrared light reflected from the marker surface can be easily captured by the the VICON Vantage camera. The errors cause by the location of each marker is less than 2𝑚𝑚[25]. The sampling rate of the system is 10 frames per second.
5.1.2 mmWave Testbed. The millimeter-wave radar we used in this paper is TI AWR1843BOOST, which is a commercial and portable (8.3𝑐𝑚× 6.4𝑐𝑚, 30𝑔) mmWave device produced by TI [13]. We also utilize TI DCA1000EVM to enable real-time data capture and stream-ing from mmWave radar, as shown in Figure 5(b). The mmWave device contains 3 transmitting antennas and 4 receiving antennas.
The 3 transmitting antennas emit FMCW wave chirps in turns. The emitted RF singal will be reflected by the human body and the surroundings, then received by the 4 receiving antennas. For each FMCW chirp, the frequency of RF will increase from 77 GHz to 80.9 GHz. The mmWave device is set to send 10 frames per second. Here each frame is composed of 128 chirps, and each chirp is composed of 256 sampling points. Based on our device setting, the maximum sensing range of the mmWave device is about 11 m, the range res-olution is about 4.3 cm, the maximum sensing velocity is about 4.5 m/s, and the velocity resolution is about 7.1 cm/s. To enable a real-time system, a UDP-based program is developed to collect packets from the device and parse the packets into the mmWave data frame. In the experiment, we place the mmWave testbed on a table (the height is about 92 cm), and the distance between the mmWave testbed and the activity area is about 1.5 m.
5.2 Data Collection and Preprocessing 5.2.1 Data Collection. In the experiment, 20 volunteers (includ-ing 13 males and 7 females) are asked to perform 8 daily activities within the activity area. The 8 activities include: (1) torso rotations; (2) clockwise walking; (3) counter-clockwise walking; (4) arm swing (the subject can randomly swing his/her arms horizontally or up-ward or downward); (5) walking back and forth; (6) walking back 274 mmMesh: Towards 3D Real-Time Dynamic Human Mesh Construction Using Millimeter-Wave MobiSys ’21, June 24–July 2, 2021, Virtual, WI, USA Figure 5: Testbeds and the basic scenario of mesh construction and forth with arm swing; (7) walking in the place; (8) lunges (the subject keeps performing lunge pose alternatively use his/her left and right leg). For each activity, the subject keeps performing it for 5 minutes (i.e., 3000 frames per activity per subject).
5.2.2 Ground Truth Mesh Construction. In our experiment, we use SMPL model to generate the ground truth human mesh to train our proposed deep learning model. Specifically, we take the pose information, shape information, translation information, and gender information of the subjects as the input of SMPL model.
The pose information and translation information can be ob-tained from the VICON system as described in Section 5.1.1. Note that the pose representations obtained from the VICON system are the absolute positions of the joints. As shown in Figure5(a), the location of each joint is obtained by averaging the locations of the two markers that are nearest to the joint (the two markers are in the front and the back of the human body, respectively). Since the pose representations are the rotation vectors of the joints, we then calculate the rotations on the joints using the absolute positions obtained from the VICON system. It is notable that the joints from VICON system and the input pose vectors of SMPL model are not one-to-one mapping, the SMPL model has more pose vectors than the joints from VICON system. Since the missing joints have little effect on the designed daily activities, we simply set those rotation vectors with constant values.
For the shape information, we use the approach in [5] to obtain the ground truth shape vector for each subject in a canonical pose.
To best match the human mesh model with the ground truth height of the subject, we also manually adjust the shape vector values.
5.2.3 Point Cloud Generation. After obtaining the frames of the mmWave data, we first calculate the Range-FFT and Doppler-FFT.
Then a static clutter removal algorithm is used to remove the static background noise. The algorithm subtracts the average value of the Doppler-FFT heatmaps from all receiving antennas, which is helpful to reduce the energy reflected from static ambient objects.
Traditionally, CA-CFAR [8] algorithm is usually applied on the Doppler-FFT heatmap to select prominent pixels as potential 3D points using fixed threshold. However, in our work, we directly use the Doppler-FFT heatmap pixels with the highest values as the potential 3D points. The main reason is that the heatmap energy differs from frame to frame. Using the fixed threshold will result in the number of selected points varying largely in different frames.
For example, if we use the fixed threshold, one frame may have a hundred of selected points while another frame may have only several or even zero selected points. This effect will be severe when the testing environment changes. Especially when we conduct experiment in occlude scenarios as described in Section 5.5.4, the energy distribution changes largely when the signal from the device is occluded by objects. Though we can manually set the threshold for each environment, we choose to select 128 heatmap pixels with the highest values for each frame to generate consistent numbers of point clouds among different frames and various environments. The noisy points generated by the multi-path effect is also alleviated in this step, since the signal that has been reflected several times tends to have lower energy value than the directly reflected signal.
Then, we calculate the 3D coordinates of the points based on the the selected pixels. Finally, we take the x-y-z coordinates, the range value, the velocity value, and the Doppler-FFT value of the point as the input feature vector of each 3D point to feed to the deep learning model.
5.3 Model Setting and Model Training In this section, we describe the setting of the deep learning model.
In Base Module, we use 3 layers of shared MLPs and the sizes of the layers are 8, 16, and 24, respectively. In Global Module, we also use 3 layers of shared MLPs and the sizes of the layers are 32, 48, and 64, respectively. The LSTM in Global Module has 3 layers and the size of each layer is 64. In Anchor Points Module, we use 81 anchor points which construct a 3 × 3 × 9 3D cubic lattice. The distance between a pair of neighboring anchor points is set to 0.3 m. The 275 MobiSys ’21, June 24–July 2, 2021, Virtual, WI, USA H. Xue et al.
number of grouped points around each anchor point is set to 8. The size of the shared MLPs in Anchor Points Module is the same as that in Global Module. We use 3 layers of 3D CNN to aggregate the featueres of anchor points into a vector with size 64. Similarly, there are 3 layers of LSTM in Anchor Point Module whose sizes are all set to 64. The FC has 2 layers in SMPL Module, which maps the concatenated vectors into a parameter vector with size 158.
During model training, we use the first 2400 frames (i.e., 80% of the data) of all subjects’ activities for training, and the remaining 600 frames (i.e., 20% of the data) for testing. The learning rate is set to 0.001. The batch size is 32. The sequence length for training is 64. The number of training batches is 500 K. The weights assigned to different losses in Eq. (3) are set to 𝛼𝑉= 0.001, 𝛼𝐵= 0.1, and 𝛼𝑆= 𝛼𝛿= 𝛼𝐺= 1.0. Note that the ground truth gender is used to select the mesh model in the SMPL Module during the training.
However, during testing, we only use the predicted gender to select the mesh model. We use PyTorch to implement our deep learning model, and TITAN V is used to train the model.
5.4 Baselines and Metrics 5.4.1 Baselines. Since there is no existing model to reconstruct dynamic human mesh from point clouds, we design the baselines by removing or replacing the modules in the architecture of the proposed model as following: B+G+S (Baseline A). In this baseline, the Anchor Point Module is removed. We inherit the Base Module, the Global Module, and the SMPL Module from the proposed mmMesh model without any change.
B+G-Max+S (Baseline B). This model shares the same structure with Baseline A except that the attention-based grouping is replaced with max-pooling operation in Global Module.
B+G+FPS-ATTN+S (Baseline C). In this baseline, besides inher-iting the Base Module, Global Module, and SMPL Module from the proposed mmMesh model as in Baseline A, we use FPS-based sampling [28] and aggregate the features of grouped points using attention mechanism.
B+G+FPS-Max+S (Baseline D). This model is very similar to Base-line C except that we replace attention-based aggregation method with the max-pooling operation. For this baseline, the model design to learn the local structure is the same as that of PointNet++ [28] which utilizes the FPS-based sampling and max-pooling operation based aggregation method.
5.4.2 Metrics. We use the the following metrics to evaluate the performance of our proposed framework: Average Vertex Error (V) [6, 48]. We compute the average vertex error by averaging the Euclidean distance between the vertices lo-cated on the predicted human mesh and the corresponding vertices on the ground truth mesh for all the subjects and activities. This metric can evaluate the overall performances of the location error, pose error, shape error, and gender error.
Average Joint Localization Error (S) [16, 48]. This metric is de-fined as the average Euclidean distance between the joint locations of the predicted human mesh and the ground truths for all the subjects and activities.
Average Joint Rotation Error (Q). Besides the joint position, joint rotation is also critical when generating the pose. This metric is reported as an additional metric to evaluate the accuracy of the constructed pose. It is defined as the average differences between predicted joint rotations and the ground truth rotations. As de-scribed in Section 5.2.3, some joint rotations in SMPL model are set to constant values. There is no need to take these joints into consideration. Thus, when calculating the average joint rotation error, we only consider the rotations of shoulder joints, elbow joints, hip joints, and the knee joints from both sides of the subject.
Mesh Localization Error (T). We also use mesh localization error to assess the precision of subject localization. This metric is defined as the average Euclidean distance between the root joint location of the predicted human mesh skeleton and the ground truths for all the subjects and activities.
Gender Prediction Accuracy (G). We also calculate the accuracy of the predicted gender to evaluate if the proposed model can dis-tinguish gender of the subject.
5.5 Experiment Results 5.5.1 Qualitative Results for Basic Scenario. We first qualitatively evaluate the proposed framework in the basic scenario that is shown in Figure 5(c). The setting of the training phase for the basic sce-nario is described in Section 5.3. The qualitative results are shown in Figure 6, in which rows (a)-(c) show 3 male subjects conduct-ing activities 8, 5, and 4, respectively. Rows (d)-(f) show 3 female subjects conducting activities 1, 6, and 7, respectively. As we can see, the six subjects in this figure have different shapes. The first picture in each row shows the video frame when the subject con-ducting the activity. The second picture and the third picture show the corresponding ground truth human mesh generated by the VI-CON system and the predicted human mesh based on our proposed mmMesh model, respectively. The results show that our generated meshes look realistic. From this figure, we can see the shapes of the generated human meshes are very similar to the corresponding subjects in the video frames. In addition, our model can predict the correct gender of each subject, which demonstrates that our model is able to correctly sense the gender information of the subjects and generate the human meshes with reasonable shapes, even if the subjects in our experiment have different heights and shapes. The results in this figure also show that our proposed mmMesh model can accurately estimate the human poses. This demonstrates that our model is able to capture the subtle body structure information from the local structure of the point cloud.
The rows (g)-(l) in Figure 6 show the consecutive frames that one subject is conducting clockwise walking (activity 2) within the activity area. The first, second, and third columns show the video frames, ground truth meshes, and the human meshes generated by our model, respectively. To better show the activity process, we pick every other frame in the video (i.e., the time gap between each pair of consecutive frames is 0.2𝑠). We can see that the constructed mesh in consecutive frames looks not only very similar to the ground truth meshes, but also very smooth. This is achieved by taking advantage of LSTM layers in our model, which encodes the temporal information in the network. This result proves that our model can generate smooth dynamic human meshes.

The results are shown in Table 1. As can be seen, for all five metrics utilized in this paper, our proposed mmMesh model achieves the best results.
This demonstrates that our model is able to generate more accurate poses, shapes, genders and translations of the subjects than all the baselines.
To study the difference between the attention-based aggrega-tion method and the max-pooling-based aggregation method, we compare the performance of baselines A and B as well as that of baseline C and D. Baseline A and baseline B share the same structure except that baseline A uses attention mechanism while baseline B uses max-pooling operation. args.summary:
mmMesh is a system presented at MobiSys '21 that constructs real-time 3D dynamic human meshes using commercial portable millimeter-wave devices (TI AWR1843BOOST radar). The system uses a deep learning framework that processes sparse 3D point clouds generated from mmWave signals reflected off the human body. Key challenges addressed include: (1) sparsity of point clouds (only dozens of human body points per frame), solved by encoding the SMPL parametric human model which uses only 86 parameters to represent a full mesh; (2) accurately aligning 3D points with body segments despite ambient noise and multipath effects, addressed through attention mechanisms, dynamic anchor point grouping, and local structure learning; (3) missing body parts due to RF signal specularity, solved using LSTM to leverage temporal information from previous frames.

The system was evaluated with 20 volunteers (13 male, 7 female) performing 8 daily activities. Using a VICON motion capture system for ground truth, mmMesh achieved an average vertex error of 2.47 cm, average joint localization error of 2.18 cm, average joint rotation error of 3.80°, mesh localization error of 1.27 cm, and 99.8% gender prediction accuracy. The system outperformed all baselines (which removed or replaced modules like anchor points, attention mechanisms, and LSTM components). The model also demonstrated robustness across different training rates and occluded scenarios.

# Abstract

| In this paper, we present mmMesh, the first real-time 3D human mesh estimation system using commercial portable millimeterwave devices. mmMesh is built upon a novel deep learning framework that can dynamically locate the moving subject and capture his/her body shape and pose by analyzing the 3D point cloud generated from the mmWave signals that bounce off the human body. The proposed deep learning framework addresses a series of challenges. First, it encodes a 3D human body model, which enables mmMesh to estimate complex and realistic-looking 3D human meshes from sparse point clouds. Second, it can accurately align the 3D points with their corresponding body segments despite the influence of ambient points as well as the error-prone nature and the multi-path effect of the RF signals. Third, the proposed model can infer missing body parts from the information of the previous frames. Our evaluation results on a commercial mmWave sensing testbed show that our mmMesh system can accurately localize the vertices on the human mesh with an average error of 2.47 cm. The superior experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed human mesh construction system. |

# M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction

###### Abstract

Human mesh reconstruction (HMR) provides direct insights into body-environment interaction, which enables various immersive applications. While existing large-scale HMR datasets rely heavily on line-of-sight RGB input, vision-based sensing is limited by occlusion, lighting variation, and privacy concerns. To overcome these limitations, recent efforts have explored radio-frequency (RF) mmWave radar for privacy-preserving indoor human sensing. However, current radar datasets are constrained by sparse skeleton labels, limited scale, and simple in-place actions. To advance the HMR research community, we introduce M4Human, the current largest-scale (661K-frame) (9×9\times prior largest) multimodal benchmark, featuring high-resolution mmWave radar, RGB, and depth data. M4Human provides both raw radar tensors (RT) and processed radar point clouds (RPC) to enable research across different levels of RF signal granularity. M4Human includes high-quality motion capture (MoCap) annotations with 3D meshes and global trajectories, and spans 20 subjects and 50 diverse actions, including in-place, sit-in-place, and free-space sports or rehabilitation movements. We establish benchmarks on both RT and RPC modalities, as well as multimodal fusion with RGB-D modalities. Extensive results highlight the significance of M4Human for radar-based human modeling while revealing persistent challenges under fast, unconstrained motion. The dataset and code will be released after the paper publication.11
1
[Project page](https://fanjunqiao.github.io/M4Human-site/)

## 1 Introduction

Perceiving 3D human motion is essential for human-centric Physical AI systems to understand users’ behavior and respond to their needs. A key enabler is markerless 3D human pose and shape regression, a core human sensing task that supports many applications such as human-robot interaction, rehabilitation, healthcare monitoring, surveillance, and VR/AR [Stenum et al. 2021](#bib.bib38); [Avogaro et al. 2023](#bib.bib6). Classic human pose estimation (HPE) represents the human body as a graph of keypoints and infers their 3D locations [Zheng et al. 2023](#bib.bib51). Moving beyond sparse landmarks, human mesh reconstruction (HMR) estimates both pose and shape of the human body as a dense surface mesh that can be used to model human-environment contact, enabling advanced applications such as VR fitness gaming, virtual try-on, avatar creation, and computer-assisted coaching [Liu et al. 2024](#bib.bib29); [Tian et al. 2023](#bib.bib39). However, current HMR systems are predominantly built on Line-of-Sight (LoS) camera (e.g., RGB and depth) and trained on large-scale video datasets (e.g., Human3.6M [Ionescu et al. 2013](#bib.bib22), 3DPW [Von Marcard et al. 2018](#bib.bib40)). This raise two practical issues: (i) visual data exposes personal appearance, often inaccessible for privacy-sensitive scenarios, such as children and elderly care, and public sharing is frequently restricted [Morgan et al. 2023](#bib.bib31); (ii) LoS cameras are usually vulnerable to adverse illumination like low-lighting and strong sunlight, and susceptible to occlusion, such as thick clothing or smoke [Chen et al. 2022](#bib.bib7); [Ding et al. 2025](#bib.bib11).

There is a growing interest in millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar-based human sensing, positioning it as a complement, or even an alternative to vision-based systems [Zhang et al. 2023](#bib.bib46). As a radio-frequency (RF) sensor, mmWave radar actively emits radio waves to sense human targets and analyzes the returned echoes to recover spatial information (range and angle) [Rao 2017](#bib.bib34). This sensing principle enables deployment in complex real-world conditions, with robustness to variable illumination and occlusion, while preserving user privacy and facilitating data distribution. Moreover, mmWave radar operates in a higher-frequency band (e.g., 77GHz), offering higher spatial resolution than other RF sensors (e.g., Wi-Fi), making it well-suited for HMR that demands fine-grained data.

Despite these advantages, existing large-scale HMR datasets/benchmarks remain largely RGB image-centric, with mmWave-based approaches rarely explored. As summarized in Tab. [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction"), most existing mmWave radar-based human sensing datasets [An and Ogras 2021](#bib.bib3); [An et al. 2022](#bib.bib5); [Yang et al. 2023](#bib.bib44); [Zhao et al. 2018](#bib.bib48); [Rahman et al. 2024](#bib.bib33); [Ho et al. 2024](#bib.bib20) are oriented for coarse-grained HPE and provide only sparse skeleton annotations. These labels are typically derived from RGB(D) cameras via existing pose estimators or multi-view optimization and thus inevitably noisy, introducing ground-truth (GT) bias that hinders high-fidelity sensing. Two RF-based HMR datasets have recently been released [Xue et al. 2021](#bib.bib43); [Chen et al. 2022](#bib.bib7), but they remain limited in scale and focus primarily on simple, in-place daily activities, constraining their application to dynamic and diverse scenarios. In terms of the modality, most datasets rely on low-resolution Texas Instruments (TI) radars that output only very sparse radar point clouds (RPC) [Fuhrmann et al. 1992](#bib.bib17), discarding much valuable signal information. While recent efforts [Rahman et al. 2024](#bib.bib33); [Ho et al. 2024](#bib.bib20) have begun to explore raw radar tensors (RT) to preserve more contextual information, they remain centered on coarse-level HPE and do not support fine-grained HMR.

To bridge this gap, we introduce M4Human, the largest-scale multimodal dataset that supports high-fidelity RF-based HMR. It comprises 999 sequences and 661K (>>15h) synchronized samples across RGB and depth images plus multi-level radar data—raw tensors (RT) and point clouds (RPC)—captured by a high-resolution Vayyar mmWave radar tailored to human sensing. M4Human includes high-quality marker-based motion capture (MoCap) annotations to provide 3D HMR GT, along with an abundant set of meticulously designed daily, rehabilitation, and sports activities. To the best of our knowledge, M4Human is the first and largest benchmark (about 9×9\times larger than the prior largest mmBody [Chen et al. 2022](#bib.bib7)) to enable mmWave tensor–based HMR across diverse, dynamic, and unconstrained indoor scenarios. Its key features and contributions are summarized as follows:

Complementary Sensing Modalities. M4Human contributes to multimodal human sensing by combining complementary sensing modalities, including line-of-sight (LoS) cameras and radio-frequency (RF) mmWave radar. It provides four synchronized modalities: RGB frames, depth frames, raw radar tensors (RT), and radar point clouds (RPC). The inclusion of both raw and processed radar data supports research at different levels of RF signal processing and understanding.

High-Fidelity Motion Annotations. The dataset includes marker-based motion capture (MoCap) annotations to support high-quality GT annotation, including 3D human mesh, human dense pose, 2D/3D skeleton keypoints, full-body position tracking under dynamic free-space sport activities, and abundant action categories.

Diverse Action Sets. M4Human includes 50 categories of human actions, spanning in-place daily activities, clinically guided rehabilitation exercises, and non-in-place sports motions. This diversity supports applications in smart home, healthcare research (e.g., evaluation and rehabilitation of neurological or physical impairments), and human–computer interaction (e.g., virtual fitness gaming).

Wide Human Sensing Tasks.
The high-quality motion annotations in M4Human enable novel tasks such as simultaneous human tracking and mesh reconstruction under free-space and complex sports motions. The rich data modalities further support multi-modal fusion and cross-modal supervision for RF-based human sensing. M4Human also supports critical research problems, including HMR using different radar modalities, and generalization across unseen subjects and action categories.

Extensive Benchmarks. To support and evaluate radar-based HMR, M4Human benchmarks state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods on both raw radar tensors (RT) and radar point clouds (RPC). We further compare with RGB-D modalities and evaluate the fusion of radar and visual RGB-D data for enhanced mesh reconstruction. We analyze model performance under varying dataset scales, highlighting the importance of large-scale datasets. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of radar-based HMR in supporting downstream human activity recognition.

## 2 Related Works

mmWave-based Human Sensing.
RGB cameras are ubiquitous for human sensing tasks (e.g., HMR [Kocabas et al. 2020](#bib.bib25); [Dwivedi et al. 2024](#bib.bib13)), but raise privacy concerns in sensitive settings and degrade under occlusion and poor lighting [Chen et al. 2023](#bib.bib8). As reported in [Chen et al. 2022](#bib.bib7), camera-based methods suffer remarkable error increases: depth (rain 56.4%, smoke 336%), RGB (dark 42.8%, smoke 16.2%) on HMR. Commercial mmWave radar has therefore emerged as a privacy-preserving and robust complement for indoor human sensing. Early radar-based works used low-resolution RPCs to tackle coarse-level motion tracking [Zhao et al. 2019](#bib.bib50); [Gu et al. 2019](#bib.bib19); [Cui and Dahnoun 2021](#bib.bib9); [Zhang et al. 2024](#bib.bib47), where human motion was reduced to a single-point trajectory and tracked using clustering and RNNs under simple walking scenarios. Subsequent studies targeted human action recognition for daily actions and HCI gestures [Singh et al. 2019](#bib.bib37); [Alam et al. 2021](#bib.bib2); [Liu et al. 2020](#bib.bib28); [Li et al. 2022](#bib.bib27). More recently, whole-body keypoint estimation from sparse RPCs has been explored via datasets and methods such as mRI, mm-Fi, and others [An and Ogras 2021](#bib.bib3); [An et al. 2022](#bib.bib5); [An and Ogras 2022](#bib.bib4); [Yang et al. 2023](#bib.bib44); [Sengupta et al. 2020](#bib.bib35); [Ding et al. 2024](#bib.bib10); [Fan et al. 2024](#bib.bib15). To alleviate the information loss during radar point cloud generation, RETR [Yataka et al. 2024](#bib.bib45), RT-Pose [Ho et al. 2024](#bib.bib20) and more [Rahman et al. 2024](#bib.bib33); [Wu et al. 2022](#bib.bib42); [Lee et al. 2023](#bib.bib26) operate directly on raw radar tensors for human pose estimation. A few recent works, such as mmBody [Chen et al. 2022](#bib.bib7) and mmMesh [Xue et al. 2021](#bib.bib43), investigate mesh reconstruction from RPCs, but they remain limited to daily actions and in data scale, which limits their application scope and generalizability.
To date, no works have explored RT-based HMR.

mmWave-based Human Pose Datasets.
The success of RGB-based HMR methods has been driven by large-scale image-based datasets (e.g., MPI-INF-3DHP [Mehta et al. 2017](#bib.bib30), Human3.6M [Ionescu et al. 2013](#bib.bib22), 3DPW [Von Marcard et al. 2018](#bib.bib40)), which provide high-quality 3D annotations from marker-based or markerless multi-view MoCap systems. In contrast, early mmWave HPE datasets [An and Ogras 2021](#bib.bib3); [Zhao et al. 2018](#bib.bib48) focus on simple in-place daily activities and provide only sparse RPC from low-resolution (LR) radars (e.g., 4 Tx/Rx channels, 4 GHz bandwidth; see Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")). mRI [An et al. 2022](#bib.bib5) and mm-Fi [Yang et al. 2023](#bib.bib44) expand to in-place rehabilitation movements but still rely on synchronized RGB to annotate 3D skeletons, which is inevitably noisy and hard to support high-fidelity human sensing. More recent datasets [Lee et al. 2023](#bib.bib26); [Wu et al. 2022](#bib.bib42), such as MMVR [Rahman et al. 2024](#bib.bib33), RT-Pose [Ho et al. 2024](#bib.bib20), explore raw radar tensors (RT) for coarse-grained HPE, often using cascaded LR radar chips or multi-view setups to boost spatial resolution at the cost of harder synchronization and calibration. For HMR, mmMesh [Xue et al. 2021](#bib.bib43) first reconstructs MoCap-annotated meshes from LR RPC, but its dataset is not publicly available. mmBody [Chen et al. 2022](#bib.bib7), employs a high-resolution automotive radar for indoor perception but lacks access to more informative RT data. Moreover, its RPC contains substantial background returns, leaving only a small fraction from the human foreground (c.f. Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Datasets ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")(a)). In addition, existing radar datasets remain limited in scale and largely restricted to simple, in-place actions, which constrains their utility for broader and more dynamic human activities (c.f. Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Datasets ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")(b)).

## 3 Datasets

Overview.
At the core of our contribution is M4Human, a large-scale multimodal dataset designed for fine-grained human mesh reconstruction (HMR). As illustrated in Fig. [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Datasets ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction"), we build a unified sensing platform that integrates a high-resolution mmWave radar, an RGB–D camera, and a Vicon MoCap system. During capture, subjects are instructed to perform a diverse set of actions while the RGB-D camera and radar record synchronized multimodal data, and the Vicon system captures precise 3D marker positions for accurate mesh annotations. Our dataset is characterized by (i) *diversity*: 661K frames across 999 sequences, involving 20 subjects and 50 meticulously designed action classes; (ii) *multimodality*: synchronized RGB, depth, radar point cloud (RPC), and raw radar tensor (RT) with precise cross-modal calibration; (iii) *high-quality annotation*: dense and time-aligned 3D meshes derived from marker-based Vicon capture with human-in-the-loop verification.

### 3.1 System Setup

We use an Intel RealSense D435 stereo depth camera [Intel RealSense 2023](#bib.bib21) that integrates an IR projector, an RGB camera, and a stereo IR pair to acquire synchronized RGB–D image frames. Raw resolution is up to 1280×\times720; for storage efficiency and faster I/O, we downsample to 640×\times480. mmWave data are captured using the commercial Vayyar vTrigB imaging mmWave radar [vay 2023](#bib.bib1). The device integrates a proprietary human-sensing mmWave Software on Chip (SoC) and outputs both raw radar tensors (RT) and processed radar point clouds (RPC). With 7 GHz bandwidth and a large 20 Tx/Rx antenna array, it provides markedly better range and angular resolution than common 3-4 Tx/Rx TI radars [Rao 2017](#bib.bib34). The mmWave radar and RGB–D camera are mounted on a 3D-printed bracket fixed to a tripod (c.f. Fig. [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Datasets ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction") (a)), connected to a unified recording PC. Subjects are recorded at distances of 0.5–6 m from the platform, within a motion area of approximately 6×5.5​m26\times 5.5\mathrm{m}^{2}, with multiple facing orientations for data diversity. A Vicon MoCap system is installed overhead, providing high-precision position measurements of 3D markers attached to anatomical keypoints during action execution.

### 3.2 Human-centric and Multi-level Radar Data

The Vayyar radar used in M4Human is tailored to fine-grained human sensing. To show its superior sensing ability, we define an effective RPC ratio metric as the fraction of points near humans relative to all points per frame (c.f. Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Datasets ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")(a)). M4Human attains a substantially higher effective RPC ratio than mmBody [Chen et al. 2022](#bib.bib7), which employed automotive radars designed for broad scene sensing rather than human targets, yielding much more background targets. With more human-concentrated returns, M4Human supports simultaneous global tracking and high-fidelity mesh reconstruction for diverse, non-in-place dynamic activities in open spaces. Furthermore, M4Human provides two complementary radar modalities: raw radar tensor (RT) and radar point cloud (RPC). RT is a 3D intensity volume obtained via FFT-based processing of time-domain signals across range, azimuth, and elevation axes, then mapped into Cartesian coordinates (X-Y-Z). RPC is derived from RT using CFAR [Fuhrmann et al. 1992](#bib.bib17), which retains only salient reflections above adaptive thresholds. As illustrated in Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Datasets ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")(c), CFAR removes sub-threshold structures and suppresses much of the spatial intensity context. Therefore, RT generally contains richer information than RPC. To support clearer interpretation and more comprehensive learning from mmWave signals, M4Human releases both RT and RPC modalities for public usage.

### 3.3 Calibration

For spatial calibration between the Vicon system and sensor platform, we affix six non-coplanar MoCap markers to a chair placed in the motion area (Fig. [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Datasets ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction") (b)). We record their 3D positions in the Vicon frame 𝐗iV\mathbf{X}\_{i}^{V} (i∈[1,..,6]i\in[1,..,6]) and manually annotate the corresponding 2D pixel locations 𝐱i\mathbf{x}\_{i} in the RGB image. With chessboard-calibrated camera intrinsics 𝐊∈ℝ3×3\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}, we solve a Perspective-nn-Point (PnP) problem [Fischler and Bolles 1981](#bib.bib16) to estimate the camera extrinsics (𝐑C←V,𝐭C←V)(\mathbf{R}\_{C\leftarrow V},\mathbf{t}\_{C\leftarrow V}), such that 𝐱i∼𝐊⁡(𝐑C←V​𝐗iV+𝐭C←V)\mathbf{x}\_{i}\sim\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{R}\_{C\leftarrow V}\mathbf{X}\_{i}^{V}+\mathbf{t}\_{C\leftarrow V}). We obtain the radar–camera extrinsic calibration (𝐑C←R,𝐭C←R)(\mathbf{R}\_{C\leftarrow R},\mathbf{t}\_{C\leftarrow R}) following a similar procedure but using radar-visible targets (e.g., corner reflectors) instead of MoCap markers. With both transformations, any 3D Vicon point 𝐏V\mathbf{P}^{V} can be first transformed into the camera frame as 𝐏C=𝐑C←V​𝐏V+𝐭C←V\mathbf{P}^{C}=\mathbf{R}\_{C\leftarrow V}\mathbf{P}^{V}+\mathbf{t}\_{C\leftarrow V}, and then to the radar frame via 𝐏R=𝐑C←R−1​(𝐏C−𝐭C←R)\mathbf{P}^{R}=\mathbf{R}\_{C\leftarrow R}^{-1}(\mathbf{P}^{C}-\mathbf{t}\_{C\leftarrow R}). This calibration process yields precise cross-modal alignment among the Vicon, RGB–D camera, and radar data.

### 3.4 Time Synchronization

In our setup, the Vicon system and the sensor board run on seperate PCs. Radar and RGB-D streams are polled alternately at 12Hz by the same PC, yielding well-aligned sensor frames. To synchronized with Vicon, subjects are instructed to perform a *trigger* gesture when recording starts: after a T-pose, they rapidly swing their head to the right (c.f. Fig. [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Datasets ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction") (c)). We detect the Vicon start frame as the first time the head-top marker’s displacement exceeds 10 cm, and we manually locate the corresponding RGB start frame and trim earlier radar/RGB–D frames accordingly. Because the Vicon stream has a higher frame rate (100Hz), each sensor frame is then temporally matched to its nearest Vicon frame.

### 3.5 Subjects and Actions

Subjects. M4Human dataset features a high diversity of human subjects, comprising 20 volunteers with varied heights (1.5–1.8m) and weights (45–90kg), balanced genders (12 male, 8 female), and heterogeneous ethnic backgrounds. This wide range of subject attributes ensures the dataset’s versatility and generaliability to a broad population. All participants have been informed that the data will be made publicly available for research purposes, and were instructed to wear caps and masks for de-identification.

Actions. M4Human meticulously curates 50 actions spanning three categories: (i) daily activities (e.g., waving, walking in a curve, sit-and-stand), targeting smart-home applications and human–computer interaction; (ii) rehabilitation exercises (e.g., upper limb extension, high knees) motivated by clinical practice to support routine training [Zhao and Krebs 2024](#bib.bib49) and recovery assessment [Kidziński et al. 2020](#bib.bib24) in healthcare applications; and (iii) non-in-place sports actions (e.g., basketball, badminton) that require substantial whole-body coordination, supporting dynamic motion analysis and VR/AR applications.

During capture, each subject performs all 50 actions, with at least 550 frames captured per action at 12 Hz. This led to a total of 999 valid sequences, ∼\sim661K valid synchronized multimodal frames, and ∼\sim15.3 hours of motion capture.

### 3.6 Body Mesh Annotation

We obtain high-precision human body mesh annotations via a three-stage pipeline. (i) *Marker-based capture*. We record human motion with a Vicon MoCap system that tracks the subject as a non-rigid body parameterized by 37 anatomically distributed markers (Fig. [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Datasets ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction") (d)). This yields accurate 3D whole-body trajectories and stable root motion, providing higher-fidelity labels than the purely image-based annotation approaches common in prior RF datasets. (ii) *Human-in-the-loop cleanup*. The automatically labeled Vicon sequences are inspected frame by frame to correct typical MoCap errors (marker swaps, short-term occlusions, missing markers), so that the final marker trajectories are temporally consistent, stable, and avoid drifting. (iii) *Mesh reconstruction and validation*. Cleaned marker trajectories are fed to SOMA [Ghorbani and Black 2021](#bib.bib18), a neural marker-to-body reconstructor, to estimate full-body pose, global trajectories, and SMPL-X-style meshes [Pavlakos et al. 2019](#bib.bib32). The reconstructed meshes and joints are then visualized together with the RGB-D and mmWave data to verify spatial-temporal alignment (Fig. [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Datasets ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction") (e)).

## 4 Benchmark and Evaluation

#### Overview.

M4Human enables a comprehensive benchmark across sensing modalities and tasks. We evaluate mmWave-based HMR with two radar representations, RPC and RT (Sec. [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Radar-based HMR Benchmark ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")); comparing radar- and image-based HMR to quantify each modality’s strengths and remaining gaps (Sec. [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Comparison to RGB(D)-based Methods ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")); and exploring modality fusion to show how mmWave radar benefits multimodal HMR (Sec. [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Multimodal Fusion ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")). Since no prior works have used RTs for HMR, we propose a simple baseline supporting the RT modality (Sec. [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 RT-Mesh: A Baseline for RT-based HMR ‣ 4 Benchmark and Evaluation ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")). We further demonstrate that the scale of M4Human improves the generalizability of radar-based HMR (Sec. [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 In Depth Analysis of Dataset Scale ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")), and that radar-predicted human meshes support downstream human action recognition (HAR) (Sec. [5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 Downstream HAR Benchmark ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")).

### 4.1 Benchmark Setup

Protocol. We define three evaluation protocols aligned with action groups to assess performance under varying difficulty levels. Protocol 1 (P1) covers 30 *in-place* daily and rehabilitation activities. Protocol 2 (P2) focuses on five *sit-in-place* daily and rehabilitation exercises. Protocol 3 (P3) comprises all *non-in-place* daily/sports activities, which are more challenging due to larger displacements and rapid motion. We also report results on the full set (ALL).

Split.
The dataset is divided into train/val/test with a ratio of 75:5:20, yielding ∼\sim496K/34K/132K samples. We evaluate under three split settings: (S1) Random, all clips are randomly assigned to non-overlapping subsets, modeling seen-subject and seen-action cases; (S2) Cross-Subject, no subject in training appears in testing (two males and two females), modeling unseen-subject generalization; (S3) Cross-Action, a *group-stratified* split with disjoint action classes; the test set includes 20% of classes sampled from each action group (i.e., in-place, sit-in-place, non-in-place), assessing unseen-action generalization.

Metrics.
We evaluate the mesh reconstruction performance using four classic metrics, all computed in the *world* frame without root/Procrustes alignment and reported in millimeters/degrees. Mean Vertex Error (MVE) is the average Euclidean distance between predicted and ground-truth SMPL-X vertices over all 10,475 vertices. Mean Joint Error (MJE/MPJPE) is the mean Euclidean distance between corresponding 3D joints using the 22-joint SMPL-X set. Mean Rotation Error (MRE) is the geodesic angular error on S​O​(3)SO(3) between predicted and ground-truth joint rotations, averaged across joints; it emphasizes pose and is invariant to global translation. Translation Error (TE) is the Euclidean distance between predicted and ground-truth global root translations.

### 4.2 RT-Mesh: A Baseline for RT-based HMR

Problem Formulation.
Following prior works [Yang et al. 2023](#bib.bib44); [An and Ogras 2022](#bib.bib4); [An et al. 2022](#bib.bib5), we allow a short temporal context of radar frames. We stack TT = 44 consecutive RTs, forming a 4D tensor XRT∈ℝT×X×Y×ZX\_{\text{RT}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times X\times Y\times Z}, where (X,Y,Z)=(121,111,31)(X,Y,Z)=(121,111,31) in our dataset. Given XRTX\_{\text{RT}}, our goal is to regress the SMPL-X parameters (α,β,τ,θ)(\alpha,\beta,\tau,\theta): root orientation (axis–angle) α∈ℝ3\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, body shape β∈ℝ10\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{10}, global translation τ∈ℝ3\tau\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, and body pose θ∈ℝ22×3\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{22\times 3}. We also regress gender probability g∈[0,1]g\in[0,1] to select the appropriate male/female SMPL-X template. Supervision for (α,β,τ,θ,g)(\alpha,\beta,\tau,\theta,g) comes from our MoCap-derived mesh annotations (Sec. [3.6](#S3.SS6 "3.6 Body Mesh Annotation ‣ 3 Datasets ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")).

Model Architecture. We propose RT-Mesh, the first HMR method that operates directly on RTs.
Compared with RPC, RT retains richer human return signals but at much higher volume, making full-volume 3D/4D convolutions computationally prohibitive. To improve the model efficiency with losing key context information, RT-Mesh is specifically designed as a two-stage structure (c.f. Fig. [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.5 Subjects and Actions ‣ 3 Datasets ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")): it first localizes the human foreground RoI amid clutter using a collapsed 2D BEV tensor, then operates on a local 3D RT crop to regress the final SMPL-X mesh parameters. Detailed architecture and training loss designs are provided in the supplementary.

### 4.3 Competing Methods

RGB(D) Modality.
For the RGB setting, we adopt the SOTA TokenHMR method [Dwivedi et al. 2024](#bib.bib13) and follow its practices: persons are first detected using Detectron2 [Wu et al. 2019](#bib.bib41) and cropped for local mesh recovery. To obtain the best performance, we initialize the model with its large-scale pretrained weights and fine-tune it on our dataset. For the depth setting, we back-project depth pixels to 3D point clouds and apply the point cloud-based HMR method P4Transformer [Fan et al. 2021](#bib.bib14).

mmWave Modality.
To comprehensively benchmark radar-based HMR, we include SOTA methods from existing mmWave HPE and HMR datasets for both RPC and RT modalities. For RPC-based methods, we select two representative HMR approaches: LSTM-based mmMesh [Xue et al. 2021](#bib.bib43) and transformer-based P4Transformer [Fan et al. 2021](#bib.bib14) applied in the mmBody [Chen et al. 2022](#bib.bib7) dataset. Since no existing HMR method is designed for RT, we adopt SOTA models from the latest RT-based HPE datasets: MMVR [Rahman et al. 2024](#bib.bib33) and RT-Pose [Ho et al. 2024](#bib.bib20). Specifically, RT-Pose [Ho et al. 2024](#bib.bib20) adapts HR-Net to radar, using a high-resolution 3D convolutional network as a backbone. RETR [Yataka et al. 2024](#bib.bib45) from MMVR extracts features from two complementary views—X-Y BEV and X-Z side view—and fuses them using a transformer-based architecture. We preserve the original RT feature extractors, replace their HPE heads with HMR heads, and retrain the models on our dataset.

## 5 Results and Discussion

### 5.1 Radar-based HMR Benchmark

Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Benchmark Setup ‣ 4 Benchmark and Evaluation ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction") compares radar-only HMR methods across two radar modalities, RPC and RT. Under the random split (S1), both modalities performs strongly: P4Trans. (RPC) [Chen et al. 2022](#bib.bib7) and RT-Mesh (RT) reach ∼\sim70mm MVE on In-Place actions and ∼\sim90mm overall, exceeding reported results on prior radar-based HMR/HPE datasets. This underscores the quality of our dataset and shows that high‑resolution mmWave radar alone can support accurate HMR in privacy‑sensitive or vision‑impaired scenarios. Our dataset poses additional challenges for another two protocols and split settings, and resulted in performance drop. P2 (Sit-In-Place) suffers from frequent self-occlusion and chair-induced multipath noise, while P3 (Non-In-Place) require jointly tracking and pose/mesh estimation under rapid, dynamic motion. S2 (Cross-subject) and S3 (Cross-action) settings also remain challenging, highlighting the need for better generaliability.

Comparing two radar representations, RT and RPC perform similarly on S1, but RT outperforms RPC on S2 and S3, indicating stronger generaliability. RT preserves denser, more continuous spatial evidence, whereas RPC is sparse and susceptible to missed detections of body parts (c.f. Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.1 Radar-based HMR Benchmark ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")). Especially for novel subjects and actions, these gaps can induce overfitting and yield twisted meshes. Moreover, our proposed RT-Mesh attains markedly higher efficiency than existing RPC- and RT-based methods, particularly those that process full-volume RT. It achieves 2.74 ms latency and 2.6 GFLOPs, making it deployable on edge devices. As a simple and efficient baseline, RT-Mesh is designed to encourage exploration into RT-based HMR, which remains an underexplored direction. We believe future work can build on this foundation to develop models with higher spatial precision, temporal consistency, and integration of human priors.

### 5.2 In Depth Analysis of Dataset Scale

Fig. [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.1 Radar-based HMR Benchmark ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction") presents an in-depth analysis of how the training dataset size influences the performance of radar-based HMR. We evaluate models trained with 25%, 50%, and 100% of our training data under different split settings, where 25% approximates the size of existing radar HMR datasets such as mmBody [Chen et al. 2022](#bib.bib7). For cross-subject (S2), this corresponds to using 4, 8, and 16 training subjects; for cross-action (S3), we use 10, 20, and 40 training action classes, respectively.

We find that the scaling law [Kaplan et al. 2020](#bib.bib23) holds for mmWave-based HMR: enlarging the training set consistently improves performance across splits and metrics, particularly for S2 and S3. For instance, RT-Mesh improves from 161.0mm to 135.1mm MVE on S2, and from 174.9mm to 143.1mm on S3. A richer dataset provides essential diversity for learning robust mappings between human motion and radar reflections, which helps mitigate the common challenges of multi-path interference and body-part miss-detection inherent to RF sensing. These results demonstrates the importance of large-scale training data in advancing mmWave-based human sensing and modelling, potentially enabling hard use cases (e.g., HMR for sports) and narrowing the gap to RGB-D systems.

### 5.3 Comparison to RGB(D)-based Methods

Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.1 Radar-based HMR Benchmark ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction") (Single) compares the best RPC- and RT-based model against RGB(D)-based methods (c.f. Sec. [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Competing Methods ‣ 4 Benchmark and Evaluation ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction")). With higher-resolution radar, radar-only models achieve comparable performance to RGB-D. Under S1 and S2, radar surpasses RGB and approaches depth. Notably, the translation error (TE) of radar matches depth and clearly outperforms RGB, which lacks explicit range information. We attribute this to radar’s higher sensitivity to moving foreground and suppression of static background, yielding more reliable root tracking in fast, non-in-place motions. Under S2 and S3, all modalities degrades largely, indicating that generalization to unseen subjects/actions remains difficult, even for camera-based HMR models that benefit from large-scale pretraining. We expect M4Human to serve as a strong benchmark for advancing generalizable HMR across all modalities.

### 5.4 Multimodal Fusion

Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.1 Radar-based HMR Benchmark ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction") (Fusion) benchmarks multi-modal fusion for HMR. For this experiment, we apply intermediate feature fusion, where features from each modality are concatenated before the HMR prediction head. On S1 and S3, RPC+RT remarkably outperforms either RPC or RT alone. This result highlights the complementary value of RT and underscores the significance of M4Human as the first dataset supporting RT-based HMR. We argue that learning jointly from two radar representations is mutually reinforcing: RT preserves dense spatial context while RPC emphasizes salient targets with pronounced motion. Moreover, fusing RT with RGB and depth images also yield significant gains, especially in TE for root-trajectory tracking. This demonstrates that radar can be a strong complementary modality to many camera-based systems for real-world applications.

### 5.5 Downstream HAR Benchmark

Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.1 Radar-based HMR Benchmark ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction") evaluates skeleton-based HAR with two inputs: (i) MoCap-de skeletons GT and (ii) RT-estimated skeletons extracted from meshes predicted by RT-Mesh. Under S1 (random split), BlockGCN [Zhou et al. 2024](#bib.bib52) attains ∼\sim75% Top-1 accuracy using MoCap skeletons, highlighting that our dataset is challenging due to dynamic, non–in-place actions. Moreover, RT-estimated skeletons already exhibit considerable accuracy, reaching 64.82% (Top-1), indicating that the proposed RT-Mesh can effectively support downstream HAR. Cross-subject generalization is still challenging for radar-based HAR, given additional performance drops in S2.

## 6 Conclusion

We present M4Human, a large-scale multimodal benchmark for mmWave radar–based human mesh reconstruction. The dataset comprises 661K synchronized frames spanning 50 actions and 20 subjects, captured with high-resolution mmWave radar, RGB, and depth modalities, and annotated with marker-based 3D meshes. M4Human provides both raw radar tensors (RT) and radar point clouds (RPC) to enabling research across different RF representation levels. We also propose RT-Mesh, a simple but effective baseline—the first method to perform HMR directly from raw RTs. Extensive experiments establish single- and multi-modal benchmarks across radar and RGB-D modalities, revealing the potential of mmWave radar for fine-grained, privacy-preserving human sensing. We expect M4Human to serve as a foundation for advancing RF-based 3D human modeling and its applications in Physical AI systems.

args.summary:
# M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction

**Summary:**

M4Human is a large-scale multimodal benchmark dataset for human mesh reconstruction (HMR) using millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar. It is the largest dataset of its kind, containing 661,000 frames (over 15 hours) across 999 sequences, involving 20 subjects and 50 diverse action categories. The dataset provides synchronized data from four modalities: RGB, depth, raw radar tensors (RT), and radar point clouds (RPC), captured using a high-resolution Vayyar mmWave radar and an Intel RealSense D435 camera.

Key features:
- **Scale:** 9× larger than the prior largest radar HMR dataset (mmBody), with 661K frames
- **High-quality annotations:** Marker-based Vicon MoCap system provides accurate 3D mesh annotations (SMPL-X), global trajectories, skeleton keypoints, and dense pose labels
- **Diverse actions:** 50 action categories spanning in-place daily activities, sit-in-place rehabilitation exercises, and non-in-place sports (basketball, badminton, etc.)
- **Dual radar modalities:** Both raw radar tensors (RT) and processed radar point clouds (RPC) are provided
- **Privacy-preserving:** Subjects wore caps and masks for de-identification; radar sensing does not capture visual appearance

The authors propose RT-Mesh, the first baseline method for direct HMR from raw radar tensors, achieving 2.74 ms latency and 2.6 GFLOPs. Benchmarks compare radar-only, RGB-D-only, and fused multimodal approaches across three evaluation protocols (in-place, sit-in-place, non-in-place) and three split settings (random, cross-subject, cross-action).

Key findings:
- RT-based methods outperform RPC-based methods on cross-subject and cross-action generalization
- Radar-only models achieve comparable performance to RGB-D under random splits, with radar excelling at translation/root tracking
- Multimodal fusion (radar + RGB-D) yields significant improvements, especially for translation error
- Scaling up training data consistently improves performance (scaling law holds for mmWave HMR)
- Radar-predicted meshes effectively support downstream human action recognition (HAR)

The dataset is designed to advance RF-based 3D human modeling for applications in smart homes, healthcare, rehabilitation, VR/AR, and Physical AI systems. Dataset and code will be released after paper publication.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Chinese academic survey paper titled "Overview on Human Pose Estimation Based on Deep Learning" published in Advances in International Computer Science (2025, Vol.5, No.1) by Yun Jiang and Shumin Liu from Jiangxi University of Science and Technology. The paper systematically reviews deep learning-based human pose estimation algorithms.

**Key Content:**

1. **Introduction**: Human pose estimation involves locating human key points (head, shoulders, elbows, wrists, etc.) from images/videos and is foundational for action recognition, intelligent driving, security, and human-computer interaction. Early methods relied on hand-crafted features (SIFT, HOG), but deep learning has become dominant.

2. **Single-Person Pose Estimation Algorithms**: Reviews algorithms including DeepPose (first DNN-based approach), Soft-argmax (heatmap integration regression), CPM (Convolutional Pose Machines), Hourglass network, HRNet (High-Resolution Network), LiteHRNet, LitePose, Graph-PCNN, TokenPose, and Hourglass Tokenizer (HoT). A performance comparison table is provided.

3. **Multi-Person Pose Estimation Algorithms**: Divided into Top-Down and Bottom-Up approaches. Top-Down methods (e.g., Mask R-CNN, AlphaPose) first detect persons then estimate poses. Bottom-Up methods (e.g., OpenPose, Lightweight OpenPose, YOLO-Pose, YOLOv5-v8 variants) detect all key points first then group them. A performance comparison table is provided.

4. **Datasets & Evaluation Metrics**: Key datasets include Human3.6M (360K 3D images), LSP, FLIC, FreeMan (11M+ frames), COCO (200K images), HiEve, MPII, AI Challenger, CrowdPose, and PoseTrack. Evaluation metrics include OKS (Object Keypoint Similarity), AP (Average Precision), PCP, PCK, and APK. Performance of major algorithms on COCO2017 dataset is tabulated.

5. **Challenges & Future Directions**: (1) Large model parameters requiring high computational resources; (2) Need for improved detection accuracy and efficiency; (3) Susceptibility to environmental factors (occlusion, lighting, clutter); (4) Insufficient datasets lacking diversity and coverage of complex scenarios.

The paper concludes that deep learning-based methods represent the future direction, with potential for expanding into video-based applications.
</summary>

<summary>
This paper presents a lightweight infrared human pose estimation system designed for the Jetson Xavier NX embedded platform. The authors address two key challenges: accuracy degradation under low-light conditions and large model parameters hindering deployment on embedded devices. 

The proposed method is based on an improved HRNet architecture. Key contributions include: (1) introducing a residual module with transfer learning between visible and infrared domains, using COCO 2017 grayscale images for pre-training and UCH-Thermal-Pose dataset for fine-tuning; (2) incorporating a channel pruning module (P-Bottle Neck and P-Basic Block) to eliminate redundant branches, achieving 46% parameter reduction versus the original HRNet; (3) optimizing the model using TensorRT for FP16 precision and deploying it on the Jetson Xavier NX platform.

Experimental results show the improved model (P-HRNet) achieves 75.3 mAP on COCO dataset (vs 75.9 for original HRNet) and 74.2 mAP on UCH infrared dataset, with only 15.5M parameters and 63.8M model size. After TensorRT acceleration on Jetson Xavier NX, the system reaches 33 fps detection speed, representing a 61% improvement over the original model. The system is designed for real-time human pose estimation (standing, sitting, lying detection) in low-light environments using infrared cameras.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed academic review article titled "Deep vision-based real-time hand gesture recognition: a review," published in PeerJ Computer Science on June 24, 2025, by Cui Cui, Mohd Shahrizal Sunar, and Goh Eg Su. The review provides a comprehensive analysis of vision-based real-time hand gesture recognition (HGR) using deep learning, covering studies from 2018 to 2024.

**Key focus areas:**
1. **Deep learning models**: The review examines CNN, LSTM, and attention mechanisms, analyzing their utilization rates, contributions to accuracy/efficiency improvements, and roles in recognition stages (e.g., feature extraction). CNN is the most widely used, with feature extraction being the most researched key stage.
2. **Evaluation metrics and datasets**: Metrics are categorized into accuracy and efficiency. Datasets are analyzed from self-created to public datasets. Ablation studies are summarized across four aspects: similar underlying models, integrating specific models, pre-processing, and others.
3. **Research gaps and future directions**: Discusses remaining challenges in accuracy, efficiency, application range, and environmental adaptation.

**Methodology**: The authors followed the PRISMA framework, searching six literature repositories (IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, Scopus, Springer, ACM Digital Library, Science Direct) with keywords related to vision-based, real-time HGR and deep learning. Initial search yielded 1,375 studies, narrowed to 47 final studies after duplicate removal, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and quality assessment.

**Key findings**: 
- Deep learning has improved issues like edge blurring from complex backgrounds (CNN), rotation inaccuracy from fast movement (LSTM), and response delays (attention mechanisms).
- The trend of deep learning model usage in HGR peaked in 2022.
- Feature extraction is the most researched key stage in HGR pipeline.
- Previous reviews lacked analysis of the relationship between model improvements and their roles in HGR stages.

**Applications** of vision-based HGR include robotics, military, clinical operations, risk warning, agriculture, remote collaboration, augmented reality, entertainment, and education.
</summary>

The paper explores how RFID backscatter communication enables marker-less passive sensing that can simultaneously distinguish multiple sensing objects. Key challenges include: 1) cross-domain sensing lacking theoretical model support, 2) sensing signals susceptible to environmental interference, and 3) bonded/non-bonded sensing lacking methodological guidance.

The paper identifies three new opportunities for RFID passive sensing:
1. From "single-tag sensing" to "tag array sensing" - expanding sensing dimensions
2. From "absolute positioning" to "relative positioning" - improving sensing sensitivity
3. From "single RFID sensing" to "multi-modal RFID sensing" - expanding sensing scope

It categorizes sensing approaches into three types:
- **Bonded sensing**: Tags attached to objects for high-accuracy perception (e.g., RF-Kinect for limb tracking, RF-Glove for micro-gesture recognition)
- **Non-bonded sensing**: Tags deployed around objects for contactless perception (e.g., RF-finger for high-precision gesture sensing)
- **Hybrid sensing**: Combining both approaches (e.g., RF-ECG for vital sign monitoring including respiration and heartbeat)

The paper concludes that passive sensing technology will develop in two directions: "expanding sensing scope" (from positioning to posture tracking, micro-motion perception, and vital sign monitoring) and "exploring sensing limits" (from decimeter-level to centimeter or even millimeter-level precision). Future work requires "feature imaging" and "intelligent reasoning" using deep learning and reinforcement learning for data-driven inference.

The system uses a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) with three convolutional layers and three fully-connected layers (totaling 8.7M weights) to directly process RSS data from passive RFID tags, avoiding manual feature selection and cascade object-use detection approaches.

The system was tested in two real-world settings: (1) a trauma resuscitation room with 16 actual trauma resuscitations (50,000 seconds of data, 12 object types, 8 antennas), and (2) a laboratory environment with staged activities. Key contributions include: (1) a deep learning model that works directly with RFID data as a multi-class classification problem, (2) analysis of features formed in convolutional layers through visualization of neuron activations, and (3) evaluation on actual trauma resuscitation data. The system also demonstrated generalizability by achieving 90.8% accuracy in a laboratory setting with different antenna configurations.

The authors note limitations including the absence of pooling layers (which could distort spatial/temporal relationships in RFID data) and the computational constraints limiting testing to 1-4 convolutional layers. The system uses only RSS data, as Doppler shift was found inaccurate and phase angle measurements were affected by frequency hopping regulations.

The paper systematically reviews RFID-based passive (battery-less) sensing technologies.

**Main Topic:** The paper examines RFID-based passive sensing research, analyzing how RFID technology has evolved from simple object identification to sophisticated sensing capabilities. **Key Findings by Layer:**

1. **Sensing Sources (Signal Channels):** The paper categorizes sensing signals into application layer (tag read rates), link layer (signal strength RSS and phase), physical layer (raw signals), and multimodal sensing. RSS provides coarse-grained sensing (meter-level accuracy) while phase enables centimeter-level precision. Physical layer raw signals capture the most detailed information but require specialized hardware (USRP).

2. **Sensing Methods:** Covers device deployment (single antenna, dual antenna, multi-antenna, dynamic antenna), tag attachment methods (device-based vs. device-free sensing), and inference approaches (model-driven vs. data-driven). 3. **Sensing Targets:** Includes indoor localization (from meter-level to millimeter-level precision), trajectory tracking, and other sensing forms (vibration frequency, breathing, heart rate, gesture recognition).

4. **Sensing Applications:** Covers object state tracking (inventory, localization, query), human behavior recognition (body, limb, finger movements, physiological signals), and anti-counterfeiting/authentication.

**Key Performance Metrics:** Phase-based positioning can achieve accuracy as high as 0.6 cm (RF-Dial system) and angle sensing accuracy of 4° (Tagyro system). RSS-based methods achieve approximately 30 cm accuracy with reference tag models.

**Future Directions:** The paper identifies four key future research directions: (1) deepening RFID communication models and discovering new signal features, (2) combining multiple signal sources in sensing methods, (3) expanding RFID sensing capabilities, and (4) exploring novel RFID application modes.

--- SOURCE 1: End-to-End Ultrasonic Hand Gesture Recognition ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11086334

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper, published in Sensors (Basel) on April 25, 2024, presents a novel end-to-end machine learning-based ultrasonic hand gesture recognition (HGR) system using low-cost MEMS ultrasonic transducers. The key innovation is that the ML model processes raw echo samples directly in the time domain, omitting computationally intensive pre-processing steps like the Fourier transform that previous work relied upon.

The authors (from Infineon Technologies AG and the University of Granada) used four MEMS ultrasonic transducers in three different geometrical arrangements (linear, center, and corner). They benchmarked five ML architectures: CNNs, GRUs, LSTMs, Vision Transformers (ViT), and Cross-Attention Multi-Scale Vision Transformers (CrossViT). The LSTM, ViT, and CrossViT models achieved over 88% accuracy.

The system recognizes 4-6 swipe gestures (swipe left, swipe right, push-pull, double tap, and optionally swipe up/down) depending on the transducer arrangement. The datasets were acquired from 6-9 test persons. This approach is compared favorably to vision-, radar-, WiFi-, and other ultrasound-based HGR systems, with the key advantages being low cost, low power consumption, privacy preservation, immunity to electromagnetic interference, and robustness in harsh environments. The paper claims this is the first ultrasound-based HGR implementation operating exclusively in the time domain.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The most important innovation described in this research paper is that we were able to demonstrate that little pre-processing is necessary to obtain high accuracy in ultrasonic HGR for several arrangements of cost-effective and low-power MEMS ultrasonic transducer arrays., To the authors' knowledge, this is the first implementation of ultrasound-based hand gesture recognition using raw echo data and, in fact, the first implementation in the time domain only., Direct processing of the sensor signals by a compact model makes ultrasonic hand gesture recognition a true low-cost and power-efficient input method., The three last-mentioned ML models [LSTM, ViT, and CrossViT] reached more than 88% accuracy., Ultrasound-based HGR systems offer several potential advantages, including luminance invariance, immunity to electromagnetic interference, high detectability, cost-effectiveness, small form factor, and energy efficiency.

The article addresses limitations in existing ultrasonic gesture recognition methods, which are often susceptible to invalid user gestures and struggle to correct misclassified gestures in real time. This academic paper, published in September 2024 in the journal "Computer Science and Application," presents a high-precision real-time fall detection system based on a multi-model fusion approach. The research was conducted by Chao Zan, Shuai Cai, Xinyi Wan, and Kanglong Tan from Hanjiang Normal University, Shiyan, Hubei.

**Main Topic:** A real-time fall detection system for elderly and disabled populations using computer vision.

**Methodology:** The system combines three key technologies:
1. **Faster R-CNN** – for precise human bounding box regression and object detection
2. **Mediapipe** – for human pose estimation by extracting 2D spatial coordinates of skeletal feature points
3. **Improved Spatiotemporal Graph Convolutional Network (DCST-GCN)** – Enhanced with a temporal deconvolution (DC) module to improve temporal feature extraction for behavior classification

**Key Results:**
- On the NTU-RGB+D60 dataset (cross-view/CV), the proposed method achieved **93.5% Top-1 accuracy** and **86.7% cross-subject (CS) accuracy**, outperforming baseline models including ST-GCN (88.3% CV), IndRNN (89.0% CV), and Cross-Attention (89.3% CV)

- Compared to other human pose detection models on COCO dataset, MediaPipe achieved 73.3% AP@0.5:0.95, outperforming OpenPose (61.8%) and Detectron (67.0%)

**Datasets Used:** NTU-RGB+D60 (56,880 action samples including 40 daily, 11 interactive, and 9 health-related behaviors including falls) and Kinetics-400

**Conclusion:** The fusion of MediaPipe with DCST-GCN provides a robust, accurate real-time fall detection system, though some misclassifications of fall-like behaviors (e.g., sitting down) remain. The team plans to further refine the recognition algorithm and validate in practical applications.

URL: https://tns.thss.tsinghua.edu.cn/wst/docs/model

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a comprehensive tutorial on applying deep learning to wireless sensing, using Wi-Fi-based human gesture recognition as a primary example. It covers three main deep learning architectures: CNN, RNN (CNN+RNN), and Adversarial Learning, plus a Complex-valued Neural Network (CVNN) for signal enhancement.

**CNN Approach:**
- Uses commodity Wi-Fi with 1 transmitter and 6 receivers in a classroom to recognize 6 human gestures (from the Widar3.0 dataset)
- Extracts Doppler Frequency Shift (DFS) from raw Channel State Information (CSI) signals
- Architecture: 3D Conv layer → MaxPooling3D → Flatten → Dense(256) → Dropout → Dense(128) → Dropout → Softmax output
- Implemented with Keras/TensorFlow; uses RMSprop optimizer, categorical crossentropy loss
- Data preprocessing includes normalization to [0,1] per time snapshot and zero-padding to align variable-length samples

**CNN+RNN Approach:**
- Combines Conv2D (via TimeDistributed) with GRU recurrent layer for temporal modeling
- Architecture: TimeDistributed(Conv2D+MaxPooling2D+Flatten+Dense128+Dense64) → GRU(64) → Dropout → Softmax

**Adversarial Learning:**
- Addresses domain misalignment where human location affects DFS measurements
- Uses a shared feature extractor (CNN+RNN) with two branches: a gesture classifier and a domain discriminator (location predictor)
- The domain loss is weighted negatively (adversarial) to encourage location-invariant features
- Custom loss functions implement categorical crossentropy for both label and domain predictions

**Complex-valued Neural Network (CVNN) for Signal Enhancement:**
- Designed to eliminate spectral leakage caused by FFT windowing effects
- Uses PyTorch (instead of Keras) to implement custom complex-valued linear layers
- Generates synthetic training data: ideal spectrums → apply windowing convolution matrix + complex Gaussian noise → train SEN to recover ideal spectrum
- Architecture: 5 complex-valued fully-connected layers with tanh activation
- Training minimizes L2 loss between enhanced and ideal spectrums
- Key function `generate_blur_matrix_complex` creates the convolution matrix of the window function to model the leakage process

The tutorial includes complete code for data loading (`load_data`), normalization (`normalize_data`), zero-padding (`zero_padding`), one-hot encoding, model building, training, and evaluation with confusion matrices and accuracy metrics.
</summary>

This paper, published in *Patterns* (March 10, 2023), introduces **SenseFi**, a comprehensive open-source library and benchmark framework for deep-learning-based WiFi human sensing using Channel State Information (CSI) data. This paper presents SUPER (Seated Upper Body Pose Estimation using mmWave Radars), a framework that uses dual-mmWave radars to estimate seated upper body human poses. The system utilizes two Texas Instruments IWR6843ISK radars oriented perpendicularly to improve spatial resolution. A novel dual-radar masking algorithm fuses data from both radars to generate two complementary point cloud types: intensity point clouds (IPC) which characterize low-motion body areas like the torso, and Doppler point clouds (DPC) which capture motion information of extremities.

The pipeline generates dense point clouds through spatial oversampling and MVDR beamforming, then applies a 3D CFAR algorithm for point cloud trimming. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a survey paper (published May 6, 2019, in Remote Sensing) that reviews deep learning (DL)-based human activity recognition (HAR) using radar. It covers three main areas: deep learning techniques, radar systems, and DL approaches for radar-based HAR, organized by the dimension of radar echoes (1D, 2D, and 3D).

**Key Points:**

- **Radar advantages for HAR:** Privacy protection, contactless sensing, robustness to light/weather, through-wall detection, no need for body-attached tags.
- **Limitations of conventional ML:** Hand-crafted feature extraction is time-consuming, task-specific, and has limited generalization. Deep learning automatically extracts high-level features hierarchically.
- **DL models covered:** CNN (spatial feature extraction), RNN/LSTM (temporal modeling), Auto-Encoders (unsupervised feature learning), and hybrid models (e.g., CNN+LSTM for spatial-temporal features).
- **Radar systems:** Doppler radar (captures Doppler shifts for velocity), FMCW radar (range and Doppler simultaneously), Interferometry radar (tangential motion), UWB radar (high range resolution, penetration capability).
- **1D echoes (HRRP):** Time-series data; limited DL work exists but RNNs are suitable.
- **2D echoes (time-Doppler, time-range, range-Doppler maps):** Most commonly used; treated as images with CNNs. Hybrid 2D maps (combining multiple map types) improve accuracy.
- **3D echoes (time-range-Doppler data cube):** Contain richest information; 3D CNNs and CNN+LSTM hybrids (e.g., Google Soli) used; processing is more complex.
- **Future directions:** Complex activity recognition, real-world scenario deployment (lightweight models, continuous activity segmentation, multi-target recognition), and unsupervised learning (transfer learning, cross-modal knowledge distillation).

**Conclusion:** DL shows strong potential for radar-based HAR, though radar HAR still lags behind vision-based technologies. Key advantages include environment insensitivity and privacy protection.

## Summary of ProbRadarM3F: mmWave Radar-based Human Skeletal Pose Estimation

This paper introduces **ProbRadarM3F**, a novel model for estimating human skeletal poses using millimeter wave (mmWave) radar signals. The model addresses privacy concerns associated with RGB cameras in sensitive environments like nursing homes and hospitals by using non-visual radar signals.

**Key Innovation:** The model uses a dual-branch feature extraction framework:
1. **FFT Branch** - Traditional Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) method to generate range-Doppler-angle heatmaps
2. **ProbPE Branch** - A novel probability map-guided positional encoding method that extracts positional features from radar signals

The two branches produce multi-format features (frequency features from heatmaps and positional features from probability maps) that are fused together using 3D convolutional layers and a cross-self-attention mechanism.

**Methodology:**
- The FFT branch performs 4D FFT on raw radar ADC data to extract range, Doppler, azimuth, and elevation information
- The ProbPE branch uses 2D CFAR detection to filter targets, generates probability maps from range-azimuth-elevation vectors, then applies sine positional encoding
- Multi-frame temporal information (8 frames) is used to improve accuracy
- A Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) refines keypoint predictions
- Binary cross-entropy loss is used for end-to-end training

**Results:**
- Evaluated on the HuPR dataset (raw radar signals from two vertically placed TI IWR1843 radars)
- Achieves **69.9% AP** (Average Precision), outperforming the state-of-the-art HuPR baseline (63.4% AP) and RF-Pose (41.4% AP)
